0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
The message. Ephesians tells ordinary believers who they are. Before the world was made, the Father chose a people in his Son; at the cross the Son bought them with his blood; by the Spirit he has made them alive, sealed them as his own, and joined Jews and Gentiles, once enemies, into one new people. That people, the church, is the first sign of what God means to do with the whole universe: “to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth” (1:10). So the letter says two things, in this order: this is what God has made you in Christ; now live as what you are. It has been called the most majestic of Paul’s letters: less a letter than a window thrown open onto the purposes of God.

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul as its author (1:1; 3:1), writing as a prisoner, “an ambassador in chains” (6:20). This was most likely his house arrest in Rome, about AD 60–62, while he waited to be heard by Caesar (Acts 28:16, 30–31). Colossians was written at the same time, and Tychicus carried both (6:21–22; Colossians 4:7–9).

The first readers. Several of the oldest manuscripts lack “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and the letter has none of the greetings you would expect from a man who had lived there nearly three years, so it was probably a circular letter for Ephesus and the other churches of the province. Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age, including yours.

Ephesus. Ephesus was a great port on the west coast of what is now Turkey and the leading city of the Roman province of Asia. Its pride was the temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world and also a great bank. The city was famous for magic; its written charms were known across the empire as the “Ephesian letters”. When Paul’s preaching hurt the trade of the silversmiths’ guild, which made shrines of Artemis, they filled the theatre with a riot (Acts 19:23–41).

Paul and the church there. Paul first called briefly, leaving Priscilla and Aquila there (Acts 18:18–21). Then he stayed longer than anywhere else on his journeys, teaching in the synagogue and then for two years in the hall of Tyrannus, “so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:8–10); he later spoke of “three years” there (Acts 20:31). When the gospel took hold, former practitioners of magic burned their scrolls in public, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:18–19). The church was mostly converted pagans, “you Gentiles in the flesh” (2:11), with Jewish believers among them, and the wonder of their being one body runs through the letter (2:11–22; 3:6). They had grown up with temple feasts, drunken festivals and magic, in households where the master ruled wife, children and slaves; many commands in chapters 4–6 assume that background.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, citing its long sentences, unusual vocabulary, close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written alongside Colossians and carried by the same man. A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. Chapters 1–3 tell what God has done. Chapter 1 praises the Father for every spiritual blessing in Christ, from election to the Spirit’s seal, and prays that the readers may see it. Chapter 2 tells how the dead were made alive by grace (2:1–10) and Jews and Gentiles made one new people through the cross (2:11–22). Chapter 3 tells of Paul’s calling to make this mystery known, and ends in a prayer to know “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (3:19). Then comes the hinge: “I therefore … urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called” (4:1). Chapters 4–6 show how such people walk: in unity as one body, built up by the gifts of the ascended Christ, putting off the old self and putting on the new (chapter 4); in love, as children of light, and wisely, filled with the Spirit, a life that reaches the home, beginning with marriage (chapter 5); as children and parents, slaves and masters, and as soldiers in the armour of God (chapter 6). The commands always rest on the facts. An adopted child does not help at home to earn a place in the family; he helps because he already has one. We obey not to be accepted, but because we are.

Where it leads: to Christ. The heartbeat phrase is in Christ: with “in him” and “in the Lord”, it comes more than thirty times. Chosen, redeemed, raised and seated, built together: all in him. The letter is not first about what Christians must do but about who they already are, and the doing flows from the being. The risen Christ is seated far above every power, and God “gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body” (1:22–23). He himself is our peace, who has broken down the wall between Jew and Gentile (2:14). He loves his church as a bridegroom his bride, giving himself up for her and washing her for the wedding day (5:25–32). The church is not a human institution God blesses but the centre of his plan, through which his “manifold wisdom” is made known to the unseen powers (3:10). Follow the argument and you end where Paul did, on your knees (3:14), asking to grasp a love no one can measure (3:18–19).

For us. Ephesians gives a believer a place to stand: in Christ you are not on probation, but chosen, adopted, forgiven and sealed before you did anything. It gives you a people, a body where old walls of race and class have come down, and a battle fought in God’s armour, not your own. Its question to every part of life is that of 4:1: this is who you are; are you walking like it?

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus: <sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, <sup>4</sup>even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love <sup>5</sup>he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, <sup>6</sup>to the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved. <sup>7</sup>In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace, <sup>8</sup>which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight <sup>9</sup>making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ <sup>10</sup>as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him. <sup>11</sup>In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, <sup>12</sup>so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup>In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup>who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory. <sup>15</sup>For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, <sup>16</sup>I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, <sup>17</sup>that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, <sup>18</sup>having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, <sup>19</sup>and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might <sup>20</sup>that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, <sup>21</sup>far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <sup>22</sup>And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, <sup>23</sup>which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything God gives his people, he gives in Christ, and all of it is a reason to praise him. After greeting the saints (vv. 1–2), Paul blesses God for every spiritual blessing (v. 3) and traces it to each person of the Trinity: the Father, who chose us before creation and adopted us as his children (vv. 4–6); the Son, in whom we have redemption, insight into God’s plan to unite all things in him, and an inheritance (vv. 7–12); and the Spirit, who seals us as God’s own and guarantees what is to come (vv. 13–14). Each part ends in the same refrain: to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (v. 4), before they had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). Whether he chose those he foresaw would believe is weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: why did God choose?” at the end of the note on v. 4.

Its purpose reaches beyond the saved: it is to the praise of his glorious grace (v. 6). In the coming ages God will show in his people the riches of his kindness in Christ (2:7), so that the church is the living evidence that the undeserving can be made heirs.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is given not to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance (see “Before the foundation of the world” in the note on v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesians lived in the shadow of the temple of Artemis, among religions that promised to take people higher through secret ceremonies and secret knowledge. Paul tells them they already have every spiritual blessing, not through ritual or achievement but by being joined to Christ.

Now: Many people today assemble their own spirituality from books, practices and experiences. Ephesians 1 says every spiritual blessing is in Christ. In Christ what the heart most needs is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes with Christ’s authority to ordinary believers whom God has made his holy people in Christ. The greeting already sounds the letter’s themes: everything begins with the will of God, and believers are who they are because they are “in Christ”.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (one sent) was an envoy carrying the full authority of the one who sent him. Paul was one of those personally commissioned by the risen Christ to lay the church’s foundation (2:20; Galatians 1:1), so his words carry Christ’s authority. He writes as a prisoner, probably in Rome (3:1; 6:20; see the introduction).

By the will of God. Not a modest disclaimer, but the only explanation for his being an apostle at all. His apostleship began on a road, with letters in his pocket authorising the arrest of Christians (Acts 9:1–2): he was not recruited from among the interested but intercepted mid-crime. A man who talked himself into a ministry can be talked out of it; a man stopped in the road by the risen Christ cannot.

To the saints. Say saint today and people picture an exceptionally good person in a stained-glass window. Paul uses the word (hagioi, holy ones) for every Christian in the city, including some he will soon tell to stop lying and stealing (4:25, 28). It is not his verdict on how they are getting on but his statement of who owns them. “Holy” means set apart, like a temple bowl, holy not because it was unusually clean but because of whose it was. Christ did not wait for Saul of Tarsus to become suitable, and he took idol-worshippers in a city of spells and called them his holy ones. If you are in Christ, “saint” is not a title to earn; it is the name on your post.

Faithful in Christ Jesus. “Faithful” here means believing. And in Christ is the key phrase of Ephesians, used more than thirty times in different forms. It means union with Christ: believers are joined to him, so that what is true of him becomes true of them. When a penniless woman married a rich man, his name, home and wealth became hers, not because she earned them but because she was joined to him, and Paul uses that very picture of Christ and the church (5:31–32).

Two addresses. This one line carries two: a settled identity in Christ, and a difficult postcode on earth, a city built around the temple of Artemis and living in fear of spiritual powers (see the introduction). Much of the letter answers that fear: Christ is above every power (1:21), and his people are safe in him. Put your own town in place of Ephesus; the letter is written to you at both addresses.

What it does not mean. Calling every believer a saint does not mean that how we live does not matter. Paul will spend half the letter calling saints to live like saints (4:1). But the order is everything: first who you are, then how to live.

Where Christians differ: did Paul write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, citing its long sentences, unusual words and overlap with Colossians, and honest readers feel the question. This commentary’s view: Paul is the author. The letter claims him twice (1:1; 3:1) and speaks of his chains and his messenger (6:20–21), the early church received it without dispute, and its differences fit a letter of praise written alongside Colossians (see the introduction).

Textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts (the papyrus P46 and the great fourth-century copies Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) omit “in Ephesus”, and the letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years there. This commentary’s view: probably a circular letter to the churches of Asia, carried by Tychicus (6:21), with Ephesus as its chief destination. That does not lessen its authority; it widens its reach.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets them with God’s free favour and the peace it brings, both coming from the Father and from Jesus Christ together. There is no verb in the Greek: this is not a polite formula but something close to a blessing pronounced over them.

Grace to you. Paul bends the ordinary Greek greeting, chairein, into a word that sounds like it and means far more: charis, God’s free favour to people who have earned only its reverse (2:8–9).

And peace. Eirēnē translates the Hebrew shalom, the Jewish greeting. So a Greek word and a Jewish word stand together in one breath, as Jew and Gentile will in chapter 2 (2:14–16).

What peace is. Shalom is not a mood but wholeness, everything in its right relation and working as it was made to. A Christian can have it in a hospital bed, and a man be without it on a beach, because it depends on the central relationship of life: first peace with God, under whose wrath we once stood (2:3), then peace between people once divided (2:14–17).

The order. In every greeting Paul wrote, grace comes first and peace last (the letters to Timothy put mercy between them), because one produces the other. Many people want peace without grace, reached by managing their lives well enough to deserve it, and it cannot be done in that direction. Peace is the state of a person against whom nothing is any longer held, and only grace can produce that: justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). First the gift, then the quiet.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. One source, two persons: Paul puts Jesus beside the Father as the giver of gifts only God can give, something no Jew would say of a mere man, a quiet witness to Christ’s deity two verses into the letter. And our: an apostle and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves address the same Father.

Peace with a name. In the next chapter Paul gives peace a name: “he himself is our peace” (2:14). Aaron’s blessing ended with the LORD giving Israel peace (Numbers 6:26), and that peace came in a person, the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). It was not a kind wish but a purchase: he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The grace is his favour, freely given; the peace is his finished work, never to be unmade.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise God, because in Christ he has already given his people every blessing his Spirit brings. Verses 3–14 are one sentence of praise in the Greek, and this verse is its headline.

One great sentence. The sentence is shaped by the Trinity: the Father chooses and adopts (vv. 4–6), the Son redeems (vv. 7–12), the Spirit seals (vv. 13–14), and each part ends with the same refrain, to the praise of his glory (vv. 6, 12, 14). Paul is so caught up in praise that he cannot find a place to stop.

Blessed be God … who has blessed us. To bless (eulogeō, to speak well of) works two ways. When we bless God, we add nothing to him; our blessing is praise. When God speaks good over someone, he gives the very thing it names (Genesis 1:28). So the sentence swings on a hinge: we bless God with our lips because he has first blessed us with his hand. And God is named here by his Son: we know him truly only as the Father of Jesus.

Every spiritual blessing. Every: the whole treasury; a believer is not waiting for some further blessing to make him complete in Christ. And spiritual does not mean wispy or unreal but given and applied by the Holy Spirit, who is himself their down payment (vv. 13–14): the Giver has moved in with the gift. Your salary is temporary and your health is on loan; your adoption is not.

Not a circumstance. In common speech a blessing is a circumstance that has gone well: the promotion, the clean scan. But the man writing is in chains, his readers include slaves, and Christians in their province would soon die for the name (Revelation 2:13). If blessing meant circumstances going well, Paul would be an unblessed man writing to unblessed people about how blessed they are. Not one item in the list that follows is a circumstance, and not one can be lost in a redundancy, a diagnosis or a bad year.

Has blessed. Past tense: already given, though much is still to be enjoyed in full (vv. 14, 18). Asking God for good things is right (Matthew 7:11), but “Lord, bless me”, prayed as though the cupboard were bare, misunderstands where we stand. The Christian is not a beggar hoping the door will open; he is an heir who has not yet read the inventory, and Paul opens it in the next eleven verses.

In the heavenly places. The phrase appears five times in Ephesians and nowhere else in Paul. It cannot simply mean heaven as the home of the redeemed, for the spiritual forces of evil are there (6:12). It is the unseen realm of spiritual reality, immediately behind everything we can see, and it holds the treasury of blessing (1:3), Christ’s throne (1:20), your seat with him (2:6), the watching powers (3:10) and the battlefield (6:12). For Ephesians who had spent their lives managing unseen powers with amulets and spells, it was no abstraction to learn that they are seated with Christ above everything they used to fear. Yet the letter ends at home, with marriage, children and daily work (5:22–6:9): knowing where the throne is does not lift you out of your Tuesday; it tells you who is over it.

In Christ, through a curse. The blessing comes in Christ because it was his before it was ours: chosen, beloved, heir, anointed with the Spirit, the blessings that follow belong first to the Son, and reach us only because we are joined to him. But a curse stood in the way, God’s just sentence on everyone who breaks his law, and Christ moved it by becoming a curse for us, so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:13–14). The hand that blesses us is the hand that laid our curse on his Son.

What it does not mean. Not a promise of earthly comfort, health or wealth; the prisoner who wrote it had none of those.

In everyday life. When someone asks how you are on a bad day, you may say honestly that the day is hard, and that you are blessed. Both are true, and the second is the deeper one.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the world existed, God chose a people for himself in Christ, in order to make them holy. This is the first blessing, and it explains all the others: salvation begins not with our choice of God but with his choice of us.

Even as he chose us. “Even as” ties this to v. 3. The verb means chose for himself: this is election, God’s free decision to save particular people, and it is personal: us.

In him. Election is never apart from Christ, who is himself the Chosen One: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1). God chose a people in his Son, their head and Saviour, so that his standing becomes theirs. So the question “am I chosen?” is not answered by peering back into eternity, where you cannot see, but by looking at Christ: whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Before the foundation of the world. Before the light was made, there was nothing about you for God’s love to be based on: no faith, no obedience, not even existence (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 1:9). A love that began before you were anything cannot be ended by your turning out to be something disappointing. Your worst week did not alter its basis, because the basis was never you.

Holy and blameless before him. “Blameless” is the word for a sacrifice without blemish. God chose us for holiness, not because of it, and before him: not before neighbours who grade on a curve, but before the God at whose holiness the seraphim cover their faces (Isaiah 6:2–5). Paul means two things. Now, in Christ, you are already counted holy and blameless (Colossians 1:22): God does not pretend you have never sinned; he credits you with his Son’s perfect record (2 Corinthians 5:21). And one day he will present you without fault before his glory (5:27; Jude 24). So the believer who sinned badly this week does not come back to God with a smaller holiness, because it was never measured by this week. That is not permission to sin (Romans 6:1–2); it is the mercy that makes repentance possible.

What it does not mean. Not fatalism, as if it does not matter what we do. Nor a reason for pride: election leaves no room for boasting (2:9). Nor is it given to make anyone anxious; Scripture teaches it to comfort believers that their salvation rests on God, not on themselves.

Common questions. If God has chosen, why preach the gospel? Because God chose the means as well as the end: the chosen come to faith through hearing the gospel (v. 13; Romans 10:14), and election is why mission cannot fail: “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). What about my own choice? Scripture holds both: the letter that says you were chosen pleads with you to walk worthy of your calling (4:1). Your believing was truly your own (v. 13); God’s rule runs underneath your choice, not instead of it, and how the two fit together he has not told us (Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 9:20). How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking for a secret sign, but by trusting Christ and seeing the fruit of holiness he produces (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10).

Is there any point praying for my unbelieving son or daughter, if God has already chosen? Every point, because prayer is one of the means God has chosen. No one believed in election more firmly than Paul, and his heart’s desire and prayer to God was for his unbelieving people to be saved (Romans 10:1). Election makes your prayers not pointless but hopeful: you are asking the God who raises the dead (2:5) to do what he delights to do. You do not know who is chosen, and you are not meant to. So pray by name, keep loving, keep speaking of Christ, and leave the timing with him. Augustine’s mother prayed for him for years before he was converted.

Where Christians differ: why did God choose? Arminian Christians, a large Protestant tradition that includes most Methodists and many evangelicals, hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29; 1 Peter 1:2), out of real concern for God’s fairness and human responsibility; they love Christ as truly as anyone. This commentary’s view: unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.5): God’s choice rested on no condition he saw in us. Paul roots it in God’s love, will and purpose (vv. 5, 9, 11), never in anything foreseen; and we were chosen to be holy, which makes no sense if God chose us for foreseen holiness. Faith is the result of election (Acts 13:48), not its cause. Is it unfair? The question assumes we were owed a choosing, and we were not; left to justice, every one of us would be passed by (Romans 3:23). The wonder is not that some are not chosen, but that any are: that grace should reach into a mass of the justly condemned and lift out a people who deserved what the rest received. No one perishes who wanted Christ and was refused.

Where Christians differ: chosen as individuals, or as a group? Some (following Karl Barth, and some Arminian scholars) hold that God chose Christ, and the church only as a group in him; individuals become elect when they join themselves to Christ by faith. This commentary’s view: God did choose a people in Christ, but the people are made up of persons. He chose us and predestined us for adoption (v. 5), which is personal, and elsewhere election is clearly of individuals: Jacob, not Esau (Romans 9:11–13); names written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8). The group and the individual belong together.

Uncertain wording. The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, so “in love” may end verse 4 (holy and blameless before him in love) or begin verse 5 (in love he predestined us); both are grammatical. The ESV links it with verse 5, which fits Paul’s stress on God’s motive, and is more likely.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of love, God decided beforehand to make us his own children through Jesus Christ, simply because it pleased him. Predestination is not a cold decree but the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children.

He predestined us. “Predestined” is marked out beforehand (our word horizon shares the root). Election (v. 4) is God choosing whom; predestination is God deciding what he would make of them, and here Paul names it: his children. In Scripture, predestination is almost always spoken of to comfort believers about their destiny, not to make them speculate about others.

Adoption as sons. “Adoption” (placing as a son) was a Roman legal act: a new father and name, old debts cancelled, full rights of inheritance, and it could not be undone. We were by nature children of wrath (2:3), outsiders; God brings us into his family as heirs (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:15–17). Sons inherited, and every believer, man or woman, receives a son’s full inheritance (Galatians 3:26–28) and belongs to himself.

Why adoption, and not only forgiveness? God could have pardoned us and left us as forgiven servants at the kitchen door. Instead he seats us at his table as his children. Forgiveness deals with our guilt; adoption gives us a Father, a family, a home and an inheritance: in the words of the Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 34), we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God. The Judge who acquits us steps down from the bench and takes us home.

Through Jesus Christ. God has one eternal Son by nature; we become children by grace, by being joined to him. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). He took our place outside, under the law and its curse, so that we could take his place inside, at the Father’s table, and pray his own word, Abba (Mark 14:36).

According to the purpose of his will. Literally the good pleasure of his will: nothing outside God moved him to it, and that is why it is permanent. A choice that rested on something in us could be undone by something in us. This rests on his good pleasure alone.

What it does not mean. Not that all people are God’s children in this sense. All are his creatures and his offspring as their Creator (Acts 17:28), but adoption comes through Christ, received by faith (John 1:12).

Did God also predestine some people to hell? Scripture speaks of the two very differently, and so must we. Those God saves, he actively chose, predestined and brought to life. Those who are lost, he passed by, leaving them in the sin they love; they are condemned for their sin, never for want of being chosen (Westminster Confession 3.7), and no one in hell will be able to say that he wanted Christ and was kept from him. Even Paul’s wording marks the difference: God prepared the vessels of mercy beforehand for glory, while the vessels of wrath are simply said to be prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22–23). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered freely to all. Your question is not what God decreed about others, but whether you will come to Christ today.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved us so that his free grace would be seen and praised, and he gave it to us by joining us to his beloved Son. This is the first of three refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), each closing the work of one person of the Trinity: salvation has a goal beyond the saved.

He has blessed us. Literally which he graced us with, a verb used only once elsewhere in the New Testament, by Gabriel to a girl in Nazareth: greetings, O favoured one (Luke 1:28). Mary had done nothing to deserve it; the whole course of her life ran from God’s free favour. Paul uses the word of dockworkers and slaves in Ephesus. In this one respect, being singled out by sheer favour, what was true of Mary is true of you.

In the Beloved. Paul could have said “in Christ” again. He chooses instead the title the Father spoke from heaven over his Son: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). The love that falls on you is not a second-class affection God worked up for sinners. You are inside the Beloved, and the love that has always passed between the Father and the Son runs over you too, as Jesus prayed on the last night: “that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me” (John 17:23). Not somewhat as. Even as.

Is that not vanity? We do not admire a man who arranges every conversation to end in applause for himself. C. S. Lewis was troubled by exactly this, until he noticed what praise actually is. We spontaneously praise whatever we enjoy, music, a landscape, a friend’s cooking, because delight overflows into speech: the finest view is only half enjoyed until you say to someone, “Look at that.” Praise is enjoyment reaching its full form. If there is a being of infinite goodness, calling creatures to praise him is not vanity but honesty about the most valuable thing there is, and kindness, because it points them to their deepest joy. A father who tells his son to come and look at the sunrise is not fishing for compliments on his taste. He wants the boy to see it.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Christ died in our place, we are set free and our sins are forgiven, as fully as God’s grace is rich. The verb is present tense: this is a possession now, held on the worst day of your life as securely as on the best.

In him we have redemption. “Redemption” (release by payment of a ransom) is the language of the slave market and of the exodus. A slave cannot buy himself; someone else pays, and he walks out having contributed nothing but his chains. In Egypt on the last night, what stood between a household and the destroyer was not its record or remorse but blood on the doorpost (Exodus 12; see Passover). In both scenes the freedom is real, total, and entirely someone else’s doing.

Through his blood. “Blood” means his life given in a violent, sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). The price was not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19).

The forgiveness of our trespasses. “Forgiveness” is sending away; “trespasses” are false steps, plural and particular. The account that was cancelled had your name at the top and your own specific items listed beneath it, including the one you have never told anyone, and the one you did again last week. Those. Paid for, by blood, and gone.

According to the riches of his grace. Not measured by our need but by his wealth, proportioned to the riches of God himself. No sin is too great for riches like these.

Why blood? He tells us to forgive freely; why does he require a death before he does it himself? Because nobody forgives a real wrong without cost. If someone smashes something of yours, either he pays, and then nothing has been forgiven, only settled; or you forgive him and absorb the loss: the thing stays broken and you carry it. The damage never simply evaporates, which is why forgiving a real injury hurts. So when God forgives, he is not shrugging off a small debt. Every one of us has done real wrong to a holy God, and it has to go somewhere. A God who ignored it would not be gracious but indifferent, as a judge who dismissed every case would not be loving but corrupt. God did what every true forgiver does, at a scale beyond measuring: he absorbed it himself. The blood is the measure of what it cost him.

In everyday life. The letter will ask you to forgive as God in Christ forgave you (4:32), which means bearing the cost of a wrong instead of passing it on. Is there a debt someone owes you that you could carry today?

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slow to catch up with facts, and you have an accuser who works on them (Revelation 12:10). First ask whether the guilt points at something specific you have not yet brought to God or put right with someone; if so, confess it plainly, and where you have wronged a person, go to them (1 John 1:9). If the sin is already confessed, the guilt is not God’s voice but an echo, and the answer is not more penance but the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Tell yourself what is true: Christ died for that sin, God has sent it away, and he does not bring it up again. If the feeling will not lift, talk to your pastor. Sometimes the gospel needs a friend to say it aloud.

Where Christians differ: how does the cross save? Some modern writers deny that Christ’s death was a substitute bearing our penalty, seeing it only as an example of love or a victory over evil. This commentary’s view: penal substitution is central: Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place. Scripture joins blood, redemption and forgiveness: a price paid, a penalty borne (Romans 3:24–25; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 9:22). His victory over evil (Colossians 2:15) and his example of love (5:2) belong with it, not instead of it.
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God poured out his grace on us without measure, and with it gave us the wisdom to understand what he has done.

Lavished. Made to overflow: God did not measure out grace carefully. He poured. How like God to pour where we would have measured.

In all wisdom and insight. “Wisdom” is the deep grasp of how things truly are; “insight” is its practical cousin. One sees; the other knows what to do on Monday morning. The grace that saves you does not rescue you and then leave you baffled about what has happened. He gives the gift, and then he gives the eyes to see the gift. That is why this letter can spend three chapters on the eternal purposes of God and still expect ordinary believers in Ephesus to follow every word.

Wisdom with a face. Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). The wisdom poured out on us is not a technique for success but the knowledge of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and weakness to Jews, and the very wisdom by which God saves (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). To be given wisdom is to be given eyes to see Christ, and in him everything else, from your sins to your sufferings.

Uncertain wording. “In all wisdom and insight” may describe God’s wisdom in planning salvation, or the wisdom he gives us to understand it; the Greek allows either. The second is more likely: the nearest parallel prays for believers to be filled “in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (Colossians 1:9), Paul prays for this wisdom in v. 17, and the sentence runs straight on, “making known to us the mystery of his will” (v. 9). Nothing is lost if a reader takes it the other way, for God’s plan is supremely wise (3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has let us into his secret plan: to bring the whole broken universe back together under Christ as its head. This is the summit of verses 3–14, and the rest of the letter unfolds it.

The mystery of his will. In Paul a mystery is not a puzzle or something unknowable, but a truth once hidden in God and now revealed (3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). And he has made it known “to us”: God lets sinners in on the purpose of the ages before it is complete.

Set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time. Christ has been the centre of God’s plan from the beginning; history was planned around him. “Plan” is household management (oikonomia, hence economy): a good steward of a great house knows what is to happen in every room and when. God runs history like that. “The fullness of time” is the moment history reaches its goal, begun at Christ’s coming (Galatians 4:4) and completed at his return.

To unite all things in him. One long Greek verb, meaning to sum up, as a column of figures is added into one total, or to gather under one head (v. 22). Sin broke the universe apart: it separated people from God and from each other (chapter 2), left creation groaning (Romans 8:20–22), and set spiritual powers in rebellion. God’s plan is to bring it all back into order under its true head. And all things, not only all people: not only the rescue of souls out of a ruined world but the restoration of everything to its right relation with Christ, the material creation renewed, not discarded (Revelation 21:1–5). Every rival throne set up since the first sin will end, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11).

Already, and not yet. God’s plan has truly begun. Christ has been raised and seated above every power (1:20–22), and the powers were disarmed at the cross (Colossians 2:15). When a Jew and a Gentile sat down at one table in Ephesus, that was the future arriving early (2:14–16; 3:10), and the rest of the letter shows the same uniting at work. But it is not yet finished: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.” But we see him, Jesus (Hebrews 2:8–9). That is the honest Christian position, and it is enough to go on with.

What would it look like? A world under one head is a world where the ground no longer throws up thorns and the body no longer grows tumours; with no funerals, because there is nothing left to bury, and no armies, because there is nothing left to defend against; a world in which you are no longer divided against yourself (Romans 7:19). Now we pray, “your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), a prayer that admits a gap. Then the gap closes: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3), and the glory and honour of the nations are brought in (Revelation 21:24–26). Everything you have ever loved is kept; everything that spoiled it is gone.

A Person, under whom everything fits. That homesickness you feel under the best music and the worst news, for a world that holds together, is the memory of what the world was made for, and Paul gives it a name: not a system or a golden age, but a Person. What a Saviour, that the universe should find its meaning in the one who was crucified outside a city wall. And what a God, to tell us his secret before it is complete, so that we may begin now the praise all creation will one day sing: “to the praise of his glory”.

In everyday life. Your fractured world, family, nation or church, has a future in Christ. Every genuine reconciliation you work for now is a small patch of that future showing through.

A grand story, in an age suspicious of grand stories. The French philosopher Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern mood as “incredulity toward metanarratives”: a refusal to believe any single story that claims to explain everything. He had his reasons: the twentieth century was wrecked by grand stories, the master race and the march to the workers’ paradise, each licensing whatever it took to reach its ending. So we ask of every big story: whom does it serve, and who gets crushed? Paul’s story can bear the question. The suspicion is itself a story, of the powerful and their victims; nobody lives without one. And the one at the centre of Paul’s did not take power by crushing anyone. He was crushed, and he reigns from a cross. A story whose hero is the victim cannot be used to make victims without betraying itself.

Where Christians differ: will everyone and everything finally be saved? Some, from Origen in the third century to modern universalists, read uniting all things as a promise that every person, and in some versions even the devil and fallen angels, will finally be reconciled to God. This commentary’s view: no. To unite under one head is to bring everything under Christ’s rule, not to save everything. In this same letter the immoral have no inheritance in the kingdom and God’s wrath comes on the disobedient (5:5–6). Some will bow in joyful worship, and others in defeat (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Philippians 2:10–11). Everything will be put in order; not everything will be saved.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ believers have been given an inheritance that cannot fail, because the God who carries out everything he purposes has destined it for them, for his glory. Everything in this sentence hangs on two words: “in him”.

Obtained an inheritance. Literally were allotted a share, recalling the land divided by lot among Israel’s tribes (Joshua 14:1–2; on the wording, see below).

God himself is the portion. When the land was divided, the other tribes walked away holding a map. Levi was handed nothing, and God explained: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20; see Priests and Levites). The others were given things God had made; Levi was given God. Test it on yourself. If you were given everything you have ever wanted, your health back, every broken relationship mended, the people you have buried returned, and God himself were not there, would that be heaven? “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). Everything else you own can be taken by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

And the glory to come. The inheritance has real content: a body, raised imperishable and like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21); a world, the new heavens and new earth the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5; Revelation 21:1–5); a face, “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4), the one thing Moses asked for and was not given; a likeness, “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). We are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17): whatever belongs to the Son is being settled on you.

Having been predestined. The main verb is past: we have obtained. Your share has already been assigned to you; it only waits to be handed over.

Who works all things. God is not reacting to history but carrying it out, every event, according to his own wise decision (Romans 8:28; Proverbs 16:33), and he is the one who promised you the inheritance. Nothing can stop him handing it over.

The first to hope. Probably Jewish believers, Paul included, who had hoped for the Messiah and believed first; verse 13 turns to “you also”, the Gentiles, and the two become one people (2:11–22). Their hope too is “to the praise of his glory”, the second refrain.

The Heir who was killed. The inheritance is ours only because it was first Christ’s: God appointed his Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2). Jesus told of tenants who saw the owner’s son coming and said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7). A will takes effect only at the death of the one who made it, and Christ died so that “those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance” (Hebrews 9:15–17). What the tenants tried to steal by killing the Heir, the Son leaves to his people in his will.

In everyday life. This is rest for the heart that must control everything. The person who has to hold every outcome lies awake, trying to do God’s job; the believer may plan carefully and then sleep (Psalm 127:2).

What it does not mean. Not that God is the author of sin. He governs evil without doing evil or approving it, and turns it to good, as at the cross (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). Every person remains responsible for what he chooses (James 1:13).

Where Christians differ: does God govern all things, or only some? Many Christians hold that God sets the overall direction of history but leaves most events to human free choices, which he foresees and responds to; open theists go further and say God does not know free choices in advance. This commentary’s view: Paul says God works all things according to his will, not only the big things. Scripture shows him governing the fall of a sparrow (Matthew 10:29), the casting of lots (Proverbs 16:33), the decisions of kings (Proverbs 21:1) and even the wicked acts that crucified Christ (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). This does not make human choices unreal. Joseph’s brothers chose freely and sinned, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God works through our choices, not around them; how both are true is beyond us, but Scripture teaches both, and the cross proves them both at once. Nothing in your life is outside his purpose.

Uncertain wording. “We have obtained an inheritance” is one Greek verb (eklērōthēmen, we were allotted) that can mean we were given an inheritance, or we were made God’s own allotted portion (Deuteronomy 32:9). Both are true (vv. 14, 18), and the ESV’s reading fits the “inheritance” of v. 14. And “the first to hope” most likely means Jewish believers (see above), though some take it of all believers, who hope in Christ before he comes again.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you heard the gospel and believed, God put his Holy Spirit in you as his mark that you are his, and as the first instalment of everything he has promised. Now the Gentiles, “you also”, share fully in everything just described (2:11–22).

When you heard … and believed. This is how God’s eternal choice becomes real in history: through ordinary preaching and real faith (Romans 10:14–17). Election never bypasses the gospel; it works through it. You heard, you believed, you were sealed: one moment, not three stages. For most of the first readers this was a memory: they had heard it from Paul himself in the hall of Tyrannus, “so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:9–10).

Were sealed. On the dock at Ephesus a merchant pressed his signet ring into hot wax across the bindings of his cargo. Every man on the quay could read the mark: this is mine, hands off; this is genuine, not a substitute swapped in on the way; this is protected, and whoever breaks the seal answers to the man whose ring made it. God’s seal is not wax but a Person: he marks you as his own, genuine and protected, by coming to live in you himself. That is his answer to the question of whether you will arrive safely (4:30).

With the promised Holy Spirit. Promised by the prophets (Ezekiel 36:26–27), poured out by the exalted Christ (Acts 2:33), and first borne by him: “On him God the Father has set his seal,” Jesus said (John 6:27), and at the Jordan the Spirit came down on him as the Father named him his beloved Son (Matthew 3:16–17). You are sealed because you are in the Sealed One, and the mark says of you what it said of him: this one is mine.

Who is the guarantee of our inheritance. “Guarantee” (arrabōn) was a down payment, the first instalment of the very same thing, committing the giver to the rest. So what you have of the Spirit now is not a lesser thing than heaven but heaven’s first payment, in heaven’s own currency: the peace that came when nothing in your circumstances explained it, the joy that caught you in a hymn, the love you find you have for people you would never have chosen. It also explains why the Christian life aches. You hold the deposit, not the estate, and the deposit was designed to make you homesick, as an engagement ring makes a man not less eager for the wedding but more eager, and more certain.

Until we acquire possession of it. Until the day of redemption (4:30; on the wording, see below). Note who would lose if that day never came: the one who paid the deposit. God has put down a pledge he does not intend to forfeit.

To the praise of his glory. The third refrain. Father, Son and Spirit have each done their part in the one salvation, and each part ends in the same song.

Where Christians differ: when are believers sealed? Some Pentecostal teaching, and some Reformed writers such as Martyn Lloyd-Jones, treat the sealing as a further experience after conversion, an overwhelming assurance to be sought, out of a real hunger for more of God that is nothing to despise. This commentary’s view: the text ties it to believing: having heard and believed, you were sealed; the Greek participle describes what happened together with believing, not a later stage. Every believer is sealed with the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9). Believers may still seek to be filled afresh (5:18), and God may give special seasons of assurance; but no Christian is unsealed. Check it not by hunting for a feeling but by the marks the Spirit leaves: that you call God Father and mean it (Romans 8:15–16), that sin now grieves you, that Christ has become precious to you and not merely true.

Where Christians differ: can a sealed believer be lost? Those who hold that true believers can finally fall away read the seal as a mark that can be broken, and point to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6), which are real and must be heard. This commentary’s view: the seal is God’s, set until the day of redemption (4:30), and the guarantee pledges the full inheritance; a pledge God gives is not withdrawn. Of his sheep Jesus says, they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). Those who abandon Christ show they were never truly his (1 John 2:19); the warnings are among the means God uses to keep the people he has sealed. So if you are afraid you are drifting, take that fear as the seal at work, not as its breaking: those who have truly let go of Christ do not lie awake over it.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s Greek is compressed: literally until the redemption of the possession. The possession may be the inheritance believers will at last take hold of, as the ESV renders it, or God’s own people, whom he will finally claim in full (compare 1 Peter 2:9, “a people for his own possession”). Either way the pledge holds: the Spirit guarantees the day when God’s people and God’s promises are finally brought together.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers need not more blessings but eyes to see the ones they have, above all the power of God that raised Christ and set him over everything for his church. Paul thanks God for their faith and love (vv. 15–16) and asks the Father to give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, to know him (v. 17). He prays that they may see the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people and the greatness of his power toward them (vv. 18–19): the power that raised Christ, seated him far above every rival power, and gave him as head over all things to the church, his body (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of God (v. 17). The Spirit who inspired Scripture is also needed to give light to its reader. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: Scripture needs no outside proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces certainty of it in the believer’s heart.

So Bible reading and prayer belong together. The Puritans habitually prayed for light before they opened the book, because the eyes of the heart do not open themselves. Paul’s prayer for the Ephesians is a prayer every reader of Scripture can pray.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians, but he can pray, and he prays not for his own release but for their understanding.

Now: We have more sermons, commentaries and Bible apps than any generation before us, and we still need what the Ephesians needed: not more content but opened eyes, the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has given them so much, Paul never stops thanking him for their faith and love, or praying for them. Knowing God’s purposes does not make prayer unnecessary; it gives prayer its confidence.

For this reason. Because of everything in vv. 3–14, Paul falls to his knees. This is the first of the letter’s two prayers (the second is 3:14–21), and both come before a single command (4:1), because Christians obey best when they know what they have.

Because I have heard. Paul is under guard in Rome (Acts 28:16, 20) and may never see these people again, so he carries them to God. Prison did not reduce his ministry to prayer; it showed that prayer had always been the larger half of it. Your quiet faith may be reported somewhere too, to people you will never meet.

Faith and love. The two marks of genuine Christianity, always together: faith looks up to Christ; love looks sideways at the people he died for and calls them family (Galatians 5:6; 1 John 3:14). And all: Jews and Gentiles raised to think each other unclean now passed the same cup. Not warmth towards the agreeable, but love for the whole awkward set of them, the only kind that proves anything. Christ, who prayed for all who would believe through his apostles’ word (John 17:20), was answering that prayer in a port city of idols.

I do not cease to give thanks. Paul thanks God, not the believers, for their faith and love, because these are God’s gifts. He has plenty to correct, but the first thing he says about this church is gratitude for what God has already done in them.

A prisoner who prays, and a Priest who never stops. Behind Paul’s prayer stands a greater one. Israel’s high priest bore the names of the twelve tribes on his breastpiece, on his heart before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). Christ is the high priest that picture promised, and he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Paul prayed when news reached him; Christ never waits for news, and carries every one of his people on his heart, without a break, for ever.

In everyday life. Think of a Christian, or a church, with a long way still to go. Thank God for what he has already done in them, and then tell them.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “your love”, reading “faith … toward all the saints”. The longer text is probably original (compare Colossians 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks God to give them, by his Spirit, a true and growing knowledge of God himself. They already have every blessing (v. 3); what they need is to see what they have, and to know the God who gave it.

The God of our Lord Jesus Christ. As a man, Jesus prayed to the Father and called him “my God” (John 20:17). Paul prays to the God Jesus prayed to, and asks for what Jesus had in full: Isaiah foretold a king from the family of Jesse, David’s father, on whom the Spirit of wisdom would rest (Isaiah 11:1–2). And this knowledge comes through the Son, for “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27). To know God better is to look longer at Jesus.

The Father of glory. The Hebrew kābôd comes from a root meaning heavy: glory is weight, what is solid enough to matter. Money in the bank and lines on a CV feel solid, but Scripture calls such things chaff (Psalm 1:4). God has real weight, and everything else only as it reflects him. Paul worships before he asks a thing.

The Spirit of wisdom and of revelation. Paul does not assume twelve magnificent verses will be enough. He can put the truth before their minds but cannot get it into their hearts, so he turns from teaching to praying. Wisdom sees things as God sees them, your own suffering included. Revelation here is the curtain drawn back on what God has already revealed in Christ, not new truths beyond Scripture: Scripture is complete, but every believer needs the Spirit to make it clear and real to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14).

In the knowledge of him. Not knowledge about God, but of him (John 17:3; Philippians 3:10). You can know a man’s birthday, his job and the name of his dog, and never have met him. So run the test honestly: is God someone you know a great deal about, or someone you know? The two feel similar from the inside for a long time, and they are not the same.

Why this prayer? A man who does not know he has inherited a fortune lives like a pauper. Paul could have prayed for their circumstances to ease or their numbers to grow; he asked instead that they would know God, because the one who truly knows him is equipped for anything that is coming, and the one who does not is unequipped for everything, however well life is going.

How do I come to know God, and not only know about him? As you come to know anyone: by spending time in his company, listening when he speaks, and answering him. He speaks in Scripture, so read it as a letter from someone, asking what it shows you about him. Then pray it back in your own words: thanks for what he has done, confession where the passage finds you out, requests where it makes promises. Do it with other believers, because you know a person better through the eyes of friends who also know him. And obey, for Jesus promised to show himself to the one who keeps his commandments (John 14:21). It grows slowly, like any friendship, but no one who seeks him with all his heart is left a stranger (Jeremiah 29:13).

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or a spirit of wisdom? Some translations read “a spirit of wisdom”, a wise attitude or disposition. This commentary’s view: the Holy Spirit, whose work wisdom and revelation are (Isaiah 11:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12); only God gives revelation. They already have the Spirit (v. 13), so Paul is praying not for them to receive him again but for his ongoing work in their understanding.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God will open their inner eyes to see the sure hope he has called them to, and how precious his people are to him.

The eyes of your hearts. In Scripture the heart is the centre of the whole person, and it has its own eyes. Many Christians know the moment when a verse read a hundred times suddenly opens: nothing changed in the text; the lights came on in the room. Only God can turn them on, the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” and “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). When the lights come on, they always fall on him.

The hope to which he has called you. Christian hope is not wishful thinking but certain expectation: the resurrection of the body, Christ’s return, the renewal of all things, life with God face to face, all guaranteed because Jesus rose. It is an anchor gripping ground the crew cannot see, “behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:19–20). Whether you have seen it tends to show in three ordinary places: when money goes, at a graveside, and in whether your own death is a horror or a door. If those places still frighten you, that is not proof that you have no hope; it is why Paul prays this prayer for you.

God’s treasure is his people. What does the God who owns the galaxies count as treasure, bought at cost? Not the stars. His people. Any treasure is priced by what the buyer paid, and Peter gives the figure: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). For Gentiles once without hope and without God (2:12), this was astonishing. If you think of yourself as someone God barely tolerates for Jesus’ sake, this verse stands in the way. You are not what he puts up with. You are what he is inheriting.

What if I read the Bible and the lights never seem to come on? Keep reading, and keep asking. Seasons of dryness are normal, even for mature believers, and do not mean God has stopped speaking; like meals you cannot remember, Scripture has fed you even on days when nothing felt memorable. Read smaller portions, slowly. Ask what each shows you about God and what it asks of you. Pray before you start: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Read with others, who will often see what you missed. The light comes in God’s time, often when you have stopped straining for it.

Where Christians differ: our inheritance, or God’s? Some read this as the inheritance believers receive, kept among the saints. This commentary’s view: most likely God’s own inheritance, which is his people. Paul says his inheritance, and the Old Testament calls Israel the LORD’s portion and inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9; Exodus 19:5; Malachi 3:17). Both truths are biblical (v. 14 speaks of our inheritance), but here the wonder is that they are God’s treasure.

verseByVerse.quote: and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The power God now directs toward believers is the very power that raised Jesus from the dead and enthroned him in heaven. It is the third thing Paul prays they will see, and it answers the fear that people like us are too weak to make it to the end.

The immeasurable greatness of his power. Beyond measuring. Paul piles up four words, power, working, might and strength (the last two lie behind the ESV’s “great might”), and ties them all to one event.

When he raised him from the dead. Not power like resurrection power, but the same exertion, now aimed at you. Jesus had been executed in public by soldiers who knew death when they saw it (John 19:33–34), then sealed in and guarded. Death had won completely, with witnesses. Then God exerted himself, and the one power in this world that has never lost an argument with anybody gave way.

Toward us who believe. Toward is a word of direction: this power is not locked away for some future day but already moving, and aimed at you. And it is toward us who believe, not us who believe flawlessly: “I believe; help my unbelief!” cried a desperate father, and Jesus acted (Mark 9:24). It has already been used on you: when we were dead in our trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ (2:5). You were not merely helped. You were raised.

At his right hand. The place of supreme honour and authority beside a king: “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). Christ shares God’s throne and rule. He sits because his saving work is finished (Hebrews 10:12), and believers are seated there with him (2:6).

Harder than a corpse? Set your own situation beside that: the habit you have failed to break for twenty years, the person you cannot forgive, the fear you have reasoned with a hundred times, the prayer you have carried so long that you no longer expect an answer. Is any of it harder than a corpse? That is not a promise that the struggle will be over by Friday. This power often works as quietly as seed in the ground, and that you are still fighting at all is its work in you (Galatians 5:17).

Power for what? Not mostly for spectacle. Power to believe and keep believing (Philippians 2:13). Power over sin, since the strength that broke death can break the grip of an old habit (Romans 6:4–6). Power to endure: the long marriage, the chronic illness, the prayer carried for years, “strengthened with all power … for all endurance and patience with joy” (Colossians 1:11). Power to love the difficult (3:16–17). And power in weakness, made perfect exactly when human strength runs out (2 Corinthians 12:9).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always feel powerful or see miracles, or that hardship will be removed. The man writing this prayer is in chains; the power is given for endurance, not escape, to make your inner life like the Son’s.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ now reigns above every power, spiritual or human, that has ever made people afraid, and he always will.

Far above. Not only higher in rank, but in a different class altogether. Christ is not the top name on the chart; he drew the chart, for all these powers were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16). Every name that ever made a city tremble, Artemis, Caesar, the spirits of the air, has been outranked by a carpenter’s son who died on a Roman cross.

All rule and authority and power and dominion. The titles Jews and Greeks used for orders of spiritual beings, including hostile ones (6:12), and also for human rulers. To Ephesians who had lived in dread of named powers, this was liberation: every power you feared is under the feet of the one who saved you. At the cross, which looked like defeat, “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). They still oppose (6:12), but as defeated enemies, not sovereign lords: there is a vast difference between a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8) and a reigning one.

Every name that is named. In Ephesus this was an attack on an industry: in magic, to know a spirit’s name was to gain leverage over it. In the same city the seven sons of Sceva tried to use “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims” as one more name in the toolkit, and were beaten out of the house (Acts 19:13–16). His name is not a lever to be operated; he is a Lord to be belonged to, and when you have the Person, you no longer need the formulas. We have our own names: the market, the scan result, the opinion of people whose approval we have never won. We do not burn incense to them; we lie awake for them. Every one of them is under his feet.

Not only in this age but also in the one to come. Jews divided history into this present age, marked by sin and death, and the age to come, when God would put everything right. Christ’s resurrection has brought the age to come into the present, and the two overlap until his return. Every power that ever terrified anyone had an expiry date. His authority is not up for renewal at the end of history; the end of history is simply when everybody finds out.

Can curses, horoscopes or evil spirits harm a Christian? They cannot own you or undo what God has done. A believer is sealed with Christ’s Spirit (1:13), and “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4); no curse can reverse God’s blessing (Numbers 23:8). The devil can still tempt, accuse and oppose you, and must be resisted, not ignored (6:11–12; James 4:7). But have nothing to do with horoscopes, tarot cards, Ouija boards, charms or spells (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are stronger than Christ, but because consulting them looks to another lord for what only he gives. If you have dabbled, confess it and get rid of the things, as the Ephesians burned their scrolls (Acts 19:19). Then stop being afraid. You are seated with the one who is far above them all.

Is it not narrow to say Jesus is above every other name? Only if the claim were that Christians are above everyone else, and it is the opposite. The name above every name belongs to the one who took the lowest place, obedient to the point of death on a cross (Philippians 2:8–9). He reached his throne not by climbing over rivals but by dying for his enemies, and he promises them a seat beside him (Revelation 3:21). Nor is a claim arrogant merely because it excludes something; every claim does, including the claim that all religions are equally true. The real question is whether it is true, and Paul rests it on a public event: God raised him from the dead (1:20; Acts 17:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has put everything under Christ’s rule, and has given this all-ruling Christ to the church as her head.

He put all things under his feet. Paul quotes Psalm 8:6, which looks back to the rule God gave Adam over all he had made, and Adam lost by his sin. Hebrews adds the ache, “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him”, and then the turn: “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus”, crowned with glory and honour (Hebrews 2:8–9). What Adam failed to hold, Christ, the last Adam, has won (1 Corinthians 15:45). The feet once nailed to a cross are the feet under which every power is now placed. Their subjection is not yet fully visible, but it is fully real: “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Head over all things to the church. God gave the church a gift: Christ, head over all things. And the strangest words are the last three: not to the angels, nor to the nations, but to the church: ordinary people, many of them slaves and tradesmen, meeting in borrowed rooms in a city that would not have noticed if they vanished. We picture two stories, the big one out there of empires, markets and wars, and the small one in here of our own life and church. This verse says there is one story, and the big one is being run for the sake of the small one.

Head. “Head” here plainly includes authority; in 4:15–16 it is also the source from which the body is nourished and held together (Colossians 2:19). So Christ’s rule over everything is also the arrangement by which you are fed. And a body goes where its head goes: if the head is seated above every power, the body cannot be left behind (2:6).

If Christ rules all things for the church, why does the church suffer so much? Because he rules for her good, and her good is not the same as her comfort. The head over all things is the Lamb who was slain, and his body follows his way, through the cross to the crown. Persecution, decline and hardship are not signs that he has lost control: when persecution scattered the church in Jerusalem, the scattered went everywhere preaching the word (Acts 8:1–4). Nothing can separate his people from his love (Romans 8:35–37), and the gates of hell will never overcome the church (Matthew 16:18). Pray for the suffering church, and do not measure Christ’s reign by this week’s headlines.

Where Christians differ: the head of the church. Roman Catholic teaching sees the pope as Christ’s visible vicar (stand-in) and head on earth. This commentary’s view: Christ alone is head of the church (Westminster Confession 25.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.4), ruling by his word and Spirit through the elders and pastors he gives his church (Christians differ, charitably, over how those offices are arranged). No human being shares that headship.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is Christ’s body, the place he fills with his presence, as he fills the whole universe.

Which is his body. The church is not a club that admires Christ from a distance but his body: united to him, living from him, the means by which he acts in the world. A body is how a person is present to things, and Christ’s body is not a building but the people who were in the room with you last Sunday, the difficult ones included. When they carry a meal to a widow, that is Christ, present on a particular street.

The fullness of him who fills all in all. Why fills, and not only rules? A king can rule a land he has never visited; to fill is to be present within it. “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the cloud of God’s glory filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11). The one whose glory filled that temple now fills all things, the universe by his power and the church, his new temple of living stones, by his saving presence (2:21–22; 4:10). He has chosen to make poor, quarrelsome, forgiven people the place where his fullness dwells.

Who fills all in all. There is nowhere you can go this week that lies outside him: the ward, the school run, the office where nobody prays, the flat you come home to when it is empty. You do not carry him into those places like a parcel. He is already filling them, and you go in as part of his body.

Can I follow Christ without the church? Not for long, and not as he intends. The church is not a helpful extra for keen believers but Christ’s body, and a hand that has left the body does not become a freer hand, only a dying one. Many who love Jesus but not the church have been hurt by Christians, and that hurt is real and should be heard. But the remedy is a faithful church, not none. “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (5:25): you cannot hold the Bridegroom at arm’s length from his bride.

In the flow. Chapter 2 opens with a jolt: “And you were dead” (2:1). The power that raised and seated Christ (1:20) has raised and seated believers with him (2:5–6).

Where Christians differ: does the church fill Christ, or does Christ fill the church? One reading: the church completes Christ, as a body completes a head. Calvin took this view and found it moving: Christ, who lacks nothing in himself, counts himself in some sense incomplete without his people. The other: the church is filled by Christ, the place he fills with his presence, life and gifts. This commentary’s view: the second is more likely. Paul consistently speaks of Christ filling (4:10) and of believers being filled (3:19; 5:18), never of Christ being filled up by us, and Colossians 2:9–10 says the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and you have been filled in him. Christ lacks nothing. Yet Calvin’s point stands in its own way. Paul could have said king and kingdom, or master and servants; he chose the one picture in which the greater looks unfinished without the lesser. A head without a body is not a lesser head; it is a horror. Christ does not need us as we need him, but he has bound himself to us so closely that he is not ashamed to be called our head. That is not a lack in Christ. It is a measure of how far love has committed itself.

1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the first half of the letter (chapters 1–3), where Paul tells believers who they are in Christ before he tells them, from 4:1, how to live.

The message. Before you did anything, God did everything.
