The Father chose and adopted you, the Son bought your freedom with his blood, and the Spirit has marked you as God’s own: all of it yours in Christ, all of it to the praise of God’s glory. What you need now is not more blessing but eyes to see what you have, above all the power that raised Christ and set him over everything, for you.

Why it was said. Most of the first readers were Gentiles from a city of idols and magic, where unseen powers were managed with charms and spells (see the introduction). Few, new and many of them slaves, they could easily feel like second-class guests beside Jewish believers, and still at the mercy of the powers they used to fear. Paul answers both fears: they were chosen before the world began, and the Christ they belong to is seated far above every power.

How the chapter makes its case. After the greeting (vv. 1–2), one long sentence of praise (vv. 3–14) moves through the Father’s choosing and adopting (vv. 4–6), the Son’s redeeming and God’s plan to unite all things in him (vv. 7–12), and the Spirit’s sealing, which brings the Gentiles fully in (vv. 13–14), each closing with “to the praise of his glory”. Then praise turns to prayer (vv. 15–23), not for new blessings but for opened eyes: to know the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the power that raised Christ and made him head over all things for the church, his body.

Where it leads. Every blessing is “in him”: Christ is the Beloved in whom we are loved, the one whose blood redeems, the Heir whose inheritance is shared, the Sealed One in whom we are sealed, the head under whom all things will be gathered. And the chapter ends at a throne: the one crucified outside a city wall is above every name that is named, and God has given him to the church.

For us. This chapter gives you a footing before it gives you a task. Read it slowly, as an inventory of what is already yours in Christ, and then pray Paul’s prayer for yourself and others: not first for easier circumstances, but for eyes to see.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the headline over the whole chapter. Everything that follows, from election before creation to Christ enthroned above every power, unpacks “every spiritual blessing”, and all of it comes “in Christ”. It also sets the order of the Christian life: God blesses us first, and our blessing of him is the answering praise.

1.reflection:
Paul calls ordinary, struggling believers “saints” and says God chose them “before the foundation of the world” (vv. 1, 4). How does it change the way you see yourself, and your worst week, that God’s love for you did not begin with anything in you?

Verses 3–14 list blessings that no illness, redundancy or bad year can take away. Which of them do you most need to remember at the moment? Why do we so easily measure God’s blessing by our circumstances instead?

Paul prays not for easier lives but that his readers will know God and see the hope, the riches and the power they already have (vv. 17–19). What would change if you prayed this way for yourself, your family and your church?

Christ is seated “far above” every power and given as “head over all things to the church” (vv. 21–22). What fears, pressures or “names” loom large over your life, and how does Christ’s reign speak to them?

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Salvation is God raising the dead, his gift from first to last. Verses 1–3 show where we were: dead in sin, following the world, the devil and the flesh, and by nature under God’s wrath, Jew and Gentile alike. Verses 4–7 show what God did out of rich mercy: he made us alive with Christ, raised us and seated us with him, so that through all the coming ages he might display the riches of his kindness. Verses 8–10 draw the lesson: saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast, and yet created in Christ for the good works God prepared for us to walk in.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

Dead in trespasses and sins is the plainest biblical statement of what Reformed theology calls total depravity: no part of us naturally seeks God or can save itself (what the term does and does not mean is set out in the note on vv. 1–2).

Against that, God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This grace does not force the will but renews it, making the unwilling willing, and the faith through which we receive salvation is his gift (v. 8).

Verse 10 answers the charge that grace makes people passive. The law could tell us to do good, but it could not make us want to. Grace does. The person saved by grace alone no longer has to do good in order to be accepted by God. He is accepted already, and so he is free to do the good works God prepared beforehand, gladly, in the Spirit’s strength.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For Paul’s readers, dead in trespasses and sins was autobiography. Many had worshipped Artemis or practised magic; converts in Ephesus burned their books of spells (Acts 19:19). The “But God” of v. 4 was the turning point of their own lives.

Now: The same diagnosis covers everyone outside Christ, however educated, moral or sincere. A person who thinks he is merely ill will not seek the remedy for death, so the church states both clearly: dead, but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without Christ we were spiritually dead, living by the world’s ways under the power of the devil. Paul begins the gospel in the grave, so that we can see what kind of rescue God’s was.

The connection. The power that raised Christ (1:19–23) is now at work in us. The sentence begun in verse 1 does not reach its main verb until verse 5: “God … made us alive”.

You were dead. Not sick or weakened, but cut off from the life of God (4:18). A corpse can be dressed beautifully; it is still a corpse. Spiritual death means no power to perceive God (1 Corinthians 2:14), no desire for him (Romans 8:7), and no ability to change. Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him; he heard a voice speak life into death, and came out (John 11:43–44). This is the death God warned of in Eden (Genesis 2:17): Adam did not drop dead that day, but he hid from God, and death began.

In the trespasses and sins. A trespass crosses a line God has drawn; a sin misses the mark he set. Dead in them: sin is not only the cause of death but the element the dead man lives in, as water is a fish’s. So the cure cannot be moral improvement. You do not improve a corpse; you raise it.

In which you once walked. “Walk” is the Bible’s word for a way of life, and the dead were busy: careers, families, religion and pleasure, all lived as if God were not there.

The course of this world. Not the planet but human society organised without God, telling us what to want and whom to admire. It is a current, and the dead do not feel it, because nothing feels less like being swept along than swimming with the tide. You discover it only when you turn and try to swim against it (1 John 2:15–17).

The prince of the power of the air. Satan, “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31) and “the god of this world”, who blinds the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4): a real person, not a figure of speech for society’s bad habits. The air was thought the home of spirits: the powers his readers feared are real, and ruled by one evil prince, yet he is a creature, not God’s equal, and already defeated (1:21; Colossians 2:15). “Now at work” is the verb used of God’s power raising Christ (1:20): two powers are at work in the world. “Sons of disobedience” means people marked by disobedience.

Three enemies. Verses 1–3 name the world around us, the devil above us and the flesh within us. Culture makes sin normal, the devil makes it attractive, and our own nature wants it. And the dead man is not fighting them but following them: not a prisoner straining at the bars, but a body carried by the tide.

What it does not mean. Not that unbelievers are as bad as they could be, or cannot do good in a human sense. Total depravity means sin has reached every part of us, mind, will and desires, so that nothing in us can turn us back to God. Nor is everyone outside Christ consciously serving Satan; most simply follow the crowd. And it does not remove responsibility: the dead walked in their sins, doing what they wanted.

Signs of life. Corpses do not develop appetites. If you find in yourself any hunger for God, if his word sometimes lands with weight, if sin now grieves you where once it barely registered, something has happened to you that you did not do: a voice has spoken into a grave, and you heard it.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel, argue clearly, but pray first: you are speaking to people who need resurrection, not merely persuasion. And no one is too far gone, because God raises the dead.

But I know kind unbelievers. Some unbelievers are kinder and more generous than half the congregation. Think of cut flowers: a florist’s arrangement can be lovelier than anything still growing in the garden. Yet it has been cut from its root, and everything you admire about it is running on borrowed time. Paul is speaking of connection, not comparison. The kindness is real; the root is what is missing.

Where Christians differ: how dead? Semi-Pelagian traditions (which hold that the first move towards God can be ours) and Arminian ones, held by many faithful believers, teach that the fall left people weakened but still able, with God’s general help (called prevenient grace), to accept or refuse the gospel; they read dead as separated from God rather than unable, and point to Jesus’ promise to draw all people to himself (John 12:32). Reformed theology holds total inability: the fallen will is free to choose what it wants, but it does not want God, and no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44; Romans 8:7–8). This commentary’s view: total depravity and inability (Westminster Confession 9.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 9.3). Paul’s image decides it: a corpse does not cooperate with its resurrection. Yet Paul says “dead” not to crush us but to prepare us for verse 5, as a dark night makes the sunrise plain. The depth of the death is the measure of the miracle (Ezekiel 37:1–14).
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of us, Jew and Gentile alike, lived for ourselves and were by birth under God’s just anger. The trouble was not only what we did but what we were.

We all once lived. Verses 1–2 said “you”, the Gentile readers; now Paul says “we”. Paul, once the strictest of Pharisees (Philippians 3:4–6), puts Jew and Gentile in the same grave. If both were equally lost, both are saved the same way, and neither can look down on the other (Romans 3:9, 22–23).

The passions of our flesh. “Flesh” here is not the body, which God made good, but fallen human nature: the whole person turned in on itself, what Luther, following Augustine, called the heart curved in on itself, so that even its good gifts, love, work and religion, are bent back towards its own comfort and glory (2 Timothy 3:2–4). Its passions are not only sexual (Galatians 5:19–21): the flesh produces boardroom sin as readily as bedroom sin.

The desires of the flesh and the mind. Literally the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts. Paul adds the mind, so the person who thinks self-control has made him good has nowhere to hide: master your bodily appetites and you may only have moved the problem upstairs, to pride in your own cleverness, the hunger for power, the craving to be admired. A man can be sober, chaste and hard-working and still live entirely in the desires of the mind.

By nature children of wrath. Not only did we do wrong; we were wrong. “By nature” is original sin in a phrase: by birth, as children of Adam, before and beneath any choice (Psalm 51:5). We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. “Children of wrath” means people on whom wrath rests (John 3:36). Nobody has ever had to teach a child to grab, or to say “mine”: every parent is an unwilling witness to this verse.

Wrath. Not a fit of temper, and not unworthy of a loving God, but his settled, holy, just opposition to evil (Romans 1:18), always fair. A God who was not angry at child abuse, cruelty and betrayal would not be good. And this truth is the ground of deep gratitude, for the one who is forgiven little, loves little (Luke 7:47): the shallowness of our worship usually matches the smallness of our sense of what we were saved from.

Like the rest of mankind. No exceptions, but one. God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), “one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He took our flesh but not its curve inward: the only man in whom the passions of the flesh and the desires of the mind never once ruled, the only child of Adam on whom wrath did not rest by nature. Yet on the cross he stood in its path for us. Paul calls him the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45): born into the first Adam’s family, so that a new family might begin with him.

The tense is the comfort. We were children of wrath. Not are. Every dreadful word in these three verses stands in the past tense, dead, walked, followed, lived, were, held there until two words in verse 4 break over them: “But God”. If you are in Christ, this passage is not your diagnosis but your medical history. Read it as a healthy man reads the chart from the worst year of his life, and marvels that he is sitting up reading anything at all.

What it does not mean. Not that the body or physical desire is evil in itself: hunger and sexual desire are God’s gifts (Genesis 1:31). Nor does “children of wrath” mean God hates his creatures or takes pleasure in their ruin (Ezekiel 33:11). The next words are “But God, being rich in mercy”.

A common question: what about infants who die? Scripture does not answer directly, and believers should speak humbly. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3), with the Westminster (10.3), says that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases. Many in the Reformed tradition, among them Charles Spurgeon and B. B. Warfield, held that all who die in infancy are among the elect, pointing to God’s judgment according to deeds done (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10), which infants have not done, and to David’s confidence that he would go to his dead child (2 Samuel 12:23). Jesus took the little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

What is certain. If any infant is saved, it is by grace in Christ, not by innocence; and grieving parents may entrust their child to the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). If you have buried a child, this is not a cold debate: the Saviour who took children in his arms holds yours now.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagius (fifth century) taught that each person is born innocent and sins only by following bad examples. Eastern Orthodoxy teaches that we inherit from Adam mortality and a tendency to sin, but not his guilt. Augustine and the Reformers taught that we inherit both a corrupt nature and the guilt of Adam’s first sin, counted (imputed) to us, because the whole race sinned in Adam, its head (Romans 5:12–19). “By nature children of wrath” fits only the last: wrath rests on us by nature, not only after we choose. This commentary’s view: original sin as both inherited corruption and imputed guilt (Westminster Confession 6.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 6.3). What sounds unfair here is what saves us. Adam acted for all of us, as a king who declares war puts his whole people at war; Christ acted for all who are in him, and as Adam’s sin was counted to us, so Christ’s righteousness is counted to them. Nor are you an innocent bystander: born into Adam’s family, you have agreed with his choice every day since by sinning yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of rich mercy and great love, God gave life to the spiritually dead by joining them to the risen Christ.

But God. After three verses of death, the subject of the sentence finally appears. Martyn Lloyd-Jones said these two words in a sense contain the whole gospel. Had the story been “But we”, there would be no hope: dead people cannot act.

Being rich in mercy. Mercy is God’s pity moving towards misery: it sees the corpse, is not repelled, and moves first. And he is rich in it: it does not run low, or grow harder to obtain the more you have needed it.

The great love. The reason lies in God, not in us. Paul piles up the words: love, great love, love with which he loved, for the children of wrath as they were (Romans 5:8). We were not lovable; he loved us anyway, and his love made us lovely.

Even when we were dead. When there was nothing to work with and nothing to reward, he acted. That settles the anxious believer’s question, whether God might yet change his mind: you contributed nothing to your first resurrection, and your standing has never rested on your contribution.

Made us alive together with Christ. The main verb of the whole sentence: not helped or improved, but raised. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5). And it is life with Christ: not a separate miracle that resembles his, but a share in his. When Jesus came out of the tomb, you came out with him. In him your resurrection already happened, outside Jerusalem, long before you were born.

By grace you have been saved. Paul breaks into his own sentence. The Greek perfect means a completed act with lasting results: saved, and still saved.

Life before faith. Reformed theology reads this verse as showing that new birth comes before faith in order, though not in time, as a room is lit the instant the switch is turned, yet the switch comes first. We believe because we have been born again (John 1:12–13; 1 John 5:1).

I cannot remember a moment when I was made alive. You do not remember being born either, and you are plainly alive. Many believers, especially those raised in Christian homes, cannot name a day, and Scripture never asks for a date. It asks whether there is life now: not “When did I first believe?” but “Am I trusting Christ today?” The signs are a newborn’s: hunger for God’s word (1 Peter 2:2), the cry of Father to God (Romans 8:15), a new grief over sin, and love for his people (1 John 3:14). If those are there, however weak, the one who raised you knows the day. Like the man born blind, you can say that once you were blind and now you see (John 9:25).

Where Christians differ: does God’s life-giving work depend on our consent? Arminian Christians, who love the gospel of grace too, hold that God’s grace enables every person to believe but can be resisted, so that the decisive factor in who is saved is the human response. Reformed theology holds that God’s regenerating grace is effectual: when God makes alive, the dead live (John 6:37; Acts 16:14, where the Lord opened Lydia’s heart). This commentary’s view: effectual calling, God’s call that does not fail to bring the dead to life (Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1–2). God does not drag the unwilling; he makes them willing by giving them new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ, believers share not only his resurrection but his place of rest and honour at God’s right hand.

Three “with” words. Made alive with, raised with, seated with: each matches a step in Christ’s story in 1:20. This is union with Christ: we are joined to him, he acted for us, and what happened to him counts as having happened to us (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–3). When the captain lifts the cup, the whole team has won it, even the player who never left the bench.

Raised us up with him. Spiritually now, for we have passed from death to life (John 5:24); bodily at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). The first guarantees the second.

Seated us with him. Stated as a fact, in the past tense: at rest, in a place of authority. The old covenant priests stood daily at their service, for their work was never done (Hebrews 10:11); Christ “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” because his one sacrifice was final (Hebrews 1:3; 10:12). You share his rest because you are in him, and he will not be in glory without his people (John 17:24). The powers of verse 2 once ruled the Ephesians; now they are beneath Christ, and the Ephesians sit with him.

In Christ Jesus. Not by our own spiritual height, so nothing here is graded. The believer converted last Thursday, who still cannot find Habakkuk and is fighting something he has told nobody about, is seated exactly where the apostle is, because neither is there on his own account. Christ has only one seat: the highest.

Seated already, still fighting. Our experience does not yet match our position. We are seated, yet we must stand and fight (6:10–13), and in the very realm where the battle is (6:12). So this is not escapism but your position in the conflict: the difference between a soldier pinned down in a trench, who cannot see whether his side is winning, and a man beside the commander with the whole battle laid out before him. Both are in the war; only one knows how it ends. The fight is fought from victory, not for it.

In everyday life. When the accuser says you are disqualified, do not produce your record; point to your seat. The boss, the diagnosis and the fear are real, but they are beneath your Lord’s feet, and you are seated with him.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved us so that through all eternity his grace and kindness would be on display in us.

So that. As in the refrain of chapter 1 (1:6, 12, 14), the purpose is God’s glory. And his glory and our good are not rivals: he is glorified precisely by being kind to us.

In the coming ages. Ages, one after another without end. What we have tasted is the down payment; the coming ages are the feast. If grace was so real to you through a fallen mind, a weak faith and a tired body, what will it be when every barrier is gone? C. S. Lewis caught it at the end of The Last Battle: the further up and further in you go, the larger everything becomes, and the cry is, “This is the land I have been looking for all my life.”

He might show. To exhibit publicly (Romans 9:22–23), with angels and powers in the audience (3:10). What will be on display through the ages is not galaxies, which never cost God anything, but what he did with people. You are the exhibit.

The immeasurable riches of his grace. The word used of his power in 1:19: grace overflows, and eternity will not exhaust it. This turns something painful inside out. Many of us carry a chapter we would rather were left out, the wasted years, the thing we still cannot say aloud, and assume heaven will keep a discreet silence about it. But what is displayed is the riches of his grace, and grace can only be measured against what it had to overcome. A restorer’s skill is never shown by a painting that was never damaged. The chapter you would erase will testify most loudly, for ever, to what he is like.

In kindness toward us. Grace is not a judge reluctantly signing a pardon; it comes in kindness (Titus 3:4), someone leaning towards you. Eternity is God, for ever, delighting to be kind to people who had nothing coming.

In Christ Jesus. All this kindness reaches us through one channel, and the exhibit has a centre. When John was shown heaven, he saw “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6), and every creature singing to him. The risen Jesus kept his wounds and showed them to Thomas (John 20:27). The marks in his hands and side will explain every saved sinner round the throne. You will be part of the display; he will be the reason for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is God’s free gift, received by trusting him and never earned by anything we do, so no one can take the credit.

By grace. The source: God’s free favour towards those who deserve wrath (v. 3). If it is deserved in any way, it is no longer grace (Romans 11:6).

You have been saved. Perfect and passive: done to you, finished, its effect continuing. So assurance is not arrogance: a rescued swimmer who says he is saved is not boasting about his swimming but reporting what the lifeboat did.

Through faith. The means: the empty hand that receives the gift. Faith is not a contribution but trust in Christ, and its whole value lies in its object. Weak faith in a sound bridge will carry you over the river; robust faith in a rotten one will drop you into it. The father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” saw his son healed (Mark 9:24–27). So the question is never whether your faith is big enough, but what you are trusting. A trembling hand on Christ has all that he is: the empty hand does not become any emptier for shaking. We are saved through faith, never because of it.

Not your own doing. “This” points to the whole thing just described, salvation by grace through faith (see “Uncertain wording” below). Grace, salvation and the faith that receives it are all gathered into one word: gift.

Not a result of works. “Works” is anything we do to put God in our debt; Paul had the law in view, but the principle covers every attempt to earn salvation (Romans 4:4–5; Titus 3:5).

So that no one may boast. The ancient world ran on honour, and the only question was what you boasted in. Paul counted his own record as rubbish beside knowing Christ (Philippians 3:4–8). If we contributed even one per cent, we could boast: “I chose wisely when others did not.” God removes every ground of pride, so that the only boast left is in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29–31). Boasting takes quiet forms: the sense that I believed because I was wiser than others; the Calvinist who privately feels more perceptive; the long-standing member eyeing the new convert with a touch of seniority. All came to the cross with nothing and left with the same righteousness of Christ. A simple test of any gospel, or any testimony: does it leave room for anyone to boast?

What it does not mean. Not that faith is unnecessary because God does everything: no one is saved without believing. Not that good works do not matter: verse 10 follows at once. Nor does God save people and leave them unchanged; he saves us from sin, not in it. Works are never the reason God accepts us; they are what grows in the life of someone he has accepted.

In everyday life. When you feel you have been a good Christian this week and God must be pleased with you, or a bad one and he must be finished with you, come back to this verse. Your standing rests on his gift, not on your week.

If faith is God’s gift, what should I do if I do not have it? Come to Christ, and ask. God gives faith through his word, for “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). So read the Gospels, sit under faithful preaching, talk with a Christian you trust, and pray honestly, even if your prayer is only, “Lord, I want to believe; help me.” The Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13), and Jesus has never turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37). Wanting faith may be the first stirring of the life this chapter describes. Do not wait until you feel ready; turn to him now.

Where Christians differ: is faith itself a gift? Arminians hold that God offers salvation and gives everyone the ability to believe, but that faith itself is the human response. Reformed theology holds that faith, too, is God’s gift, granted to those he has made alive (Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48; 2 Peter 1:1). Even if “this” in verse 8 refers to the whole package, faith is part of the package. This commentary’s view: faith is God’s gift; we believe, but we believe because God has given us life (v. 5).

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification includes the inner renewal of the person, begins at baptism, can be increased by good works, and can be lost by mortal sin. The Reformers taught that justification is a legal declaration: God pronounces the sinner righteous, not because of any righteousness in him, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to him, received by faith alone (Romans 3:24–28; 4:5). Renewal always follows, but it is not the ground of our standing with God. This commentary’s view: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone (Westminster Confession 11.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1). Verses 8–10 say it exactly: saved not by works, but for works.

Uncertain wording. In Greek, “this” (touto) normally matches the gender of the word it refers to, and here it matches neither “grace” nor “faith” (both feminine). Some still take it as faith, others as grace, but it most naturally means the whole just described, salvation by grace through faith; and the faith that receives it is part of that whole.
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are God’s own handiwork, newly created in Christ to live the good life he planned for us beforehand. Good works do not save us; they are what God saved us for.

His workmanship. Salvation cannot come from our works, because we ourselves are God’s work. Poiēma (hence poem) appears only twice in the New Testament: here, and in Romans 1:20, of the created universe, “the things that have been made”. The word Paul uses for the galaxies he uses for you, and of the two works the second cost God far more: the first he spoke into being; the second required a death.

Created in Christ Jesus. Salvation is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), not a touching-up of the old self, though the new creature still has growing to do. You are still you, but the deepest thing about you has changed: you now love what you once ignored, God, his word and his people, because he has given you a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26).

For good works. Actions that please God: done in faith, according to his commands, from love, for his glory. They include the large and visible, mission, justice, generosity, and the small and hidden (4:25–32): the plumber who charges fairly, the employee who works as to the Lord (6:7), the parent who disciplines with warmth (6:4), the one who goes back to apologise. Masterpieces are made not to be stored but displayed (Matthew 5:16).

Which God prepared beforehand. As God planned our salvation before the foundation of the world (1:4), he planned the good works that would follow. Not that you are a robot running a script: God prepares the works, and his Spirit works in us (1:19–20). So the question is not what good works to invent, but what God has put in front of you today: the neighbour in need, the unexpected chance to serve, the gift waiting to be used.

That we should walk in them. The verb of verse 2, on the opposite road. Not admire good works, nor intend them: walk, one step at a time, usually with nobody watching. Conversion did not stop you walking; it changed the road (4:1, 17; 5:2).

Not by works, but for works. Verses 8–10 are the whole Reformation in miniature. Works are the fruit of salvation, never the root: a child obeys not to earn a place in the family but because he belongs. The faith that justifies is never alone (James 2:17–18). And since even our best works are imperfect, they are accepted for Christ’s sake, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

Copied from that one face. God works to a pattern: those he foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29). He is making each of us like Jesus, and every stroke is copied from that one face. When the finished work is unveiled, no one will admire the clay. They will praise the hands that shaped it.

The exhausting work of making yourself. Our culture hands every young person a task no earlier generation was given: invent yourself. It sounds like freedom. But the French sociologist Alain Ehrenberg, in The Weariness of the Self, argued that the rise of depression in modern societies is bound up with exactly this: when each person must produce his own identity and success, every shortfall becomes a verdict on the self, and many simply run out of strength. Paul’s word cuts the knot. You are not your own poem; you are his, a work someone else began and has promised to complete. You still walk, but on paths prepared beforehand, as a son runs errands in his father’s house, not as a man building a house to justify his existence.

Not a masterpiece? Some readers meet the word and think: “Not me.” But you are not the one asked to assess the work. You are standing inside it while it is still being made, the one place from which no work of art ever looked finished. A house halfway through renovation looks worse than before anyone touched it, and that is evidence not that the builder has failed but that he has begun. The worth of a work is set by the artist, never by the material’s opinion of itself. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

What if I miss the good works God prepared for me? You will sometimes fail to do the good in front of you: that is sin to confess, not a plan you have ruined. God prepared these works knowing your failures, and his purpose does not hang on your never putting a foot wrong (Romans 8:28). Nor are they hidden in a maze: most are plain, the commands of Scripture and the needs in front of you, met as you have opportunity (Galatians 6:10). For bigger decisions, choose wisely within what Scripture allows, take counsel, pray, and go forward without fear of having picked the wrong door. The God who prepared the road also guides the walker.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s cross has made outsiders into God’s own household. Paul asks the Gentile believers to remember what they once were: without Christ, outside Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope and without God (vv. 11–12). Now they have been brought near by Christ’s blood (v. 13). He is our peace: he broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile, made one new humanity, reconciled both to God through the cross, and gives both access to the Father in one Spirit (vv. 14–18). So they are citizens, family and a temple where God lives by his Spirit (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

We often think of Christ’s death only in individual terms, and that is true as far as it goes. But the cross also made a new community. Christ reconciled sinners to God and, in the same act, to one another: he reconciled “us both to God in one body through the cross” (v. 16).

So the unity of the church is not only a practical goal; it is something Christ bought with his blood. To keep up the walls he has torn down is to live against what the cross did. A reconciled congregation of very different people says, simply by existing, that the wall is down.

The temple picture (vv. 19–22) adds that the church’s holiness matters. The old temple was guarded because God dwelt there, and the church is now his dwelling by the Spirit. That gives every local church both dignity and responsibility.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone barrier in the temple courts, the soreg, was not a metaphor, and Paul’s Jewish and Gentile readers knew which wall he meant; now they sat side by side at the Lord’s table as members of one household.

Now: Churches still struggle with the walls Christ has torn down: race, class and political tribe can shape a congregation more than we notice. Ephesians 2 says the wall is down and the new humanity is more basic than any of those divisions. A church gladly one across them is showing what the cross accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers must remember how far outside God’s people they once stood, despised by those who bore the covenant’s outward mark.

Therefore. Because of verses 1–10. If God saved Jew and Gentile alike by grace alone, the wall between them has no ground left to stand on.

Remember. Forgetting comes easily: the believer of thirty years drifts towards feeling like the sort of person God would naturally have wanted. God trained Israel in deliberate recollection, nearly always tied to a command about somebody else: remember you were a slave, therefore release your servant generously (Deuteronomy 15:15); you know the heart of a stranger, therefore do not oppress him (Exodus 23:9). About to tell a mixed church to live as one body, Paul reminds the Gentile half how far outside they once stood.

You Gentiles in the flesh. By birth: Gentiles were not born into God’s covenant people.

The uncircumcision. Circumcision was God’s covenant sign to Abraham (Genesis 17:9–14) and had become the badge of Jewish identity, and many Jews called Gentiles “the uncircumcision” with contempt, as David spoke of “this uncircumcised Philistine” (1 Samuel 17:26). The name labels a whole people by what they lack, and Paul quotes it so that his readers will never be comfortable using its like about anybody else: a man who remembers being on the outside cannot easily keep another there. And he says “called” of both groups: both labels are human names, not God’s final verdict.

Made in the flesh by hands. In the Greek Old Testament “made with hands” is used of idols (as in Isaiah 46:6): circumcision valued for itself is merely human. God always wanted circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and in Christ believers receive “a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11).

The offspring the mark pointed to. Circumcision was the sign of a promise with a person at its heart: in Abraham’s offspring all the nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), and that offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So the Gentiles of Ephesus did not slip in by a side door; they arrived where the mark had always pointed, and in him became “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). Christ was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), bearing in his body the very mark the nations lacked, and kept the covenant every son of Abraham had broken. Then on the cross he bore the curse of the covenant breakers, Jew and Gentile alike (Galatians 3:13).

What it does not mean. Not that circumcision was a mistake or God’s covenant with Israel worthless: it was his gift and pointed to Christ (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). Paul objects to the outward sign being treated as the ground of standing with God, and used to despise others.

How to remember. Not by dwelling on old guilt, dealt with at the cross, but by keeping your story straight, so that grace stays astonishing and you stay kind. Tell your story honestly, and read verses 1–3 and 12 as a description of yourself. Come to the Lord’s Table as Jesus told you, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), bringing nothing but your need, and he gives you himself. And let the memory turn outward, as it always did in Israel. Timothy Keller argued in Generous Justice that people who know they were spiritually bankrupt and rescued by sheer grace will be drawn to the poor and the outsider, because they recognise themselves there. The test of a good memory is how you treat the newcomer, the awkward one, the person from the wrong background, this Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outside Christ the Gentiles had lost everything that matters most: the Messiah, God’s people, his promises, hope, and God himself. Paul lists five losses, each deeper than the last, so that the rescue in verse 13 lands with full weight.

1. Separated from Christ. The hope of the Messiah belonged to Israel (Romans 9:5); Gentiles had never been promised a Saviour, so they were not even waiting for one.

2. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. Israel was the people God had formed, ruled and lived among; Gentiles had no citizenship in it and could only watch from outside.

3. Strangers to the covenants of promise. A covenant is a solemn, binding promise that creates a relationship, as wedding vows do. God made covenants with Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), with Israel at Sinai and with David (2 Samuel 7), and promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34), all carrying one promise: “I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” A stranger had no claim on what God had bound himself to give.

4. Having no hope. No sure hope beyond death. The ancient world was full of temples but had no certain promise that death was not the end; a common epitaph ran: “I was not; I was; I am not; I do not care.” Paul speaks elsewhere of those who “grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

5. Without God in the world. Greek atheoi, in a city crowded with gods: they did not know the one true God who had revealed himself by name and kept his promises. Gods everywhere, and God nowhere.

The vocabulary of exclusion. If you have ever stood at the edge of a group and known you did not belong, you know the taste of every word here, and it was once your standing before God. The outsiders were not given advice, a procedure or a probation. They were brought near, in a single movement, by somebody else’s blood, and the five losses are reversed one by one: in Christ, citizens, heirs, holding an inheritance, his dwelling. Every privilege on this list was Christ’s by right as Israel’s Messiah, and he shares every one with those who had none. The answer to the whole catalogue of exclusion is not a policy but a Person.

Can a life be good without hope and without God? Many thoughtful people say yes: we make our own meaning, and it is braver to face the dark without comfort. Bertrand Russell gave that view its most honest form in his 1903 essay “A Free Man’s Worship”: since all we achieve will one day lie buried in the ruins of an indifferent universe, the soul’s dwelling can be safely built only “on the firm foundation of unyielding despair”. There is nobility and honesty in that. But meaning you make for yourself is only as strong as you are. Paul does not say the old life had no joys; he says it had no future and no Father. The gospel does not ask you to pretend. It gives you a hope with a name, and a God who came looking for people who were not even waiting for him.

What about people who have never heard of Christ? Paul does not soften it: outside Christ there is no hope, for there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). But God’s judgment is perfectly fair. No one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ he never heard of; people are judged for their sins against the light they had, the witness of creation and conscience, which all of us have resisted (Romans 1:20; 2:12–16). No one is innocent, and no one will call God unjust. That is why the church sends missionaries: how can anyone believe in one of whom he has never heard (Romans 10:14)? God has people in every tribe and language, and he will gather them (Revelation 5:9). So leave the judgment to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and give, pray and go.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s death, people who were far from God have been brought right into his presence.

But now. Matching “But God” in verse 4: there from death to life, here from distance to nearness. And in Christ Jesus reverses “separated from Christ” (v. 12): the first loss is undone, and with it all the others.

Far off … brought near. Almost technical terms: Jewish writers seem to have used “far off” for the Gentile world and “brought near” for a proselyte, a Gentile admitted into the covenant people. Isaiah had promised “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19), and Peter preached that the promise is “for all who are far off” (Acts 2:39). Paul blows the standard meaning apart: not admitted to an outer court, but within nine verses fellow citizens, family and stones in God’s own temple. The verb is passive: we did not travel the distance; we were carried. And “near” means welcome: your sins no longer stand between you and God, and you may come to him as his child at any hour (Romans 5:1–2).

By the blood of Christ. “Blood” means life given up in death, especially in sacrifice: “the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement” (Leviticus 17:11). The distance was not of miles or race but of sin, which goodwill could never close, and it was never only a Gentile problem: the Jew inside the barrier watched the high priest go into God’s presence for him, once a year, and never without blood (Hebrews 9:7). The wall kept Gentiles out of the court; sin kept everybody out of the holiest place. So blood is not the outsider’s entry fee but the only door, and at the cross the final sacrifice was offered once, and both walked through it together (1:7; Colossians 1:20).

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles now join Israel by becoming Jewish, nor that Jews remain near without Christ: both come near in exactly the same way, through Christ, by the Spirit (v. 18). Nor is the nearness undone when you feel far from God; it rests on an event outside you. A believer may feel a long way off on a Tuesday afternoon and still be, in the only sense this verse means, near.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself is the peace between Jew and Gentile: in his death he tore down the hostility that divided them and made the two one.

For he himself. “He” comes first, with emphasis: peace is not a treaty or a feeling but a Person. “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27): the world manages conflict; Christ gives himself. Micah promised a ruler from Bethlehem of whom it would be said, “he shall be their peace” (Micah 5:5), and Isaiah named the Messiah the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). This peace has two sides, between peoples (vv. 14–15) and with God (v. 16), and the second is the foundation of the first.

Has made us both one. Jew and Gentile, the deepest religious division of the ancient world: not brought closer but made one. Two people each joined to Christ are thereby joined to each other, whatever their cultures say, because the ground at the foot of the cross is level (Galatians 3:28).

The dividing wall of hostility. In the temple a stone balustrade fenced the Court of the Gentiles off from the inner courts, with notices (one found in 1871) warning any foreigner who passed it that he would be responsible for his own death. Paul himself was nearly lynched when accused of bringing a Gentile past it: Trophimus, an Ephesian (Acts 21:28–29). When Paul wrote, it was still standing; it fell with the temple in AD 70. But in God’s eyes it had already fallen at the cross, the day “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). The wall of stone expressed a wall in hearts, mutual contempt and suspicion, and Christ did not lower it; he broke it down.

In his flesh. On a Roman cross, on a particular Friday, not by education or goodwill. The one who hung there took both hostilities, between God and man and between Jew and Gentile, into himself, and did not pass them on (Colossians 1:20–22).

It was expensive. For a Jewish believer it meant eating at a Gentile’s table, setting aside food laws his forebears had died rather than break; for a Gentile, accepting salvation through a nation he thought peculiar. Acts shows how hard it proved (Acts 10; 15), and Peter himself later withdrew from Gentile tables until Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Paul announces an accomplished fact, and spends the rest of the letter urging the church to live inside it.

Was the Son undoing the Father’s work? If the separation between Jew and Gentile was God’s own doing, through the law, circumcision and the rules that kept Israel apart, how can Christ be praised for demolishing it? Because he is finishing it, not undoing it. The separation was like a cast on a broken limb: it preserved the people through whom the Messiah would come, and taught the world that God is holy and access to him no casual matter. The law was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:23–25). When the bone has knitted, the cast comes off, not because it was a mistake, but because it has done its work.

Is it wrong to have separate churches for different languages or cultures? Not in itself. Where people cannot understand one another, a congregation in their own language may be the loving thing, and the apostles took practical care that Greek-speaking widows were not overlooked (Acts 6:1–6). It becomes wrong when the arrangement becomes a wall: when a church is closed in practice to people unlike its members, or Christians pick a church to avoid people of another colour, class or background. Would a stranger from another culture be welcomed and given a full share, including in leadership? Christ has made us one; our churches should look, as far as we can make them, like people who believe it.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
By setting aside the law’s regulations that kept Jew and Gentile apart, Christ created one new people out of the two.

By abolishing … the law of commandments expressed in ordinances. To put out of action. Paul means the law given through Moses as the arrangement under which Israel lived with God, especially the parts that marked Israel off from the nations: circumcision, food laws, sacrifices, the calendar of feasts and Sabbaths, purity rules (Colossians 2:14–17). These were God-given and good (on why Christ could end them, see “Was the Son undoing the Father’s work?” in the note on v. 14), but they also made Jew and Gentile two peoples who could not eat together.

Create in himself. Creation language, as of you personally in v. 10. Committees found institutions every week, but nobody can make a creature. God made the church’s unity, and the most any of us can do is refuse to damage it.

One new man. Not Jews absorbing Gentiles, nor Gentiles absorbing Jews, but a third thing: a new humanity in Christ, in which the old division no longer defines anyone (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). A Jew does not stop being a Jew, nor a Gentile a Gentile (1 Corinthians 7:18–20), and Scripture’s last picture of the redeemed is not a uniform crowd but a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). Neither a melting pot nor a federation keeping a polite distance: the differences remain and simply stop deciding anything. Your background is still yours; it is no longer your standing.

So making peace. Peace was made, with materials, labour and cost: his flesh, a crucifixion, everything he had. So peace in a church is never simply the absence of friction but the keeping of something expensive that somebody else paid for, which is why Paul says to maintain it, not create it (4:3).

What it does not mean. Not that God’s moral will has been abolished. Paul quotes the fifth commandment in this very letter (6:2–3), and chapters 4–5 are full of moral commands. Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). What is abolished is the law as a covenant that divided and condemned, not God’s holy will, and Christians keep that will from a new heart, by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

How do I know which Old Testament commands I should still keep? Read each through Christ, and ask what the New Testament does with it. The sacrifices, priesthood, food laws, feasts and purity rules pointed to him and are fulfilled in him: you keep them by trusting the sacrifice they foreshadowed, not by repeating them (Hebrews 10:1–14; Mark 7:19; Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation are not a code for modern states, though they still teach principles of justice and mercy (Westminster 19.4; 1689 19.4). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in loving God and neighbour, still shows how God’s children live, and the New Testament repeats it again and again (Romans 13:8–10). You obey it not to be saved, but because you have been.

The Sabbath. Here Reformed Christians differ. Many godly brothers keep the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, as the Christian Sabbath set apart for worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), a view that deserves respect; others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Colossians 2:16–17) and still gladly give the Lord’s Day to worship. This commentary takes the second view: Christ is our Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift rather than the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, so no one should bind another’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5).

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists, among them many devoted students of the Bible, hold that Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct promises: the church is a parenthesis, and God will resume his earthly plan for national Israel in a future millennium. Some have taught that the church has simply replaced Israel, leaving the Jewish people no further place in God’s purposes. Covenant theology holds that there is one people of God throughout history, the one olive tree of Romans 11, now including believing Jews and Gentiles together, and that the promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his church. This commentary’s view: one people of God in Christ, as “one new man” and “one body” say. Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, not planted beside it (Romans 11:17). But God has not finished with the Jewish people: Paul expects many Jews to come to faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26), and they will come into the same one body, not a separate one.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the cross Christ brought Jew and Gentile together to God in one body, and put to death the hostility that stood in the way.

Reconcile. To turn enemies into friends by removing the cause of the hostility: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The trouble was never that God was distant and we were confused. There was hostility, which is why the remedy had to be a death and not an explanation.

Us both to God. The logic of the whole passage. Jew and Gentile could not be at peace with each other while both were at war with God. Call our quarrel with God the vertical problem, and our quarrels with one another the horizontal one: the vertical lies beneath the horizontal. When both are reconciled to God through the same cross, they find themselves standing side by side. Purely social attempts at unity cannot last, because they leave things with God unmended.

Whose hostility? Ours to God is real (Romans 8:7; Colossians 1:21), but we were also children of wrath (v. 3), under God’s just opposition. Reconciliation deals with both. At the cross God’s wrath against sin was borne by Christ as our substitute (Romans 5:9–10; 2 Corinthians 5:21), removing the cause of enmity on God’s side; through the gospel our hearts are won, removing it on ours.

In one body. Probably both Christ’s body on the cross (Colossians 1:22) and the church (1:23; 4:4): one body died, so that one body might live. You are not saved privately and later invited to consider joining a church. The act that brings you to God sets you down among people you did not choose, and who did not choose you.

Killing the hostility. Not soothed or managed but put to death, because hostility has a life of its own, grows when fed and outlives the people who started it. Human hostility usually kills people. They took Christ out and killed him, and in being killed, he killed the thing that was killing everybody: hostility did its absolute worst and was destroyed by the very thing it did. Christ did not kill his enemies; he died for them.

What it does not mean. Not that the cross changed God from hating to loving: God’s love sent Christ (Romans 5:8), and God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfied his own justice. Nor is everyone reconciled automatically: reconciliation is received through faith, which is why the next verse speaks of preaching (v. 17; 2 Corinthians 5:20).

In everyday life. If you are at odds with a fellow believer, the order is not negotiable: vertical first. Go to the cross and look at what was forgiven you there, as the servant forgiven ten thousand talents should have done before collecting a hundred denarii (Matthew 18:23–35).

Why could God not simply forgive, without a cross? Because real forgiveness always costs the one who forgives. Forgive the man who wrecked your car, and the damage does not vanish: you pay for it instead of him. Sin against God is real damage, to his honour, his world and his creatures, and a holy Judge cannot pretend it never happened (Proverbs 17:15). At the cross God paid for it himself, in his Son, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The cross is not God being paid off by someone else; it is God bearing the cost of his own forgiveness.

Must I be reconciled with a believer who wronged me and will not admit it? You must forgive, and you must be willing; but full reconciliation takes two. Forgiving means letting go of revenge and handing the account to God (Romans 12:19; Mark 11:25), and that you can do alone, today. Reconciliation means restored trust, and that needs repentance on the other side (Luke 17:3). So do what lies with you: pray for him, refuse to speak against him, and go to him privately; if he will not listen, follow the steps Jesus gave (Matthew 18:15–17). You are to live at peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), and not further. Where there has been abuse, forgiveness never means returning to danger. Get safe, tell the elders, and report any crime to the police. Trust, once broken, is rebuilt slowly, by evidence of real change.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ announces peace to outsiders and insiders alike, and through him both now come freely to the Father by the same Spirit.

He came and preached peace. Paul is echoing Isaiah: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (Isaiah 52:7), and “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19). Jesus never preached in Ephesus; Paul means chiefly the risen Christ, preaching through his messengers by his Spirit (Romans 10:14–15). When the gospel is faithfully preached, even by somebody nervous and doing it badly, Christ himself is preaching. His first words to his gathered disciples after rising were, “Peace be with you” (John 20:19–21).

Far off and near. Both needed it equally: nearness was not peace. Those raised in the church, fluent in its songs, need it preached on exactly the same terms.

Access. Being ushered into a king’s presence by someone with the standing to bring you. Under the old covenant Gentiles could go no further than the outer court, only priests entered the holy place, and only the high priest the Most Holy Place, once a year (Hebrews 9:7). Now every believer can come straight to God, at any time, with confidence (3:12; Hebrews 10:19–22). The torn curtain (Mark 15:38) meant the same as the broken wall.

In one Spirit. The Spirit makes the access real today. God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6), so the very cry of “Father” in your prayers is the Spirit at work. And it is one Spirit: not a Jewish route and a Gentile route, but the same welcome for both (1 Corinthians 12:13).

The Trinity. Through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father, and the goal of access is family. Whenever a believer prays, however haltingly, the Father is approached through the Son who opened the way, by the Spirit who carries the prayer from within (Romans 8:26–27). The Son holds open the door into the throne room of heaven, and the King has made his throne a place where children are expected.

What it does not mean. Not that every religion or sincere seeker has access to God: access is “through him”, through Christ alone (John 14:6). Nor that we need no mediator: we need exactly one, and we have him (1 Timothy 2:5). No priest, saint or ritual stands between the believer and the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers now belong fully to God’s people and God’s family, built on the apostles’ teaching, with Christ as the stone that holds it all true.

So then. Paul gathers up verses 11–18 and reverses the losses of verse 12 in three pictures: a city, a family, a temple. The movement is from the edge to the centre, from outside to home.

No longer strangers and aliens. A stranger passes through; an alien lived in the city as second-class. The Gentiles had been both. Now neither.

Fellow citizens with the saints. Roman citizenship was the most prized status in the empire. The officer who nearly flogged Paul had bought his for a large sum; Paul replied, “But I am a citizen by birth” (Acts 22:25–29). These Gentiles are full and equal citizens of a commonwealth beside which Rome is a temporary local arrangement, and they did not buy it; they were born into it (Philippians 3:20). And this exposes a quiet idol: many of us draw our worth from some lesser citizenship, a nation, a class, a profession, a church tradition, the circle we were admitted to. None is wrong, but none can carry the weight of who you are, and each tempts you to look down on outsiders. The citizen of heaven has nothing left to prove.

Members of the household of God. Warmer still: not a guest on probation, but family, with a Father who provides, brothers and sisters in every nation, and a home that cannot be taken away (1 Timothy 3:15).

Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Now the picture becomes a building, temple language on purpose, and a foundation is laid once. The prophets here are most likely New Testament prophets (3:5; 4:11), and they are the foundation in their teaching: the revelation of Christ they received and passed on, now preserved in the New Testament. Calvin said the foundation is the doctrine they preached; move away from it and the building falls. So sola Scriptura, Scripture alone as the final authority over all the church believes and does, is not a preference but a structural necessity. A church that leaves apostolic teaching does not build higher; it builds on sand.

The cornerstone. Most likely the foundation cornerstone, laid first, from which every other stone took its line and level (see “Uncertain wording” below). So an error there is never small: a wall built off a crooked corner is wrong all the way up, more obviously the higher it rises. Churches drift that way, quietly taking their line from a founder’s personality, the culture’s instincts or whoever gives most. Isaiah promised a precious cornerstone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16); “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), and Jesus claimed it for himself (Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4–7). The builders said, “This one does not fit.” God said, “This one holds everything together.”

What it does not mean. Not that the apostles and prophets matter more than Christ: the foundation is their witness to him, and he is the stone that fixes it. Nor that new apostles and prophets with the same foundational authority continue today (see the box “Where Christians differ: the continuation of prophecy” at the end of this note).

If prophecy has ceased, does God still speak to me personally? Yes: every time you open the Bible. Scripture is not God’s old voice, now silent, but his living voice, and the Spirit uses it to comfort, warn and direct you personally (Hebrews 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). He also guides by his providence and through wise believers, and may bring a verse or a person to mind at the right moment: a kindness, but not new revelation. Test every impression by Scripture, weigh it with others, and never say that God told you something as though it bound anyone else (Westminster Confession 1.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). In his word you have everything you need for faith and life. Open the book: he is speaking.

Where Christians differ: the continuation of prophecy. Continuationists hold that the gift of prophecy continues, often as a lesser, fallible gift distinct from the foundational prophets of this verse; they point to Paul’s urging to desire the gift (1 Corinthians 14:1) and to Joel’s promise for the last days (Acts 2:17), and many faithful believers and churches hold this view with love for Scripture. Cessationists hold that apostles and prophets belonged to the foundation-laying period and ceased with it, and that God now speaks through the completed Scriptures. This commentary’s view: cessationist, held charitably. If the apostles and prophets are the foundation, they cannot also be the walls. And whatever view one takes, no claimed word today may add to or stand alongside the apostolic foundation.

Uncertain wording. “Cornerstone” (akrogōniaios) is a rare word. Most take it, with the ESV, as the foundation stone at the corner, which fits Isaiah 28:16 (“laid as a foundation”) and the picture of a building rising from it (v. 21); some take it as the capstone at the top, which completes the structure. Either way all depends on Christ; the foundation stone is more likely. “Prophets” could be Israel’s prophets, but the order “apostles and prophets” and the parallel in 3:5 point to Christian prophets.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the whole church, fitted together stone by stone, is growing into a holy temple for the Lord.

In whom. Christ is not only the first stone of the temple; he is the temple. “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” he said, of his body (John 2:19–21). The place where God meets sinners is now the risen Son, and the church is a holy temple only because it is built in him, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Being joined together. A builder’s word (again in 4:16): stones fitted so that each bears on the next. Each believer is a living stone (1 Peter 2:5), and God shapes us to fit with others, often through the friction of living with very different people. The verb says this is being done to us, and is still going on: no stone chose its neighbours, which is worth remembering when the people beside you are not the ones you would have picked. They did not pick you either. Neither of you is the mason.

Grows. Buildings do not grow; Paul mixes the pictures on purpose. The building gives the church its solidity: God is here. The body gives it life: still becoming what it is meant to be (4:15–16). Lose the growing, and you have a congregation kept open like a heritage site, where nothing happens. Lose the building, and you get warmth without shape, a movement that glows for five years and finds it has no foundation.

A holy temple. The word means the inner sanctuary. Beside the vast temple of Artemis (see the introduction), the true temple is not marble but people, and in place of the temple whose wall kept Gentiles out (v. 14), Gentiles are now part of the building (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16). It is holy because the Lord is in it and it belongs to him. That should sober us as well as comfort us (Leviticus 10:1–3): gossip, division and sin quietly tolerated in a congregation are not bad manners but the defiling of God’s house, which is why Paul warns that God will destroy anyone who destroys his temple (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Unfinished, and not ashamed of it. The building grows into a holy temple; it has not arrived. So when your church disappoints you, and it will, you are not looking at a ruin but standing on a building site. The dust and half-built walls are evidence not that the project has failed but that it is still going on, and that the Builder has not left.

In everyday life. Is anyone in your church bearing weight on you, so that your absence would be a real problem, not just an empty seat? And whose weight are you carrying? If the honest answer to both is nobody, you are living like a stone leaning against the wall, when Christ has already set you in it. The difference is invisible from the road and total in a storm. If that is because you are ill, new or lonely rather than unwilling, it is no failure: tell one person, and let the Mason fit you in.

Uncertain wording. The Greek for “the whole structure” lacks “the”, and strictly could mean “every building”, as if each congregation were a separate one; some manuscripts add “the”. Since Paul speaks throughout of one body and one temple, “the whole structure” is almost certainly right.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You too, once outsiders, are being built together with all God’s people into the home where God himself lives by his Spirit.

In him you also. The emphasis falls on “you also”: you who were far off, without God (v. 12), are now part of his dwelling. The outsiders have become the house, and each conversion adds a stone.

A dwelling place for God. The God who fills all things (1:23) has always meant to live among his people, from Eden (Genesis 3:8) onward. After sin shattered that, he told Israel, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8), and his glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Ezekiel watched the glory leave the idolatrous temple (Ezekiel 10–11), and was promised its return (Ezekiel 43:1–5). It returned in a form no one expected: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”, literally pitched his tent among us, “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). At Pentecost the Spirit came down not on a temple but on people (Acts 2:3). One day the whole new creation will be his home: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The gathered church is that story’s present chapter.

By the Spirit. God lives in the church not symbolically but really, by the Holy Spirit. When believers gather, he is not merely remembered; he is present, hearing their prayers, speaking through his word and binding them together, so that even an outsider may sense that God is really among them (1 Corinthians 14:25; Matthew 18:20).

He is not visiting. When a handful of forgiven sinners meet in his name, the God of the burning bush and the filled temple is not visiting. He lives there. He makes his home with the unworthy, and he will never move out.

The address. Many look for God’s presence in a place, a view or a quality of silence, and the hunger is not silly. But Paul’s address is a people: the awkward ones near you on Sunday, the one who talks too long afterwards, the family whose children never sit still. Together they are not the setting where you might meet God but the place where he has chosen to live. The chapter opened with corpses and ends with the same people as the house God lives in: that is the distance grace covers, in twenty-two verses.

In the flow. Chapter 3 prays for this temple, and chapter 4 urges the church to keep the unity of this one building (4:1–6): chapters 1–3 tell the church what God has made it, and chapters 4–6 how to live as what it already is.

2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with God’s mighty power raising Christ from the dead and seating him far above every power (1:19–23). Chapter 2 shows that same power at work on people: first on sinners who were spiritually dead, then on two peoples who had been enemies for centuries.

The message. You were dead and far off, and God, out of sheer mercy, has made you alive and brought you home. Salvation is not our climb towards God but his rescue of people who could not move: a resurrection given freely, by grace through faith, and a reconciliation bought by Christ’s blood, which joins Jew and Gentile into one new people in whom God himself now lives.

Why it was said. Most of the readers were Gentiles who had grown up among the gods and temples of Ephesus (see the introduction), now sharing a church with Jewish believers whose people had kept theirs at a distance. Both needed to hear that neither had anything to boast of, and that neither was a guest in the other’s house.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul tells the gospel twice. First as resurrection (vv. 1–10): verses 1–3 are the grave, dead in sin, following the world, the devil and the flesh, and by nature under wrath; then come two words, “But God”, and verses 4–7 are the rising, made alive, raised and seated with Christ, to display his kindness for ever; verses 8–10 sum it up: saved by grace through faith, not by works, yet created for good works. Then as reconciliation (vv. 11–22): remember how far off you stood, without Christ, hope or God (vv. 11–12); “But now” you have been brought near by his blood (v. 13); Christ is our peace, who broke down the wall, made one new man and reconciled both to God through the cross (vv. 14–18); so you are citizens, family and a temple for God (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. Every step happens with Christ or in Christ. His rising is our new life, his seat is our seat, his flesh broke down the wall, his blood brought us near, and he himself is the cornerstone of the house. The chapter opens with corpses and closes with the same people as the dwelling place of God. Only such a Saviour could cover that distance, and he covered it for people who were not even looking for him.

For us. No one is too dead for God to raise, and no one in Christ is a second-class member of his household. Remember what you were, so that grace stays astonishing; and look at the believer you find hardest to love as a stone set beside you in the same temple.

keyVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ
keyVerse.note: Two words turn the whole chapter.
