Everything before “But God” is a death we could not undo; everything after it is God acting, out of mercy and love, for people who could do nothing, and verse 13 tells the same story again for outsiders with its own “But now”. Salvation is not our climb towards God but his raising of the dead, and it happens in one place: together with Christ.

2.reflection:
Paul describes life without Christ as death, not sickness (vv. 1–3). How does that change the way you think about your own conversion, and about the people you long to see come to Christ?

Verses 8–9 leave no room for boasting. In what quiet ways do Christians still find something to boast about, and how does the gospel of grace answer each one?

Paul tells the Gentile believers to remember what they once were (vv. 11–12). Why should remembering our past outside Christ make us kinder to outsiders, and who might feel on the outside of your church today?

Christ has broken down the wall of hostility and made one new people, a household and a temple for God (vv. 14–22). What walls of background, class, culture or temperament still stand between believers you know, and what would it look like this month to live as one household?

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s long-hidden plan is that Gentiles share everything with Israel in Christ, and Paul’s whole life, chains included, serves it. Paul begins to pray (v. 1), but first explains the grace entrusted to him and the mystery revealed to him (vv. 2–5): the Gentiles are fellow heirs, one body and sharers in the promise (v. 6). Grace made the least of the saints its preacher (vv. 7–9), so that through the church God’s many-coloured wisdom is shown to the heavenly powers (v. 10), as he purposed from eternity, giving us bold access to him (vv. 11–12). So Paul’s sufferings are no reason to lose heart; they are the readers’ glory (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The mystery hidden and revealed

In Paul a mystery (mystērion) is a secret kept in God and now disclosed in the gospel (see the note on vv. 2–3). The inclusion of the Gentiles was not absent from the Old Testament: it was there in the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3) and in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). What waited for Christ was its full disclosure (see the note on vv. 4–5).

The whole Bible works this way: first the outline, then the real thing, as a sketch comes before the finished painting. The two Testaments are one message unfolding. So reading the Old Testament with Christ in view is not forcing something onto it. It is following where it was already going.

Paul’s description of himself as “the very least of all the saints” (v. 8) shows what grace does to a person (see the note on vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus knew plenty of riches that could be counted: the wealth of Artemis’ temple, gods who could be appeased, secrets that could be bought by initiation. Paul announces something of another kind, “the unsearchable riches of Christ” (see the note on vv. 7–8).

Now: Paul writes this from a Roman cell and tells the church not to lose heart over his sufferings (v. 13). God still carries his glorious gospel in plain containers: a persecuted church, a small congregation the world ignores. Paul calls this “treasure in jars of clay” (2 Corinthians 4:7): something priceless kept in a cheap pot, so that nobody mistakes the pot for the treasure. Such a church may look weak, yet it is where the powers are watching God’s wisdom on display.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a prisoner because he brought the gospel to the Gentiles, begins to pray for them. He breaks off mid-sentence to explain his calling (vv. 2–13) and resumes in verse 14 with the same words.

For this reason. Because of chapter 2: Gentiles have been brought near and are being built into God’s temple (2:19–22).

I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus. The emphatic “I, Paul” puts his own authority and story on the line (2 Corinthians 10:1; Galatians 5:2). Humanly, Paul was a prisoner of Rome, chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 30). But he does not write “a prisoner of Nero”. Rome believes it is holding him; Paul knows that Christ put him there, so that the gospel would spread (Philippians 1:12–14).

On behalf of you Gentiles. This is more literal than it looks. A mob seized Paul in the Jerusalem temple, shouting that he had brought Greeks past the barrier, because they had seen him in the city with Trophimus the Ephesian (Acts 21:27–29). He had not. But in a deeper sense the charge was true: Paul had insisted that the wall was down (2:14). The doctrine of chapter 2 cost him his freedom, and he is explaining it to the very people it was about.

Lord of the cell. Christ Jesus is Lord even over a Roman cell, and turns his servant’s prison into a pulpit for the nations. He himself was once bound and led away to die, so that Gentiles might go free.

In everyday life. Listen to how you describe your situation: “I am stuck here because of” the employer, the diagnosis, the person. Paul had every right to that sentence and never used it. He does not call the chains good; he says whose they are. You are not the prisoner of your situation, but a servant of Christ placed where he wants you.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s calling is a trust of God’s grace, given to him for the Gentiles’ sake, and its message was revealed to him, not worked out by him.

Assuming that you have heard. Or “surely you have heard”: polite, not real doubt. The letter probably went to several churches (see the introduction), and some readers knew Paul only by reputation.

The stewardship of God’s grace. “Stewardship” (oikonomia) is the running of a household, the word used of God’s own plan in 1:10. A steward was often a trusted slave who held the keys, kept the accounts and gave the household its food (Luke 12:42). Nothing in his hands was his, and everything in them was there to be given out; a steward who hoarded his master’s grain was not careful but unfaithful. Paul is the steward of grace, not its owner (1 Corinthians 4:1–2), and what he hands out is God’s own wealth, which never runs low.

Given to me for you. His calling as apostle to the Gentiles (v. 8; Romans 15:15–16) arrived addressed to somebody else: not for his honour, but for their benefit.

The mystery … made known to me by revelation. In English a mystery is a puzzle that cannot be solved. In Paul it is almost the opposite: a secret of God, hidden until he chose to reveal it, and now openly made known (Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26). Paul did not work it out; all his training under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3) never produced it. It was disclosed on a road, by the one he was travelling to persecute (Galatians 1:11–12), and it reached him first not as a doctrine but as a Person: “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting” (Acts 26:15). If it had to be deduced, only the clever would have it. Because it is revealed, it belongs to anyone willing to receive it.

In everyday life. Take an honest inventory: money, skills, a spare room, years of experience, the gospel itself. Do not only ask, “Am I using this wisely?” A careful man can say yes and still keep it all for himself. Ask: “Who was this given to me for?”
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul has already written in this letter lets any reader see that he understands the mystery of Christ. His authority is not a claim to be taken on trust; it can be tested by reading.

As I have written briefly. Paul means this very letter, especially 1:9–10 and 2:11–22, not an earlier, lost one. “When you read” means read aloud: letters were read to the congregation, again and again (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).

My insight into the mystery of Christ. “Insight” (synesis) is the ability to put things together: Paul’s message hangs together, and it unlocks the Old Testament promises. “Mystery” echoes Daniel, where the God in heaven reveals what no wise man could tell (Daniel 2:27–28). The readers also knew the word from the mystery cults of their cities, whose members swore never to tell outsiders their secret rites. Paul’s mystery is the opposite: announced to all nations, written down and read aloud. And the secret is Christ himself, and what God has done in him, including the joining of Jew and Gentile in one body (v. 6). What Paul received by revelation, we receive by reading, and the Spirit who gave it is glad to open it to us.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the Old Testament glimpsed, God has now revealed plainly, by his Spirit, to the apostles and prophets. The contrast is not between ignorance and knowledge, but between a promise seen from far off and its full disclosure.

Not made known as it has now been revealed. “Sons of men” means human beings, and “as” matters: not unknown, but not known as it is now. The Old Testament promised blessing to the nations (Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 49:6). What was not clear was how: that Gentiles would come in not by becoming Jews, through circumcision and the law, but directly in Christ, as full and equal members of one body.

To his holy apostles and prophets. “Holy” means set apart for this task, not sinless. These are New Testament prophets, named after the apostles (2:20; 4:11). Together they are the church’s foundation (2:20), because they received the mystery from the Spirit, the revealer, and passed it on (1 Corinthians 2:10–13; John 16:13).

Stand with the men who did not get to see it. Peter says the prophets “searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10–11). Isaiah writes of a man pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, then goes back over his own page trying to work out whose face he has described. “It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you” (1 Peter 1:12; compare Matthew 13:16–17). On an ordinary morning, with an open Bible, you know whose face it was. That is no reason for pride, but it is a reason to stop handling your Bible as a duty and start handling it as the answer to somebody else’s lifelong question, put into your hands.

When someone says “God told me”, is that the same thing? Not in the sense of this verse. The apostles and prophets received revelation binding on the whole church, written down once for all as Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). God still guides his people by his word, by the Spirit opening our eyes to it, by the counsel of others and by his providence, and a verse may come home to you with great force; that is the Spirit at work. But an impression, however strong, is not a new word from God and never carries Scripture’s authority (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). So test every “God told me”, your own included, by the Bible. If it adds to Scripture or contradicts it, set it aside; if it agrees, the authority lies in Scripture, not in the impression.

Why did God wait so long? He was not idle. The centuries of promise, sacrifice and law were a schoolroom, teaching what kind of Saviour was needed (Galatians 3:24), and Christ came in the fullness of time, not late (Galatians 4:4). Nor were those generations left out. Abraham believed the promise and it was counted to him as righteousness (Romans 4:3), and the Old Testament saints died in faith, greeting from afar what we now see (Hebrews 11:13): saved by the same Christ, looked for in advance.

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Many Christians in charismatic and Pentecostal churches believe gifts such as prophecy continue, and most agree that no such word carries Scripture’s authority. This commentary’s view: revelation of this foundational kind ended with the apostles and prophets, and we gladly honour brothers and sisters who differ.

Where Christians differ: was the church entirely hidden? Classic dispensationalists, who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras with separate plans for Israel and the church, teach that the church was wholly unknown in the Old Testament, a parenthesis in God’s programme for Israel, which will resume after the church is removed. Covenant theology, which reads the Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace, holds that the church fulfils God’s promises to Abraham and the prophets, now revealed far more clearly. Paul’s “as” implies that something was known before, and elsewhere he shows that the Gentiles’ inclusion fulfils the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:8, 29) and the prophets (Romans 15:8–12). This commentary’s view: the church is the fulfilment of God’s one plan, partly foreseen and now fully revealed. Dispensationalist believers love Christ and his word; this is a disagreement among brothers about how the Bible’s story fits together, not about the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secret, now told, is that believing Gentiles share everything with believing Jews in Christ: the inheritance, the body and the promise. They are not guests on Israel’s estate but full members of one family, brought in through the gospel.

Fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise. Three Greek compounds beginning with syn (together); the middle one appears nowhere in surviving Greek before this letter, a man reaching for a word that does not exist because the thing he describes had never existed either. Co-heirs: Gentiles inherit everything God promised Abraham and his descendants (1:11, 14, 18; Galatians 3:29), not as tenants, but equally. Co-bodied, the coined word (syssōma): not two bodies side by side, but one body with one head, Christ (2:16; 4:4); the Gentile believer belongs to the same body as you, as your hand and your foot are both you. Co-sharers of God’s promise to Abraham and his offspring, summed up in the gift of the Spirit (1:13; Galatians 3:14) and God’s pledge to be their God.

Through the gospel. The way in is the good news believed, not ancestry, circumcision or law-keeping, which is why Paul fought so hard against those who wanted Gentiles circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5; 5:2–6).

Made one where his body was broken. All of it is in Christ Jesus, the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16): the whole inheritance is his, and all who are joined to him by faith inherit it with him, his standing with the Father, his future (Galatians 3:26–29). He reconciled Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross (2:16): the one body of the church was made where his own body was broken for both. No Gentile earns his way in, and no Jew keeps his place by ancestry; both stand in the one Son.

Second-class, without anyone saying so. Nobody writes second-class membership into a church constitution. It grows quietly, in who gets treated as family and who as a guest: the convert with a visible past whom people are glad to see and slow to trust, the newcomer who has not learned the vocabulary, the one who arrives with noisy children. None is told they are lesser; they are simply never quite folded in. But fellow heir means they will inherit exactly what you inherit: not less, not later, not on conditions. The way you treat them this week is either a rehearsal for the age to come or a contradiction of it.

What it does not mean. Not that Gentiles replace Jews: fellow heirs share; they do not take over. Nor is ethnic identity erased (see 2:14). The point is equal standing before God and equal belonging in his family.

Does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Yes. God has not rejected the people he foreknew, and his gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:1–2, 29). But that purpose is not a separate road to salvation. God’s people are one olive tree, Israel, with Gentile believers grafted in as wild branches: one tree, one way in, faith in Jesus the Messiah (Romans 11:17–24; John 14:6). Many Reformed Christians, reading Romans 11:25–26, expect a great turning of Israel to Christ before the end, natural branches grafted back into their own tree; others read “all Israel” there as the full number of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. On either reading, a Jew is saved exactly as a Gentile is, by faith in the Messiah. So love your Jewish neighbours, pray for them, and share the gospel with them gladly. It came to them first (Romans 1:16), and the promises you now share were spoken first to their fathers.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s ministry is grace from first to last: God’s power made the least of all the saints a servant who announces Christ’s inexhaustible riches to the Gentiles.

I was made a minister … by the working of his power. “Minister” is servant (diakonos, from which deacon comes), a word used of a waiter at table, and “I was made” means God appointed him; he did not apply. The power is that of 1:19–20, which raised Christ from the dead. It took resurrection power to turn Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle (Acts 9:1–22), and it takes the same power to sustain him (Colossians 1:29).

Though I am the very least of all the saints. Paul bends the language: “leaster”, less than the least. It is not false modesty. “Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison” (Acts 8:3). Picture a door opening at the wrong hour, a husband or a wife dragged out past the neighbours. Decades on, an apostle with churches across the empire, this is what he still counts himself: the memory never left him, and it never disqualified him. His self-description moves: least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9, about AD 55), least of all the saints (here, about AD 61), foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15, about AD 63). The older he grew in grace, the lower he saw himself. And what had made him that man was not unbelief but religion: zeal for God, blameless by the law’s standard (Philippians 3:5–6). Religion used to earn God’s favour had made him cruel. Grace rescues the respectable as surely as the rebel.

This grace was given. Paul cannot speak of his ministry without speaking of grace (1 Corinthians 15:10). He never forgets what he was, and never doubts what he has been given. The grace was for one task: to bring the Gentiles good news (euangelisasthai, the verb behind evangelise).

The unsearchable riches of Christ. Paul has spoken of the riches of grace (1:7; 2:7) and of glory (1:18); now of Christ himself. “Unsearchable” (anexichniaston) means beyond tracing out, like a path through a forest whose tracks simply stop (Romans 11:33). These riches are not an asset Christ hands out at arm’s length; they are him: forgiveness, adoption, wisdom, the Spirit, hope, and deepest of all, “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8; Colossians 2:3). Here is a Saviour whose wealth does not shrink when it is shared, who gives himself away to the unworthy without coming to the end of what he is. And he handed these riches, for preaching, to a man who had dragged women out of their houses for believing in him.

In everyday life. Is there something in your past that you assume has ruled you out? When someone says, “God uses ordinary people”, do you add silently, “but not people who have done what I did”? Put it beside what Paul did. He is not the exception; he is the pattern. Your past does not disqualify you from serving him; only pride does.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s task is to show everyone how God is carrying out the plan he kept hidden in himself from eternity: the Creator’s plan for all he made.

To bring to light for everyone. God’s plan is public. And light does not make what it shows. Switch on a lamp in a dark room and nothing is created: the furniture was there all along, and you had been barking your shins on it. God’s plan stood complete before the world was made; at Christ’s coming the light went on. Faith does not make these things true; it opens your eyes to the room you were already standing in.

The plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God. “Plan” is oikonomia again (v. 2; 1:10). The church, one new humanity of Jew and Gentile, is not an emergency measure but what God was working towards from the beginning (1:4, 9–11). It was hidden not in the world but in the one who stands behind the world, so no searching could find it: “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:7–8).

Who created all things. The God who saves is the God who made everything. Redemption is not a repair job on a project that went wrong, but the Creator carrying through his first purpose, “to unite all things in Christ” (1:10). The new creation (2:10, 15) is what the first creation was always for.

The light has a face. What switched the lamp on was a Person. The God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). All things were made through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16). To be shown the plan is to be shown him.

Nothing wasted? If God is running his household, nothing in it is wasted: easy to write, hard to believe on a Thursday afternoon, when you can point to years in a job that led nowhere, or a decade lost to illness or a broken marriage. Paul does not deny the experience; he names who is doing the managing. Try this on paper tonight. Trace how you came to hear the gospel. Who told you? How did you come to be in that room, that school, that ward, that friendship? Follow it back four or five links, and you will find a chain of things that looked accidental, arranged by people who had no idea what they were doing. Someone moved house. Someone fell ill. Someone invited the wrong person by mistake. That is God running his household. If he managed all that without once consulting you, the years you have written off are far more likely to be rooms in the same house than evidence against it.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fellowship” (koinōnia) instead of “plan” (oikonomia), and add “by Jesus Christ” after “created all things”. This commentary’s view: “plan” is original, supported by the earliest manuscripts, and “by Jesus Christ” is a later expansion: biblical truth (Colossians 1:16), but not part of this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s purpose is that the church, a reconciled people of every kind, should show his many-coloured wisdom to the spiritual powers of the universe. This is why Paul preaches (vv. 8–9), and why the mystery was revealed at all.

Through the church. Not through the stars or the great events of history, but through ordinary people gathered in Christ.

The manifold wisdom of God. “Manifold” (polypoikilos), found only here in the New Testament, means many-coloured, a word used of embroidered cloth or a meadow of flowers. God’s wisdom shows in the variety of people he gathers: Jew and Gentile, slave and free, rich and poor, every culture, joined in one body without losing their variety, where no diplomacy had ever dissolved the old division. A church of people who are all alike shows less of it.

To the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. The audience is spiritual beings, angelic and demonic (1:21; 6:12), prominent in this letter perhaps because Ephesus was gripped by fear of named powers (Acts 19:19). Good angels watch with wonder; evil powers watch their defeat.

Crowned on a cross. The wisdom shows in the method: a crucified Messiah as cornerstone, a persecutor as chief missionary, forgiven sinners as the display of his glory (1 Corinthians 1:27–28). The cross looked like Christ’s defeat, and God made it the place where he was crowned King. How are the powers defeated, when evil is plainly still at work? At the cross Christ cancelled the record of debt that gave the accuser his case against us, put the powers to open shame, and broke the fear in which they held us (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15). Their end is fixed (Revelation 20:10), though not yet carried out, and the church is the public announcement of that victory. Every time former strangers call the same God Father, God is saying to every power in the universe, look what my wisdom has done.

The back of the cloth. From the back, embroidery is a mess: knots, loose ends, colours stopping dead in the middle of nowhere. Turn it over, and every thread was going somewhere. From where you sit, the church looks like a rota that keeps failing, two families not speaking, a treasurer worried about the roof, and a man in the third row you privately gave up on. You are looking at the back of the cloth. Paul does not say the knots are imaginary. He says the front faces somewhere else: God sees the finished picture, and he is showing it to the powers of heaven.

What the powers are watching. Not the moments anyone photographs. Two members quietly reconciling after eighteen months of coldness. A widow driven to the hospital by someone who does not much like her. Six people at a prayer meeting on a wet Tuesday. A former enemy passing the bread to a former enemy. That is the embroidery, and it tells the powers that the crucified one has won. It is also why this letter cares so much about church unity (4:1–16): not as good manners, but because the same powers are watching (6:12). The relationship in the church you have decided is not worth the effort is not a distraction from the display. It is the display.

What it does not mean. Not that the church preaches to angels, or should try to address or command spiritual powers. It makes God’s wisdom known simply by being a reconciled people. Nor does “wisdom” mean cleverness: it is God’s skill in achieving his good purposes, above all through the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

Do angels not already know everything about God? No. Angels are wise and holy, but they are creatures, and they learn as creatures do. They do not know the day of Christ’s return (Matthew 24:36), and they long to look into the things of the gospel (1 Peter 1:12). They shouted for joy at creation (Job 38:7), but they had never seen a crucified Lord gathering former enemies into one family. Heaven is not bored by your congregation on an ordinary Sunday. It is studying it.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this was God’s plan from eternity, carried out in Christ, and in him we may come to God freely and confidently, sure of a welcome.

The eternal purpose. Literally the purpose of the ages. The church is not plan B: God planned it before time (1:4, 11) and carried it out in Christ’s life, death, resurrection and ascension.

In whom we have boldness. Paul’s readers had come out of a world of spiritual dread, of gods unpredictable and unapproachable, managed by ritual. “Boldness” (parrēsia) was the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly, in his own words, without first getting permission. Listen to the praying of someone who does not believe he has that right. It is hedged. “If it be your will” comes early, not as submission but as insurance, so that nothing has quite been asked and nothing can be refused. The requests stay small. After a bad week the praying stops, as if it would be decent to stay away until things improve. Every one of those instincts belongs to a servant on probation, and Paul says that is not what you are. The grief may come out as grief, and the anger where there is anger, because a son does not brief his father the way a petitioner briefs an official.

And access with confidence. Access (prosagōgē) is entry into the king’s presence, granted by one with the standing to bring you in, and your introducer is Christ himself (2:18). Those who were far off (2:12–13) can now come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19–22). Feel what that overcomes: Isaiah, seeing the holy Lord, cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:3–5), and a careless approach to the holy place meant death (Leviticus 16:2). And the tense is present: we have it now, as did the man in chains who wrote it.

Through our faith in him. You do not come saying, “I have had a good week, so hear me”, but “Jesus died and rose for me, so hear me.” The first confidence rises and falls with you; the second stands as firm as he does (Hebrews 10:19–21).

What it does not mean. Not casualness or presumption. What we draw near to is a throne (Hebrews 4:16; 12:28), so we come with reverence and awe, but without fear of rejection, as children to a father.

In everyday life. Think of the thing you have not said to God because it seemed too small, too angry or too late. In Christ there is no wrong size and no wrong hour. The door you are hesitating at is already open.

Uncertain wording. “Through our faith in him” renders a short Greek phrase, literally “through the faith of him”, which some scholars read as “through his faithfulness”, Christ’s own. This commentary’s view: the usual translation, faith in him, best fits Paul’s usage in Ephesians, where faith is the believer’s trust in Christ (1:15; 2:8). Either way, our confidence rests on Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s sufferings are no sign that the gospel is failing; they are for his readers’ honour, so they must not lose heart. The digression ends where it began, with his chains (v. 1), and the man in the cell is worried about the morale of the people who are free.

Not to lose heart. To grow weary, lose your nerve, give up (enkakein). If the apostle of this gospel is in prison, perhaps the gospel is failing. That reasoning still empties pews, and what makes people give up is very often not their own suffering but somebody else’s. A respected pastor is diagnosed at fifty-two. A couple who prayed for years for a child end up burying one. A missionary family comes home broken. Nobody announces a change of belief; it happens quietly, in the gap between what was preached and what was watched. Paul knows the Ephesians are doing that arithmetic about him, and he interrupts it.

Suffering for you. Paul is in prison because he took the gospel to the Gentiles (Acts 21:28–29). But the words “for you” were not first his: “This is my body, which is for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24). His cell shows a servant’s life taking the shape of his Lord’s. Christ saved us not by avoiding pain but by entering it, and the Father exalted him because he humbled himself (Philippians 2:8–9). That is the way of our God: he wins by losing, gives life through death, and makes the hardships of his servants serve the joy of his people.

Which is your glory. My chains are nothing to be ashamed of; they are to your honour. They show what your salvation is worth, since a man will go to prison to bring it to you, and they carry forward the gospel through which you will share Christ’s glory and be made like him (2 Timothy 2:10; Romans 8:18, 30; 1 John 3:2). Notice Paul’s restraint. He does not explain why God allowed the arrest, or when release might come; he says what the suffering is for, and leaves the rest alone. Our comfort for one another often goes wrong by supplying reasons we do not have.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s sufferings add anything to what Christ did to pay for sin. Christ’s suffering alone saves; Paul suffers to bring that salvation to others (Colossians 1:24).

In everyday life. When someone faithful suffers, it is easy to look for the flaw, the hidden sin, the weak faith, because a flaw would explain it and leave the rest of us safe. Paul offers no flaw to find. He offers a purpose.

How not to lose heart. Paul uses the same verb of himself: “So we do not lose heart” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Four things help. Look first at the cross. The central event of the gospel looked like defeat on the day it happened, so a faithful servant’s suffering is no sign that the gospel has stopped working. Lament instead of calculating. Take the hard case to God in words, as the psalms do, rather than doing the arithmetic alone; a complaint brought to God is still faith. Ask what the suffering is serving, not only why it came. Paul gives no reason for his arrest, but he can see what his chains are doing for others. Keep the end in view. “This light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). Then write this week to the suffering friend whose story has shaken you, and tell him what his faithfulness is doing for you.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s Greek says only “I ask not to lose heart”, without saying whom he asks or who might lose heart. It could mean “I ask you not to lose heart” (the ESV), “I ask God that you may not lose heart”, or “I ask God that I may not lose heart”. The ESV’s reading is the likely one: the words that follow, “which is your glory”, show that the danger in view is the readers’ discouragement, not Paul’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks that the church may be filled with God himself, and praises the God who can do more than he asks. Kneeling before the Father of every family (vv. 14–15), he prays in a chain of steps: strength by the Spirit in the inner being (v. 16), so that Christ makes his home in their hearts and they are rooted in love (v. 17), so that together they grasp the immeasurable love of Christ (vv. 18–19), so that they are filled with all the fullness of God (v. 19). Then he gives all the glory to the God whose power is already at work within us (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The indwelling Christ and the fullness of God

This prayer names the goal of the Christian life: to be “filled with all the fullness of God” (v. 19). Paul sets no ceiling on what he asks for the Ephesians, because God sets none on what he gives.

The way to that fullness is Christ dwelling in the heart through faith (v. 17). This is called union with Christ: the believer is really joined to the risen Lord, as a branch is joined to its vine and lives by its sap. God does more than clear our record; he gives us Christ himself. The whole Christian life flows from that bond: assurance, holiness, prayer, service and joy.

The closing burst of praise, the doxology (vv. 20–21), also teaches us how to pray. God is not limited by the smallness of our asking, and the power by which he answers is already at work within us (see the note on v. 20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery cults around Ephesus promised union with the divine through costly initiation, one stage after another, always with another level to reach. Paul prays for a fullness no initiation could buy: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith and sustained by the Spirit.

Now: When we cannot find words, the Spirit helps us (Romans 8:26), and when a situation seems past recovery, we pray to the God who raises the dead. Each time the church says this doxology, it reminds itself, and the watching powers, that its God is generous beyond our prayers.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul kneels to pray to the Father, the source of all fatherhood, who is now Father of Jew and Gentile alike. “For this reason”, the words of verse 1, picks up the prayer he broke off.

I bow my knees. Jews normally stood to pray (Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13); kneeling marked unusual earnestness (1 Kings 8:54; Daniel 6:10). And this man is in custody: a prisoner going down on a stone floor, probably watched, to pray for churches he may never see again. There is nobody in that room to impress.

From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. A wordplay English loses: Father is patēr, family is patria, a family group descended from one father. To name something, in the Bible, is to give it its identity (Genesis 2:19–20). God is not called Father because human fathers exist, as if we projected the idea upward. He is Father first, eternally, and human fathers are faint copies. So if your father was absent, harsh or cruel, your experience is not the standard by which God is measured. He is the standard, and what you knew was a distortion of an original that is undistorted and unfailing (Luke 15:20–24; Psalm 68:5). And since Jew and Gentile are now one family (2:19), Paul prays to the Father of them all.

Abba, on a stone floor. Paul can kneel and say “Father” only because another man knelt first. In Gethsemane the Son knelt (Luke 22:41) and said “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). The cup he prayed about was God’s just anger against our sin, and while it stood between us and God we could never have called him Father. Jesus drank it at the cross, and because he did, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6).

What it does not mean. Not that every human being is a child of God in the saving sense. All are his creatures (Acts 17:28), but the fatherhood that saves is adoption through Christ (1:5; John 1:12): God takes sinners into his family as his own children, with full rights and a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7). And kneeling is not required for prayer: posture is a help, not a law.

In everyday life. Next time you pray, notice what face you are imagining: disappointed but too polite to say so, or already looking for the fault. That face usually belonged to somebody, a parent or a teacher perhaps, and you have been putting it on God ever since. Change it by looking at Jesus, the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3): “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Watch him touch the leper (Mark 1:41) and promise paradise to a dying thief (Luke 23:43). That is not Jesus being kinder than the Father. That is the Father, showing you his face.

Uncertain wording. Pasa patria can be read “every family” (the ESV) or “the whole family” (the King James Version); Greek usage favours “every family”, each family group owing its name to the one Father. Who the families “in heaven” are is not explained; most take them to be the ranks of angels. On any reading, no family anywhere has a fatherhood that does not come from him.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “of our Lord Jesus Christ” after “the Father”. This commentary’s view: not original. The shorter reading is found in the earliest manuscripts and makes the wordplay with “family” clearer.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the Father to strengthen believers deep within, by his Spirit, out of the limitless wealth of his glory. It is the first step of a prayer that climbs to the fullness of God.

The shape of the prayer. In Greek, verses 14–19 are one sentence, a chain of requests like steps on a staircase: strengthened by the Spirit (v. 16), so that Christ dwells in your hearts (v. 17), so that you may grasp his love (vv. 18–19), so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God (v. 19).

According to the riches of his glory. Not out of his riches, which could mean a small gift from a large fortune, but in proportion to them: without limit. The strength is not achieved; it is granted.

Strengthened with power through his Spirit. Two words for strength, piled up: not power over circumstances, good as that is to pray for, but power in the inner being. And it comes from a Person, “the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead” (Romans 8:11). God does not lend his people a little more of their own resolve; he gives his Spirit, God himself, to dwell in the hidden self and hold it fast. It is Christ’s risen life at work in you, working as it did in him: “he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). So it seldom arrives as a feeling of being strong; it arrives in weak people and carries them through. The right response to finding yourself weak is not a programme of self-improvement. It is to ask.

In your inner being. Literally the inner man: your will, your faith, your capacity to trust God when nothing visible supports it. Two people facing the same grief look alike from outside, but one is quietly falling apart while the other is held somewhere the storm cannot reach. If you are the one falling apart, this is not a verdict on you but a prayer for you, because no one can produce this strength. “Our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16), with endurance (Colossians 1:11) and a peace that does not depend on circumstances (Philippians 4:7). God’s first work is not rearranging your circumstances, but building something in you that they cannot shake.

How do I actually pray this prayer? Use Paul’s words as your outline. Take verses 16–19 slowly and turn each clause into a request, for yourself and for others by name: “Father, strengthen her inside by your Spirit; make Christ at home in his heart; root them in your love; help me grasp how wide and long and high and deep it is; fill us with all your fullness.” Do not wait to feel something first, or judge the answer by tomorrow morning’s mood. God delights to answer this prayer, because it asks for what he has already promised (1 John 5:14–15). Then close as Paul does, with verses 20–21, thanking him in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit’s strengthening is so that Christ may be fully at home in believers’ hearts through faith, as people planted and founded in his love.

So that Christ may dwell in your hearts. Not to lodge, but to settle and make a permanent home, to move in and unpack (katoikeō). The heart is the centre of the person, thought, will, desire and feeling together (see 1:18), so Christ dwelling there rules and shapes everything we are. He already lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10); Paul prays that he would be more fully at home, not visiting in a crisis but present at work, in the argument with your spouse, in the moment of temptation. The Puritans pictured a house: Christ enters at conversion, but we must open every room to him. And faith here is not a single decision but the daily turning of the heart to him (John 15:4–5).

Not a guest who keeps his coat on. The eternal Son, by whom all things were made (John 1:3), who on earth had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), is willing to make his home in a sinner’s heart, and he comes to stay.

Rooted and grounded in love. Two pictures: a tree is only as strong as its hidden roots (Colossians 2:7; Psalm 1:3), and a house only as safe as its unseen foundation (Matthew 7:24–25). The love is above all Christ’s love for us (vv. 18–19), which then produces our love for him and for others. The deeply rooted believer bends in the storm but does not fall, because he knows what the wind cannot change: I am loved. And in Greek both words describe something already done and still true: you have been rooted and founded. Trees do not plant themselves, and no building lays its own foundation. Sending your roots deeper is real work, but it answers a planting that was never your idea. You are not asked to manufacture a foundation; you are asked to build on one.

What your worst week shows. You will never discover what you are rooted in on a good day, and the most revealing storm is your own sin. After you have failed badly, what happens to your sense of being loved by God? If it collapses, and stays collapsed until you have made up the ground with better behaviour, then whatever you believe about grace, you are leaning on your own performance. Do not despair of yourself. The way back is not a better week but a fresh look at Christ: go back within the hour and tell him plainly what you did, because you are not earning your way in again; you are standing on what somebody else laid. And if, under the real grief over the sin, there is a floor you have not fallen through, the stubborn knowledge that you are loved by a God who knew about this before you did it, you have found the foundation. It is the one thing your worst week cannot get underneath.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ enters and leaves believers depending on their mood or behaviour; his indwelling is permanent (John 14:23). Nor is “love” a vague feeling: it is the self-giving love shown at the cross (5:2, 25).

What does opening a room to Christ look like? Name the room, usually the part of life where you would rather not have his opinion: money, what you watch when alone, the grudge you are keeping, the plans you have already made. Bring it to him in plain words: “Lord, this is yours too; show me what you want here.” Open your Bible on that subject. Tell one trusted believer, because rooms kept secret tend to stay locked. Then do the first obedient thing you can see, however small: give the gift, cancel the subscription, make the call, say sorry. Christ does not batter the door down; he makes his home with those who love him and keep his word (John 14:23).

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that believers may have the strength to grasp, together with all God’s people, the immeasurable size of Christ’s love.

May have strength to comprehend. The odd word comes first: strength. Nobody says he lacked the strength to follow an argument. This answers the question left open in verse 16: what is the power for? Not for miracles or great achievements, but so that you can take in how much you are loved. It takes little strength to accept a compliment, and a great deal to accept a gift you can never repay, from someone who knows exactly what you are. Everything in us resists being loved on those terms; we would rather be admired, or at least useful. To stand still and be loved, with nothing to contribute, undoes a person, and it takes the power of God in the inner man not to flinch and start earning again.

With all the saints. We grasp it together, not alone. The old saint who has suffered, the new believer full of joy, the church in another culture: each sees aspects of Christ’s love the others need, and none has ever come back reporting that it ran out.

Breadth and length and height and depth. Four directions were a common ancient way of describing the whole of space: go as far as you can in any direction, and the love is still there. Job’s friend Zophar asked who could find out the deep things of God, higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol (Job 11:7–9); Paul prays that in Christ this immeasurable love may be known. Many preachers map the four onto the cross; it preaches well, but Paul does not make that link.

Breadth. Wide enough to embrace Jew and Gentile and every nation (chapter 2): wide enough to include you, your failures, your doubts, and the person beside you whose life looks nothing like yours.

Length. From before the foundation of the world (1:4) to the ages to come (2:7). It did not begin when you became lovable, and nothing in death or life can separate us from it (Romans 8:38–39).

Height. High enough to seat you with Christ in the heavenly places (2:6) and bring you before the Father with boldness (3:12).

Depth. Deep enough to reach you where you actually are, not where you pretend to be: the shame, the addiction, the thing you have never told anyone. It went down into death itself (Romans 5:20). This is the love that held him to the cross when he could have called for angels (Matthew 26:53), and that holds his people now.

In everyday life. It is possible to describe the love of Christ accurately and not be moved at all. If you have read a passage like this, felt something begin to rise, and then found yourself changing the subject or remembering a job that needed doing, that is not a lapse in concentration. It is the very thing Paul is praying about. Stay a little longer.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not say what has this breadth and length and height and depth. Suggestions include God’s wisdom (v. 10), the riches of Christ (v. 8), and the church as God’s temple (2:21–22), measured like the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:16). The likely meaning is the love of Christ, which the next words name (v. 19), since the sentence runs straight on from the four dimensions to that love.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of the prayer is that believers know Christ’s love, which is beyond all knowing, and so are filled with everything God is and gives.

To know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. “Know” (gnōnai) is personal knowledge, as one knows a friend (John 17:3): not learning facts about Christ’s love, but experiencing it more deeply. How can you know what is beyond knowing? You can know facts about the ocean without ever standing on the shore and feeling its size. Paul wants you on the beach, knowing in your bones that this ocean has no far shore. We can know Christ’s love truly but never fully.

Filled with all the fullness of God. The summit of the prayer: literally filled up to all the fullness of God. In Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9), and the church is his fullness (1:23). Paul prays that believers would be filled with everything God is and gives, his life, love, holiness, joy and peace, as fully as creatures can be. Picture a jug held under a waterfall: the waterfall is beyond comparison larger, yet the jug can be completely full, with nothing in it but what pours from the fall. In practice it means a life increasingly marked by what God is: loving more deeply because he is love, a patience not native to your temperament, a joy that does not evaporate when things are hard.

Be filled. Passive (plērōthēte), not “fill yourselves”. The fullness of God is a gift, not the reward for a disciplined enough life. The jug does not fill itself; it holds itself under the water: prayer, the word, worship, confession, the company of the saints (5:18).

Every “you” is plural. Paul asks that a congregation, this mixed, awkward Jew-and-Gentile assembly, would together be filled (1:23). Some of the filling only ever arrives through the people you have been joined to, including the ones you would never have chosen.

The hollow. You do not pray for someone to be filled unless there is a space in them. Everyone knows the restlessness that survives getting what you wanted. The promotion is pleasant for a fortnight. The house is bought, the qualification finished, the relationship secured, and within a season the same low hum returns, the sense that something has still not arrived. We assume we picked the wrong thing, and choose another. But Paul is describing a capacity no created thing was ever the right size for. The hollow is not a design fault. It is the shape of a container built for the fullness of God, and nothing smaller will ever sit in it.

What it does not mean. Not that believers become God or lose their creaturely nature. A cup filled from the ocean is full of the ocean, but it is still a cup. The Eastern Orthodox speak of deification, believers coming to share in God’s own life; Reformed theology speaks rather of union with Christ and of being made like him (Romans 8:29). And it is a growing filling, complete when we see him face to face (1 John 3:2).

What if I believe Christ loves me but cannot feel it? Then you are in good company, and not outside this prayer. Feelings rise and fall with health, sleep, grief and temperament; Christ’s love does not, and it is measured at the cross, not by this week’s feelings (Romans 5:8). Paul prays that we may know it, so God is willing to make it more real to us, usually over time and by ordinary means. Look long at how Christ treats sinners in the Gospels. Pray this very prayer for yourself. Sing truths you cannot yet feel. Take the Lord’s Supper as his pledge to you. Stay close to believers who have known his love in dark times. This knowing often arrives slowly, like dawn, and it is no less real for being quiet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends his prayer by praising the God who can do far more than anything we ask or imagine, by the power already at work in us. He has asked for enormous things; now he steps back and says that God can do immeasurably more.

Far more abundantly. Paul stacks the words (hyperekperissou) because no single word goes far enough. Our requests are limited by our words, our imagination by our minds; God is limited by neither. And he has already done more than anyone thought to ask: he gave his Son. No one in Israel prayed for a crucified Messiah, and no Gentile imagined adoption into the family of God.

According to the power at work within us. Not distant, not dormant, not waiting to be switched on by enough faith: working now (energoumenēn), the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20) and raised us with him (2:5–6). Why does it so often not feel like it, with the same old sin and the same weakness? It works whether you feel it or not, as a seed breaks through concrete without anyone seeing it move. It is aimed first at the inner person, not the circumstances: you may be waiting for it to change your situation while God is using your situation to change you. And it shows most clearly in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9): where your own strength has run out, God’s power is not added to yours but takes its place.

The hinge of the letter. This doxology is no decorative flourish. Everything from 1:3 to here has been about what God has done: chosen, redeemed, sealed, raised, seated, reconciled, built, revealed. Apart from one call to remember (2:11) and one plea not to lose heart (3:13), three chapters have given no command. The moment the praise ends, the tone changes: “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling” (4:1). Between the doctrine and the duty Paul has put not a summary but praise: a man on his knees running out of words. That order is deliberate, and it does not reverse. Anyone who takes up chapters 4–6 without first being undone by chapters 1–3 will find the commands crushing, trying to produce by effort a life that was only ever meant to overflow from astonishment. The obedience of this letter runs downhill from a doxology. If it is running uphill in your life, you may have started in the wrong chapter.

What it does not mean. Not a promise that big prayers guarantee health, wealth or success. Paul is still in prison. God’s “more” is more of what verses 16–19 ask, and more of his good purposes than we could ever plan (Romans 8:28–32).

But my prayer was answered no. This promise can wound. Someone reads it with a prayer in mind that met a plain no: the healing that did not come, the marriage that ended anyway, years of asking met with silence. To them the verse can sound like mockery. The answer lies in two small words easily skipped: or think. God does more than we know to ask. We often ask for the lesser thing because we cannot yet see the greater, and when a loving father says no, his love has not failed; the no is his love at work. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed. The answer was no, and the “more” was grace sufficient and power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Where no better thing is yet visible, the more is not cancelled but kept, for the coming ages (2:7), for the day God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The account does not close at the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All glory belongs to God, and it is to be shown in Christ and in his church, for ever. With this Amen the first half of the letter, about what God has done, ends in worship.

To him be glory. Behind the word stands the Hebrew kābôd, from a root meaning heavy: the weight, worth and splendour of who God is (see 1:17). To give him glory adds nothing to him, as the sun does not brighten because someone looks at it. It is to recognise and declare what is already true, and to live in line with it: the goal of everything in chapters 1–3 (1:6, 12, 14).

In the church and in Christ Jesus. The two stand side by side as the places of God’s eternal glory: the risen Son, seated above every power, and a congregation with its awkward silences and its hymns nobody can quite sing. Paul does not apologise for the pairing. The church is his body, and the glory of the head shines in the body he fills (1:22–23), as a mirror displays the sun. You are one of the places where God’s glory is meant to be seen.

Throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen. Literally to all the generations of the age of the ages. Empires rise and fall; the church’s praise will never end. “Amen” is Hebrew for firm, true, so be it, the people’s response in worship (1 Corinthians 14:16; Nehemiah 8:6). Paul has written the sentence; the Amen is where the reader signs it.

Christ is the Amen. He is himself “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). Every promise of God finds its Yes in him, and so it is through him that the church says its Amen to God’s glory (2 Corinthians 1:20), generation after generation, and the song will still be his when time has finished.

Giving him glory in ordinary life. It takes three ordinary forms. Honest praise: kneeling by your bed on a Tuesday night, no audience, saying, you are good and I am not; you saved me when I had nothing, and I am grateful (Psalm 50:23). A life that points to him: when you are patient with a difficult colleague and they wonder what you have that they do not, God is glorified without a religious word spoken (1 Corinthians 10:31; Matthew 5:16). And trusting him when it is hard: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15). That may be the deepest, because it tells every watching soul that this God is worth trusting when it costs.

Is God vain to want glory? In us it would be vanity, because we are not the greatest good, and demanding praise is a lie about our size. God is the greatest good, so pointing us to himself is not vanity but truth and kindness: anywhere else he pointed us would be something less. And look at how this God seeks glory. Jesus said the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified, and he meant his death (John 12:23–24). The God who wants glory gets it by washing feet and carrying a cross.

3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 closes the teaching half of the letter. Chapter 2 ended with Jews and Gentiles built together into one temple for God (2:19–22); now Paul turns to pray for that new people, breaks off to explain his own part in God’s plan, and ends in praise, just before the “therefore” of 4:1.

The message. God’s long-kept secret is out: in Christ, outsiders share everything with God’s ancient people as full members of one family, and through this mixed and unlikely church God shows his wisdom to the universe. So the greatest thing to ask is to know the love of Christ, which is beyond all knowing, and to be filled with God himself.

Why it was said. The readers were mostly Gentiles from a city of magic, mystery cults and fear of spiritual powers (see the introduction). Their apostle was in chains, arrested over the very question of Gentiles and the temple, and they might wonder whether the gospel was failing (v. 13). They needed to know that their place in God’s family was no afterthought, and that his chains were for their honour.

How the chapter makes its case. It is a prayer interrupted by an explanation. Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then tells of the grace entrusted to him and the mystery revealed to him: the Gentiles are fellow heirs, one body and sharers in the promise (vv. 2–6). Grace made the least of the saints the preacher of Christ’s riches (vv. 7–9), so that through the church God’s many-coloured wisdom is displayed to the heavenly powers, as he purposed from eternity (vv. 10–12); so they must not lose heart (v. 13). Then he kneels and prays in a chain of steps: strength by the Spirit, Christ at home in their hearts, power to grasp his love, and the fullness of God (vv. 14–19). A doxology closes the first half of the letter (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. The secret is “the mystery of Christ” (v. 4), the riches are his (v. 8), and the prayer’s summit is his love (v. 19): wide enough to take in the nations, deep enough to go down into death, and without a far shore. The Son who knelt in Gethsemane and drank the cup opened the way for outsiders to kneel before the Father as his children.

For us. Your congregation, awkward as it is, is where heaven watches God’s wisdom; in Christ you may come to God boldly at any hour; and before the commands of chapters 4–6, Paul wants you on your knees, astonished at being loved.

keyVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter climbs to this sentence. The mystery Paul was given to preach is a love wide enough to take in the Gentiles (v. 6), and the prayer he kneels to pray is that believers may know that love, though no one will ever reach its end. The goal is not more information about God but being filled with God himself, and the way there is the love of Christ.

3.reflection:
Paul calls himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus”, not of Rome (v. 1), and tells the church that his sufferings are their glory (v. 13). What situation in your life do you tend to describe as a prison, and what would change if you saw yourself as placed there by Christ for others?

The mystery is that Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body and partakers of the promise (v. 6), and through such a church God shows his wisdom to the heavenly powers (v. 10). Who might feel like a guest rather than family in your church, and what would it look like to fold them in?

Paul prays for strength to grasp the love of Christ (vv. 16–19). Why might it take strength to accept being loved? When have you found it hardest to believe that Christ loves you, and what helped?

Three chapters about what God has done end in praise (vv. 20–21) before the commands of chapters 4–6 begin. What happens when Christians try to obey without first being astonished at grace? Which of the requests in verses 16–19 will you pray this week for someone by name?

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people called by one God must live as one. Paul’s first request is not for great deeds but for the humble, gentle, patient love that keeps the peace between believers (vv. 1–2), because the unity they must guard has already been made by the Spirit (v. 3). It rests on everything they share: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father over all (vv. 4–6). We do not create this unity; we keep it or damage it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The unity of the church

The unity of the church is not a goal to be reached but a fact to be kept (see the note on v. 3).

The four graces that keep unity, humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another, are a portrait of Christ applied to church life (see v. 2).

Seven times in verses 4–6 Paul says “one”, and that roots this unity in shared truth, not in pretending doctrine does not matter (see the notes on vv. 3 and 4–5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church gathered former worshippers of Artemis, Jewish believers, slaves and free, merchants and harbour workers. Every natural instinct pulled them apart along old social lines. Paul’s “therefore” ties his call to chapter 2: the wall has already come down, the body is already one, so walk like it.

Now: Churches still split along political, cultural and stylistic lines, and it is easy to shop for a church that suits our preferences and keeps us among people like ourselves. Paul calls for a costly unity rooted in shared confession, not shared taste. A local church that holds together through its differences, with patient and humble love, bears witness to the one God “who is over all and through all and in all”.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has called you to himself, live in a way that matches that calling. Here the letter turns from what God has done (chapters 1–3) to the life that fits it (chapters 4–6).

Therefore. The sharpest turn in the letter. For three chapters Paul has given almost no commands, only one call to remember (2:11) and one plea not to lose heart (3:13); he has been describing: chosen, redeemed, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, reconciled, built, indwelt. Chapters 4–6 hold some forty commands, and the order matters. Paul does not say, Live like this, and God will accept you, but, God has accepted you; therefore live like this. Christian ethics flows out of grace, never the other way round: the move from indicative (what is true) to imperative (what to do).

I … a prisoner for the Lord. Literally in the Lord. Paul is in prison because he obeyed Christ (3:1), so he asks nothing of us that has not cost him first. The man who tells us to walk can himself walk only the few steps of a cell.

Urge. To call alongside, to appeal (parakaleō): not a cold order but a pastor’s earnest plea. The same word is used for comfort.

To walk. After the size of chapters 1–3 you might expect something towering. What arrives is the plainest verb available, and it organises all that follows: walk worthy (4:1), not as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), as children of light (5:8), wisely (5:15). Nobody schedules walking or photographs it, and it cannot be done in bursts. The Christian life is lived not in the peaks, but in the ordinary going-along of an ordinary week.

In a manner worthy. “Worthy” (axiōs) means fitting, in keeping with. The picture behind the word is a trader’s scales. In one pan lies your calling, all that God has done for you in chapters 1–3; in the other, your daily life. You cannot add anything to the calling side; God filled it before the world was made. You are asked to bring the other side up to match it. And the weight on the calling side is Christ himself: God called you “into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Corinthians 1:9), so a worthy walk looks like his. None of us makes the scales balance. He did: from the manger to the cross he never once fell short of his Father’s will, and God counts that perfect life as belonging to everyone who trusts him. A son who bears the family name worthily is not earning the name; he already has it, and is asked to live like a man who has it.

Of the calling to which you have been called. In Paul, God’s calling is not an invitation a person may take or leave but the call that actually brings a person to Christ (1:18; Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9), and it calls us to something: to be holy (1:4), his children (1:5), one body (4:4). When you believed, more was happening than your own decision. God was calling you by name, as Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43): the call itself gave the life to answer it.

What it does not mean. Not that God calls those who are worthy; he calls the dead (2:1–5). Nor is it a life of grim effort under a heavy load. The God who called also equips (4:7, 11–12), and the Spirit works in us with the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20; 3:16, 20).

If God has already accepted me, why should I bother to obey? Because grace does not leave a person where it found him. Paul expects the question and answers it with horror: shall we go on sinning so that grace may abound? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). A man pardoned by a king and adopted into his house does not ask how little he can do now that he is safe; the grace that saves also trains us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). And if your obedience is your way of getting God to accept you, you have reversed Paul’s order. Obedience is not the price of acceptance but what accepted people do, gladly, because they love the one who accepted them (John 14:15).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church stays one through humble, gentle, patient love that carries the weight of other believers. What most often destroys unity is not doctrine but pride, so these four qualities stand between “walk worthy” (v. 1) and “maintain the unity” (v. 3).

With all humility. Lowliness of mind (tapeinophrosynē). In the Greek world it was usually a fault, the cringing posture of a slave. Christ showed what it truly is when he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17) and humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:3–8). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself but thinking of yourself less, and seeing yourself truly before God. False modesty is still focused on self.

And gentleness. Prautēs could be used of a horse broken to the bridle. The animal has lost none of its strength; the strength now answers to a hand other than its own. A naturally timid man is not gentle in this sense; he simply has nothing that needs restraining. Jesus called himself “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and he drove the traders out of the temple.

With patience. Long temper (makrothymia), the patience God shows us (Romans 2:4): above all, patience with people, the slow, the difficult, the wrong.

Bearing with one another in love. To put up with, to carry the weight of, and the weight is “one another”, other Christians. The man who tells you the same story every time you meet. The woman who is late to everything and always has a reason. The one whose theology is slightly off and who would like to discuss it after the service, at length. None of them is sinning; they are simply heavy, as people are, and the instruction is to pick up the weight and keep walking, as Christ has carried ours through every year of our wandering, and carried our sins to the cross. This is not excusing evil; Paul will command speaking the truth in love (v. 15) and exposing wrong (5:11). And love makes the other three last: without it, humility becomes self-contempt, gentleness passivity, and patience resentment.

In everyday life. It is natural to cast yourself as the one doing the bearing. Turn it round: who in your church is bearing with you? Someone finds your manner difficult or your blind spot wearing, and has decided, quietly, to put up with it and go on loving you. You are the heavy person in somebody else’s week. Once you see that, humility becomes possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians do not create unity; they guard the unity the Spirit has already made, and that takes effort.

Eager to maintain. Making every effort (spoudazontes). A house is maintained by somebody clearing the gutters in November, a marriage by two people apologising more often than they would like. And you are asked to keep unity, not build it, because it already exists. Nobody creates his own family. He finds himself in it, and what remains is how he treats people he did not choose.

The unity of the Spirit. The unity the Spirit creates. Every believer has the same Spirit (2:18, 22; 1 Corinthians 12:13), and Christ has already made Jew and Gentile one (2:14–16). This unity is a fact, not a goal; God’s work, not a human agreement. It was bought, not negotiated: Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and the Spirit bound us together with a cord no quarrel can finally cut. What we so easily fray, he wove. If you and the believer you find hardest both trust Christ, you are already joined to the same Lord by the same Spirit. You cannot cancel it. What is left in your hands is whether the way you treat each other tells the truth about that bond or hides it (John 17:21).

In the bond of peace. A bond ties together, like a cord or a ligament. Christ is our peace (2:14), and the peace he made at the cross must be lived out between people. We imagine the threat is doctrinal, and it very seldom is. Churches divide over a message never returned, a decision taken without someone who expected to be consulted, a remark repeated to the wrong person, a slight at the door that was probably not intended. Theology gets recruited afterwards, to give the wound a respectable name. The bond never breaks in the abstract, but between two particular people, and no general goodwill towards the church covers that.

What it does not mean. Not unity that ignores truth. Paul grounds it in one faith (v. 5) and the unity of the faith (v. 13), and it cannot include those who deny the gospel itself (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10). But among those who share the gospel, Christians should not divide over church government, the details of the last things or the style of worship. They may worship in different churches, but they should treat one another as brothers.

Is it ever right to leave my church? Yes, but more rarely than we think, and never lightly. It is right to leave when a church abandons the gospel, will not teach the Bible faithfully, refuses to deal with serious sin or abuse, or binds your conscience where Scripture does not; it may also be right when you move house or are genuinely needed elsewhere. It is not usually right to leave because the music changed, a friendship cooled or someone offended you; those are exactly the places where this verse is meant to be obeyed. If you do go, speak to your elders first, leave without running anyone down, and join another faithful church soon. Leaving a church is sometimes necessary. Drifting away from church altogether never is (Hebrews 10:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians are one because everything that makes them Christians is one. One body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and in verse 6 one God: seven times Paul strikes the same note.

The shape. The list is arranged around the Trinity: one Spirit (v. 4), one Lord (v. 5), one God and Father (v. 6). We are one because Father, Son and Spirit are one, and this one God has brought us all to himself: the Father is our Father, the Son our Lord, and the Spirit lives in each of us.

One body. The church, the body of Christ (1:23; 2:16): many congregations, but one church with one head.

One Spirit. There is no believer without the Spirit (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13).

The one hope that belongs to your call. God called us to a single future: the inheritance in Christ, his return, the resurrection, the new creation (1:18). And it has an edge. The same finish line means the same finishing group.
