The people you find hardest in your church are not a temporary arrangement; you will be with them, in unshadowed friendship, for ever, and learning to love them now is an early start on eternity.

One Lord. In the Roman world “Lord” was Caesar’s title; for Christians there is one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6; Romans 10:9). To say “Jesus is Lord” was to say Caesar is not, and every age has its own Caesar, whether the state, the market, the crowd or the self, asking for the bow that belongs to Christ alone.

One faith. Both our trusting and what we trust, the gospel itself (Jude 3). Christian unity is not shared feeling but shared truth.

One baptism. The sign of entry into Christ and his body, given once (Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:27), into the one name (Matthew 28:19). Some take it to mean Spirit baptism, the Spirit’s inward work of joining us to Christ, but baptism with water best fits the list. Water baptism is a sign: it shows that a person has been joined to Christ by faith. It does not do the joining.

I was baptised as a baby. Should I be baptised now? If you now trust Christ, the view this commentary takes is yes, held gently: if baptism is the sign a believer receives on professing faith, being baptised as a believer is not a second baptism but your first. Do not despise what your parents meant, for they were asking God to bless you, and do not treat paedobaptist friends as opponents. Talk it through with a pastor, read the passages for yourself (Acts 2:38–41; 8:36–38; Romans 6:3–4), and let it never become a matter of pride or quarrelling. Baptism does not save you; Christ does. But obeying his command is a joy.

Where Christians differ: one baptism, but whose? Paedobaptists (Presbyterian, Anglican and others) baptise the infants of believers as the new covenant sign, parallel to circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12). Credobaptists (Baptists and others) baptise those who profess faith, holding that baptism signifies a union with Christ by faith that infants cannot yet profess (Acts 2:41; 8:12). Sadly, many churches do not recognise each other’s baptisms. This commentary’s view: credobaptist, held charitably. Believers’ baptism best fits the New Testament pattern, but paedobaptist Christians who trust Christ are brothers and sisters in the one faith and the one body. The disagreement is real, but it must not break the unity of verse 3.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over the whole church stands one God and Father, who rules all his people, works through them all and lives in them all.

One God. “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The God who is one makes his people one, so a church that splinters over secondary things acts against its own deepest nature.

The Shema with Jesus inside it. Paul sets one Lord beside one God and Father, as in 1 Corinthians 8:6: “for us there is one God, the Father, … and one Lord, Jesus Christ”. Israel’s confession has been opened up so that Jesus stands inside it. This is not a second God: the one God has a Son, and only through the Son does anyone come to call him Father (Matthew 11:27).

And Father of all. In context, Father of all believers, Jew and Gentile together (2:18–19; 3:14–15). Stretch the word to mean every human being and you do not enlarge Paul’s point; you empty it. There are no stepchildren in God’s family.

Who is over all and through all and in all. Three small prepositions that cover everything. Over all: his transcendence; there is no committee above this Father. Through all: his providence; he is at work in every circumstance, including the ones you would never have chosen. In all: his presence; he dwells in his people by his Spirit (2:22). So nothing can reach you without first passing him. That does not make every day easy. It means no day is ownerless.

What it does not mean. Not pantheism: God is over all, distinct from what he has made. Nor that every person is God’s child whatever he believes. God made and sustains every human being (Acts 17:28), but sonship in the saving sense belongs to those who receive Christ (John 1:12); Paul has just called people “by nature children of wrath” (2:3).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “you” (in you all) or “us”. This commentary’s view: the shorter text, “in all”, is original. The addition gives the right sense, though: the “all” in view is God’s people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one body is not a uniform mass: the risen Christ gives each member grace to serve, so that the whole church grows up into him. Each believer has a gift measured out by Christ (v. 7). Like the conqueror of Psalm 68, he came down to the lowest place and ascended above all, and from the throne he shares out the spoil (vv. 8–10). His gifts to the church are ministers of the word, who equip all the saints for ministry (vv. 11–12), until the church is mature and steady against error (vv. 13–14), speaking the truth in love and building itself up as every part does its work (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The ascended Christ and the equipping ministry

Paul grounds all ministry in the ascension. It is the ascended Christ, far above all the heavens and filling all things, who gives gifts to his church as he chooses. Ministry is first his work. It is how the reigning Christ cares for his church today, not a project that people thought up.

The Reformed tradition has generally held that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet (2:20) belonged to the church’s founding, while evangelists and pastor-teachers continue (see the note at 4:11).

Verses 15–16 are Paul’s fullest picture of mutual ministry. The body grows “when each part is working properly”, not when a few are busy and the rest look on. Every member is a minister, not because everyone preaches, but because everyone brings the gift he has received to build up the whole.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul had spent about three years in Ephesus, and the elders he left knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now he was absent, and this letter itself was an act of equipping. The leaders of verses 11–12 were, first of all, those elders and teachers, charged with preparing every member to serve.

Now: A church where the congregation receives services delivered by professionals leaves believers unable to feed themselves and easily blown about by new teaching. So the leader’s question is not only how well he performs but how well he equips, and the member’s question is not only whether he is being fed but whether he is contributing.

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer has been given grace to serve, and Christ decides how much each receives. Paul turns from “all” (vv. 4–6) to “each”: the church is one, but not a uniform mass (1 Corinthians 12:12–27).

Grace was given. Not saving grace, which all share equally, but grace for service, the gift and ability to serve in a particular way (3:2, 7–8). Christ gives here (vv. 7, 11); elsewhere the Spirit distributes and the Father works the same gifts (1 Corinthians 12:4–6, 11): one divine generosity, from three Persons.

To each one of us. There are no giftless Christians, no passengers in the church (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10). The gifts may be public, like teaching, or quiet, like helping, giving, showing mercy or administration (Romans 12:6–8), and they are for building up the body (v. 12), not for anyone’s status.

According to the measure of Christ’s gift. Christ decides what each receives, and that removes both pride and envy. If your measure is smaller than someone else’s, it was measured out by the one who knows exactly what he intends to do with you, and envy is finally a complaint about his arithmetic. If your measure is larger, a bigger allocation of something you did not earn is not an achievement (1 Corinthians 12:11). Nobody in a body admires the hand and looks down on the liver.

How do I find mine? The New Testament never suggests you identify your gift first and serve afterwards. Begin with what is in front of you. What needs doing that nobody is doing? What need are you uncomfortable walking past? What do people keep thanking you for, or asking you to do? Answered honestly across a year of ordinary service, those questions will tell you more than any questionnaire. Gifts are found in use, the way a muscle is found by lifting something.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reads Psalm 68 of Christ: the risen King has won his victory, and now he shares out its spoil with his church.

Psalm 68. “It says” means God says it. Psalm 68 is a victory psalm: God marching from Sinai up to his sanctuary on Mount Zion as a conquering king, captives in procession behind him and the spoils shared out. Paul’s readers would have pictured a Roman triumph: the general in his chariot, the treasure of the defeated carried through the streets, the conquered kings walking in chains before the crowd, and at the end the spoil handed out.

When he ascended on high. God’s ascent to Zion is fulfilled in Christ’s ascension to heaven after his resurrection (Acts 1:9–11), where he is seated far above every power (1:20–21). The cross was the decisive battle; the ascension is the triumphal procession; the gifts to the church are the spoils of war.

He led a host of captives. Literally he took captivity captive: Christ’s defeated enemies, paraded in his triumph. Sin, whose penalty he bore; death, stripped of its sting (1 Corinthians 15:54–57); the devil and his powers, disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15); and the law’s power to condemn (Galatians 3:13). Some read it of the people he freed, now following him; the military picture favours the first.

And he gave gifts to men. Here is the puzzle. The Hebrew of Psalm 68:18 says the king received gifts among men; Paul says “he gave”. In an ancient triumph, receiving tribute and sharing it with one’s soldiers were two halves of one event, and Paul presses the giving half. The Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms (the Targum), probably preserving an older synagogue reading, also has “gave”, and the psalm itself goes on to describe God giving to his people (68:10, 19, 35). The King who received the spoils now distributes them, the Spirit first of all (Acts 2:33), and his gifts are people (v. 11).

That the LORD God may dwell there. The psalm gives the ascent a purpose: the conqueror received gifts “even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there” (Psalm 68:18). The ascended Christ gives gifts that build rebels into a dwelling place for God (2:22). The conqueror wants to live among the conquered.

Which part of the procession were you in? By the account of chapter 2, you were on the captives’ side of the parade: dead in trespasses, “following the prince of the power of the air” (2:1–2). The campaign that broke that camp was fought for you, not by you. That is why no one may boast about a spiritual gift (1 Corinthians 4:7). Loot is not an achievement; a soldier carried off the field does not, on receiving his share of the spoil, make a speech about his contribution. Everything in your church that actually works, the teaching, the hospitality, the administration nobody notices, the person who is unaccountably good with the dying, is plunder from a battle in which we were the ones rescued.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul bent Scripture to his argument. He interprets it, as Jewish teachers did, in the light of its fulfilment in Christ. The difference from the Hebrew is real and interpreters still weigh the explanations, but believers hold that Paul reads the psalm truly.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm pictures God ascending Mount Zion in victory, receiving tribute; Paul applies it to Christ, who in triumph gives gifts. A Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave gifts.”

parallels.desc: you ascended on high, leading a host of captives

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christ who gives these gifts first came all the way down, and has now gone up above everything, so that he fills all things. Verses 9–10 are a short aside on one word: to ascend implies a descent before it.

He had also descended. Christ must first have come down from heaven (John 3:13; 6:62), so the gifts of verses 11–16 come from a Lord who knows the lowest place as well as the highest. On “the lower regions, the earth”, see below.

The descent, step by step. “He descended” covers a very long way down. From the throne, where he was worshipped without ceasing, to a womb, and a manger (Luke 2:7). To a village with a poor reputation (John 1:46), and long years as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). To a wandering life with nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). To being thought out of his mind by his own family (Mark 3:21). To a friend’s kiss in a garden at night, and all the rest running away (Mark 14:45, 50). To a courtyard where the man who had sworn to die with him denied knowing him (Mark 14:66–72). To a rigged trial, a whipping, a crown of thorns made as a joke (Mark 15:15–17). To an execution kept for slaves and rebels, stripped, between two criminals (Mark 15:24–27). To a cry of forsakenness (Mark 15:34). To a corpse, and a grave with a stone rolled across it. Every stair goes down, and he took none of them as an observer. No angel was asked to take that road; the Lord of glory took it himself.

Far above all the heavens. Beyond every created realm, to the throne of God (Hebrews 4:14; 7:26). The one who went lowest has been raised highest.

That he might fill all things. Christ ascended not to leave the world but to fill it with his presence, power and rule. The word runs through the letter: the church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (1:23); believers are to be “filled with all the fullness of God” (3:19) and “filled with the Spirit” (5:18). He is not spread thinly through the universe like air. He is seated at the Father’s right hand, pouring out his Spirit and gifts (Acts 2:33), and by his Spirit he is with his people wherever they are (Matthew 28:20). That is why his going away was for their good (John 16:7): on earth he stood in one place at a time; now he is with all his people at once.

In everyday life. Name the one place you suspect he cannot reach, the thing that feels beyond anyone’s sympathy, his included. There is no cellar in your life with a floor lower than the one he has already stood on, and he has come up from it.

Uncertain wording. The Greek is literally “the lower parts of the earth”: either the lower parts, that is, the earth, or the parts beneath the earth. There are three main views. The incarnation: Christ came down from heaven to earth, which fits the contrast with “far above all the heavens”. A descent into Hades: Christ went to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection, perhaps to proclaim his victory; this leans chiefly on one much-debated verse (1 Peter 3:19), and lies behind the Apostles’ Creed’s “he descended into hell”. Pentecost: Christ ascended, then came down again in the Spirit to give gifts; less likely, because Paul’s reasoning puts the descent first.

This commentary’s view: the incarnation, including the whole of Christ’s humiliation down to death and the grave (Philippians 2:6–8). Paul is not mapping the afterlife but tracing the sweep from the lowest place to the highest. Calvin and the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) take the Creed’s phrase in a similar sense: for Calvin, the very anguish of hell that Christ bore on the cross in our place; for the Catechism, his remaining in the state of the dead until the third day. So a Christian can say the Creed’s words and mean them, without any legend of a tour of the underworld. Many faithful Christians, early and recent, have held the second view, and believers may differ on it without suspicion of one another.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “first” (he also descended first), as in the King James Version. This commentary’s view: an early explanatory addition, not original, though it correctly states the order.
verseByVerse.note: “The lower regions, the earth” may mean his coming down to earth in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ascended Christ gives his church people, servants of his word, as his gifts to it. Its leaders are not the church’s invention or its employees.

And he gave. Christ himself gave, and he gave not programmes or a curriculum, but people, with names, families, limited strength and phones that ring at inconvenient hours. That is far better than any resource: a book cannot sit with you in a hospital corridor at two in the morning, or notice that you have stopped coming. It also means the gift will disappoint you as a resource never would. Your pastor will preach a thin sermon in the very month you needed a good one. Churches sometimes conclude that the wrong man was given, when what has happened is that a man was given, which was the arrangement from the beginning.

The apostles. Those personally commissioned by the risen Christ as his authoritative witnesses: the Twelve and Paul, with a few others in a wider sense (Acts 1:21–26; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:7–9). They laid the church’s foundation (2:20), and their teaching is preserved in the New Testament.

The prophets. New Testament prophets, who received and spoke revelation from God for the church in the foundation-laying period (2:20; 3:5; Acts 11:27–28; 13:1).

The evangelists. Those gifted to proclaim the gospel where it has not been heard and to plant churches (Acts 21:8; 2 Timothy 4:5). The church needs them in every generation.

The shepherds and teachers. A single “the” covers both words, so this is probably one group: pastors who teach. “Shepherd” (poimēn) is the word translated pastor. A shepherd feeds, leads, protects and seeks his flock, and in the church he does it chiefly by teaching God’s word (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2). These are the elders, also called overseers (Titus 1:5–7), under-shepherds of the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4), who laid down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

The common thread. Every person on this list serves by speaking God’s word: Christ builds his church by his word, spoken by the people he gives. The list is not complete (compare Romans 12:6–8; 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, 28).

In everyday life. When did you last pray for your pastor by name, about the specific things you know he carries? Ministers often live on general encouragement and precise criticism: the criticism comes with details and dates, the encouragement as “nice sermon” at the door. Reverse those two for a year, and you would hardly recognise the man at the end of it.

Where Christians differ: apostles and prophets today. Some churches, especially in newer charismatic and apostolic movements, recognise living apostles and prophets with authority to direct the church, and speak of a fivefold ministry that must continue until we all attain to the unity of the faith (v. 13). Others use “apostle” in a weaker sense, of missionaries or church planters. Cessationists hold that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet ended with the apostolic age, because a foundation is laid once (2:20) and Scripture is now complete. This commentary’s view: cessationist, held charitably. No one today holds the apostles’ authority, and the prophetic foundation is complete in Scripture; evangelists, pastors and teachers continue, and the church needs them as much as ever. Many continuationists, who believe gifts such as prophecy continue, also deny that anyone today holds an apostle’s authority. The disagreement is among people who love the same Lord and the same Bible.
verseByVerse.note: “Shepherds” is the word often translated “pastors.”

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gives pastors and teachers to equip every believer for ministry, so that the whole body is built up. The saints are not the audience of ministry; they do it.

To equip. Setting broken bones, mending torn fishing nets (Mark 1:19), fitting out a ship: the word family (katartismos) was used of all three. Pastors and teachers mend, train and fit out the saints, which means all believers (1:1), chiefly with Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

For the work of ministry. The equipped saints do the work (on the wording, see below), and not only from a pulpit: care for the sick, the widow and the stranger (Matthew 25:35–36; James 1:27); encouragement that strengthens faith (Hebrews 3:13); discipling, older and younger, one to one (2 Timothy 2:2; Titus 2:3–5); witness to neighbours and colleagues (1 Peter 3:15); prayer (6:18); and generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–8).

For building up the body of Christ. Paul joins two pictures, a building going up (2:20–22) and a body growing. It grows as more people come to Christ, as believers become more like him (v. 13), and as they are joined more closely to one another (v. 16).

In everyday life. We usually measure a church by its minister; this verse asks whether the members are working. A church where only the pastor ministers is like a team where only the coach plays. If your pastor were away for six months, how much of your church’s ministry would stop? Ask your elders where you can serve, and start.

Uncertain wording. The weight of this verse rests on where the commas fall. The King James Version has three tasks, all belonging to the leaders: “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body”. Modern versions drop the second comma: leaders equip the saints for the work of ministry. The modern reading has the better case, though some careful scholars prefer the older one: Paul uses one word for “for” (pros) in the first phrase and another (eis) in the next two, which suggests a chain, not three tasks side by side. Leaders equip the saints; the saints do the work; the body is built up.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s gifts aim at a whole church grown up into his likeness, steady enough not to be blown about by every new teaching.

Until we all. The goal is for the whole church, not a few spiritual heroes. It will be reached fully at Christ’s return; in this life maturity is a direction of travel.

The unity of the faith. In verse 3 the church guards the unity it has; here it grows into a fuller one: shared conviction about the whole truth of the gospel (Jude 3), not a thin agreement on the few things nobody disputes.

And of the knowledge of the Son of God. Full, personal knowledge (epignōsis; 1:17). The aim of all ministry is not a better informed congregation, but one more deeply captivated by Jesus himself.

To mature manhood. Literally a complete man, a full-grown adult, in contrast with “children” in verse 14. Paul pictures the whole church, women and men alike, as one person growing up, the “one new man” of 2:15. Maturity here is not the absence of struggle but stability: a faith not easily capsized.

The stature of the fullness of Christ. Stature is height: think of a child measured against a mark on the door frame. The mark the church is growing towards is not the best Christian you know, but Christ himself (Romans 8:29; Colossians 1:28). How great he must be, if the measure of maturity is nothing less than him.

So that we may no longer be children. Children in the bad sense: unstable, gullible, easily impressed. Not the childlike trust Jesus praised (Matthew 18:3), but childishness (1 Corinthians 14:20; Hebrews 5:13–14).

Tossed to and fro. A picture familiar to a port city: a small boat with no keel or anchor, tossed by the waves of feeling and circumstance and carried about by whatever wind is blowing this season. In practice it is the Christian whose convictions can be dated by whatever he last read or listened to; who finds a new teacher every eighteen months, each the one who has finally made sense of everything; who is persuaded by whoever spoke most confidently. Paul describes a stage, not a fixed character; the only tragedy is staying there.

By human cunning. Dice-playing (kybeia), and so trickery: the sleight of hand of a cheat at dice.

By craftiness in deceitful schemes. “Craftiness” (panourgia) is the word for the serpent deceiving Eve (2 Corinthians 11:3), and the serpent opened not with a denial but with a question (Genesis 3:1). “Schemes” is the word of 6:11. Error comes warmly, from likeable and sincere people, wrapped around a great deal of truth. Nine-tenths of it is right, and the wrong tenth is the part everything else rests on, like one rotten beam under a good floor.

The setting. Paul had warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in among them, and that from their own number men would arise speaking twisted things to draw disciples after them (Acts 20:29–30). Within a few years Timothy was left in Ephesus to stop certain people teaching a different doctrine (1 Timothy 1:3).

What it does not mean. Not that mature Christians never change their minds: maturity is teachable, but stable. Nor is the cure to become suspicious of everything, which produces a hard, frightened Christian. It is to know the Son of God so well that counterfeits show themselves by contrast, as someone who handles genuine banknotes all day needs no course in forgery.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church grows up into Christ as its members speak the truth to one another in love and every part does its work. All its growth comes from Christ the head, and it grows in love.

Rather, speaking the truth in love. One Greek word (alētheuontes): truthing, living and speaking the truth. But “in love”. Truth without love wins arguments and loses people; love without truth comforts people on their way to ruin. “In love” means speaking the truth for someone instead of at them. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6).

We are to grow up in every way into him. Not knowledge while love withers, or zeal while wisdom lags, but all moving one way, into Christ. He is not only the example we copy; he is what growing up means. To mature is to become more like him and to live closer to him (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Who is the head, into Christ. The head was often seen as the source of direction and life for the body (1:22; Colossians 1:18).

From whom the whole body, joined and held together. The church grows not by human techniques but by drawing life from its head, every part fitted in its place (2:21).

By every joint with which it is equipped. Ligaments are the points of contact through which supplies pass. Much of what a Christian receives from Christ comes through other believers: the encourager who seeks out the one who is struggling, the older woman discipling a younger, the one who prays before it is light. The ligament is never seen and never applauded, but remove it and the body collapses. You may never know which of your ordinary contacts carried life to someone this week. Ligaments are not meant to know; they are meant to stay connected.

When each part is working properly. Every member has a function (v. 7); when some parts stop working, the body is weakened.

Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. A church that knows more but does not love more has not grown up; it has only grown clever (1 Corinthians 8:1). And a body overflowing with such love becomes its own best evangelism (John 13:35).

Two ways to abuse “the truth in love”. First, a man says what he has decided must be said, and afterwards feels the satisfaction of having been faithful, and everyone who heard it knows the satisfaction was the point. It cost him nothing and left the other person with no way forward: bluntness with a Bible verse pinned to the front. Second, and far more respectable: someone is drifting, a marriage is quietly failing, a man’s temper is frightening his children, and nobody says a word. We call the silence love; it is usually the avoidance of an unpleasant conversation. Three questions tell which you are doing. Have you prayed for this person more than you have rehearsed the sentence? Will it cost you something, or only them? Would you want someone to do the same for you, about your own blind spot?

When did love come to mean agreement? For many today, to love someone is to affirm them and never suggest they might be wrong, because to question how a person lives is to reject the person. It is often meant kindly, but it leaves everyone alone with their mistakes, and it makes love cheap, since agreeing costs nothing. C. S. Lewis observed in The Problem of Pain that what we really want is not so much a Father in heaven as a grandfather in heaven, who likes to see young people enjoying themselves and asks nothing of them. The God of the Bible is better than that, and harder. At the cross he told the most searching truth ever told about us, that our sin was serious enough to cost his Son’s life, and in the same act loved us more than anyone ever has. He did not affirm us as we were; he died to make us new.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers must no longer live as they once did, because they have learned Christ himself. The unbelieving world walks with an empty mind and a hardening heart, sliding into ever hungrier indulgence (vv. 17–19). But that is not how they came to know Christ (vv. 20–21). They were taught, in him, to put off the old self like a rotting garment, to be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and to put on the new self God has created, like him in true righteousness and holiness (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
The old self, the new self and the renewed mind

The old self and new self are not personality types. The Bible speaks of two human families, each with a head. By birth we all belong to Adam’s family and share his fall. The old self is the person we were there, under the rule of sin and corrupted by deceitful desires (v. 22). By faith we are joined to Christ, whom Paul calls the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), the head of a new family. The new self is the person we are in him. To become a Christian is to be moved from the old family into the new.

The renewal of the mind (v. 23) is the inward side of that move, as in Romans 12:2, and the work of a lifetime (see the note on v. 23).

The goal is “the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (v. 24): the image of God restored in Christ (see the note on v. 24). So the Christian life is not chiefly rule-keeping; it is learning to live as who you already are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus offered pleasure in every form and at every price, around the temple of Artemis, the baths and the theatre. Paul does not tell the believers there simply to try harder. He gives them a new identity. The old self’s clothes are to be taken off and thrown away, not kept for occasional wear, and the new self put on.

Now: Today’s culture offers the same temptations, faster and closer to hand, on a screen in every pocket. Paul’s answer has not changed: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind by the gospel. The believer who feeds daily on Scripture and asks the Spirit to renew his mind is not swimming against the current alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must no longer live as unbelievers do, with minds busy about things that are empty. Paul says it under oath, because old patterns do not vanish at conversion.

Now this I say and testify in the Lord. “Testify” (martyromai) is a courtroom word, from martys, witness, the root of our word martyr: Paul speaks like a witness under oath, with Christ’s authority behind him.

You must no longer walk as the Gentiles do. “Walk” picks up verse 1: verses 1–16 showed the worthy walk inside the church; verses 17–24 show it against the world outside. The readers were Gentiles by birth, but Paul now uses “Gentiles” for unbelieving pagans. Their identity has changed so completely that they no longer count as Gentiles in that sense, so they must stop living like outsiders.

In the futility of their minds. “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness: the word family the Greek Old Testament uses for idols, which cannot see, save or satisfy (Jeremiah 2:5), and for the refrain of Ecclesiastes, “vanity of vanities”, a vapour you cannot hold. “Mind” (nous) is the faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. It works well enough, but everything it decides is built around something that is not there. Ephesus, proud of its temple of Artemis (see the introduction), was busy and even religious, aimed at gods who did not exist. Today the idols have changed clothes: the bigger house, the endless scroll, the next achievement that will finally satisfy. Plenty of motion; no destination.

The hunger underneath. God made the heart for himself: “he has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11), and nothing smaller fits the space. We try to fill the ache with good things, family, work, a hard-earned holiday, never built to carry that weight, and the habit does not stop at conversion. A hungry heart is not talked out of eating. Thomas Chalmers, the Scottish preacher, named the cure: “the expulsive power of a new affection”. A child will not drop a broken toy because he is told to, but he drops it gladly for something better. So a lesser love is driven out by a greater: “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). When the itch comes, if I just had that, I would be content, name it as the old hunger, and feed it at its only source: the word, prayer, the Lord’s table, God’s people. Then the good gifts can be enjoyed as gifts, not gods.

Is it not proud to call other people’s minds futile? Only if Paul were claiming that Christians are cleverer or better, and he is not. His readers once walked exactly this way (2:1–3), and so did he (Titus 3:3). Nor is he calling unbelievers’ work, love or art worthless; those are real gifts of God. His claim is about what a life rests on. A fine house built on sand is still a fine house, but it cannot stand in the storm (Matthew 7:26–27). The Christian is not the man who found the answer by being wiser; he is the man who was found (Luke 19:10).

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unbelieving life begins in a hard heart, which darkens the mind, cuts a person off from the life of God, and gives him over to cravings that can never be satisfied. Read the chain from the inside out: the root is not in the head but in the heart. People do not reject God because they lack information; they lack understanding because their hearts are hard towards him.

Darkened in their understanding. The form is passive: they have been darkened, not only darkened themselves. This is not stupidity; these people may be brilliant. What is darkened is the faculty by which a person decides what is worth living for. Like a compass with a bent needle, it still swings confidently, but it points the wrong way. It can look entirely respectable: a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into the career, the retirement fund, the renovated house, nothing scandalous, all reasonable, aimed at a horizon that ends at the grave.

Alienated from the life of God. Picture a flower cut for the table. On Monday it looks perfect, but cut from its root it is already dying; it simply has not shown it yet. This is the spiritual death of 2:1, the very thing Christ came to reverse (John 10:10).

Because of the ignorance that is in them. Not the innocent ignorance of someone who has never heard, but wilful ignorance: the not-knowing of a man who keeps shutting his eyes against the sun and then complains that it is night (Romans 1:21).

Due to their hardness of heart. “Hardness” (pōrōsis) was a medical word for calcification, hard tissue forming where there should be living flexibility. It is not one dramatic rebellion, but small refusals piling up, each making the next easier. Pharaoh is the case study: again and again he hardened his own heart, and again and again the LORD hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12), until God gave him what he kept choosing and left him in it. That is a frightening judgment: not a bolt of lightning, but God handing a person over and no longer stepping in. So Scripture pleads, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–13).

They have become callous. Literally past feeling, like skin burned so often it no longer feels pain.

And have given themselves up to sensuality. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is appetite with the brakes removed, no longer bothering to hide. In Romans 1:24 God gave them up; here they give themselves up.

Greedy to practise every kind of impurity. “Greedy” is wanting more (pleonexia; 5:3). Indulgence does not satisfy; it inflames, and the one who thought freedom lay in removing every limit becomes a slave to cravings that cannot be fed. That endless hunger is itself a clue that the soul was made for something no craving can supply.

The sweetest reversal. Christ was handed over to death in our place, so that we need not be handed over to our cravings; he drank the bitter cup of God’s judgment to the bottom, so that the thirsty might drink the living water he gives (John 4:14). The god of this world blinds (2 Corinthians 4:4), but the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” shines in the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6), and Paul has already prayed for exactly that (1:18). A heart can harden itself, but it cannot soften itself, so God promises to do what the sinner cannot: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Because the whole slide began in the heart, a new heart changes everything that flowed from the old one.

What it does not mean. Not that every unbeliever is equally depraved; Paul describes where the road leads. Many are restrained by conscience, upbringing, law and God’s common grace, the kindness he shows to all (Matthew 5:45). And believers read this with recognition, not superiority: this was the road we were on, and grace interrupted it.

How do I know whether my own heart is hardening, and could it be too late? The warning signs are quiet: sins that once troubled you no longer do; you hear Scripture and feel nothing, and do not mind; you avoid people who might challenge you; you explain away every conviction. If you see some of that, do not despair, but act today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13): confess it plainly, get back under the word and among God’s people, and ask for the heart of flesh God promises. If you fear it is already too late, that fear is itself evidence that it is not; a heart past feeling does not lie awake worrying about it. Nor is the numbness of grief or depression the same thing: a hard heart does not want God, while a sufferer who feels nothing often longs to feel him again. Christ still promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians did not learn a set of ideas but a Person, and no one can learn Christ and keep living the old way. The Greek is emphatic: but you, not so.

You learned Christ. A phrase found nowhere else in the Bible. Not you learned about Christ, or you learned his teaching, but “you learned Christ”: a Person, not a curriculum. In the philosophical schools the master pointed beyond himself to his ideas. Here the Teacher is himself the lesson: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and the knowing never comes to an end. A disciple (mathētēs, a learner) was an apprentice to a Person whose life slowly reshapes his own, until he can say, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

The logic. You cannot learn the pure, self-giving Christ and conclude that self-serving living is fine. A man handed a rule-book keeps rules badly and resents them by Thursday. A man who has come to love a Person finds his behaviour changing from somewhere deeper than his will.

How you learn a person. Read the Gospels to watch him: how he handles interruption, what makes him angry, whom he stops for, how he speaks to people who have failed badly. Pray as conversation, not recitation. And obey, the part we leave out: whoever keeps his commandments is the one to whom he will show himself (John 14:21). Obedience is not the fee for knowing him; you learn what a person is like by doing things alongside him.

In everyday life. Try to say in one sentence what Jesus is like to deal with, not what he did or taught. If that is hard, the gap is the difference between learning about him and learning him.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The truth they were taught is not an abstract idea but a Person, Jesus, in whom they now live.

Assuming that you have heard about him. Or surely you heard him: when the gospel was preached to them, Christ himself was speaking through his messengers (2:17; Romans 10:14, 17).

And were taught in him. In him, not by him. All through this letter believers are “in Christ”, joined to him by faith as a branch is joined to a vine, so that his life flows into theirs. That is why this teaching can do more than inform: it can produce a new self (v. 24).

As the truth is in Jesus. The only place in Ephesians where Paul uses the human name Jesus alone: the man from Nazareth who touched lepers, was crucified under Pilate and rose. You could hand a man the dictionary meaning of courage, or point him to the soldier who threw himself on a grenade for his friends. In Jesus, the truth about God and about what a human life was made to be became a life you can watch. And the truth that is in Jesus (v. 21) stands against the desires of deceit (v. 22): truth against deceit is the real contest.

What it does not mean. Not that truth is relative (my truth); it is found in Jesus (John 14:6; Hebrews 13:8). Nor is every teaching that uses his name true: test it by the Jesus whom the apostles knew and wrote about in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were taught to take off the old self, the person they were before Christ, like a garment rotting through its lying desires. Verses 22–24 give the content of that teaching: put off the old, be renewed, put on the new.

The grammar. Scholars debate whether these are commands (put off!) or a description of what happened at conversion (you have put off); Colossians 3:9–10 speaks of it as having happened. This commentary’s view: both. At conversion, when the believer was joined to Christ, the old self was put off once and for all (Romans 6:6); now believers must keep living out that change day by day (vv. 25–32 give the commands). A wedding works the same way: the vows are made once, and lived out every day after.

To put off. A picture of clothing: to take off and throw away old garments (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5). Not adjusting your wardrobe, but stripping off an entire identity. Later converts took off their old clothes before baptism and put on new white ones afterwards.

Your old self. Literally the old man (Romans 6:6; Colossians 3:9): not the body or the personality, and not just bad habits, but the whole person you were before Christ, a member of Adam’s fallen family, ruled by sin (2:1–3).

And is corrupt. Present tense: is being corrupted, rotting. You do not renovate what is rotting; you put it off.

Through deceitful desires. Literally desires of deceit: they make promises they cannot keep, and there are remarkably few of them. Just this once. You have earned this; look at the week you have had. Nobody will ever know. You can stop whenever you decide to. That is nearly the whole script, and it need not be clever, because it arrives at the moment you are least inclined to examine it. Then look at what is actually delivered: ten minutes afterwards, a slight flatness, the beginning of a wish that it had not happened, and you a little further in. The trouble with the desire is not that it is naughty but that it lies, and the lie costs you something every time you believe it (Hebrews 3:13; James 1:14–15; Genesis 3:4–6).

A truer word. Every lie that desire whispers is answered by “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). And he has done more than answer it: “our old self was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). When he died, the person you used to be died with him, and sin lost its right to rule you.

How do you put off something so deep? By starting from what has already happened. A worker’s cruel boss has been dismissed. The man may still shout orders in the street, and the habit of jumping lingers, but no one has to obey him now. To put off the old self is to believe that, and to stop jumping. And you were raised with Christ too (Colossians 3:1–3), so the next word is not another command to grit your teeth, but a promise: “be renewed”.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians have two equal natures fighting inside them, or are still the old self with a new layer on top. Believers are new people (2 Corinthians 5:17). But remaining sin still lives in us and must be fought (Romans 7:21–25; Galatians 5:17), by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). The fight is real, but the identity is settled.

In everyday life. Bring to mind the thing that most reliably pulls at you, and ask what its record is. Has it ever once delivered what it promised? A desire with a perfect record of lying to you has no claim on your trust. Christ has never deceived you.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were as members of Adam’s fallen family, before we were joined to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between putting off and putting on, God renews the way believers think, from the inside, by his Spirit and his word.

And to be renewed. A daily process, done to us by God: the verb is present and, as most read it, passive. That does not mean we sit and wait, or that we change ourselves by willpower: “work out your own salvation … for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). We cannot manufacture renewal, but we can put ourselves in its way: Scripture, prayer, honest friendship, the preached word (Romans 12:2).

In the spirit of your minds. Our own inner spirit, the mindset from which our thinking flows. God does not only change a few of our opinions; he changes the way we see everything, as new glasses change every single thing you look at.

Why the mind? Because the problem began with darkened understanding (v. 18). Behaviour follows belief: what we think about God, ourselves and the world shapes what we desire and do, and changed thinking comes through the truth as it is in Jesus (v. 21). That truth has a face: we are changed into Christ’s image by beholding his glory (2 Corinthians 3:18), so the mind is made new chiefly by looking long at him.

Renewal is slow, and it is promised. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), “from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation broods over minds bent by years of sin, never hurried and never defeated. John Newton, once the hard-hearted captain of a slave ship, was renewed until that same mind gave the church Amazing Grace. Near the end, his memory almost gone, he said: “I remember two things, that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour.” The God who did it for Newton is doing it for you.

Reflexes, not only information. A renewed mind is not chiefly a mind with more in it, but one whose reflexes have changed. Someone criticises you in front of others: what happens in the first half-second, before you arrange your face? A colleague you consider less able is promoted over you: what is the first movement of the heart? Money is tight and you are awake at two in the morning: what does the mind reach for? You can agree to almost any doctrine at little cost, so measure renewal by the unguarded reaction, and be encouraged, not crushed, by what you find: this is exactly the faculty God has undertaken to renew, slowly and from underneath. The first sign is rarely that the wrong reflex has gone, but that you notice it. A year ago the resentment simply was the truth about the situation; now it arrives, and something in you recognises it as an intruder and declines to agree with it. That is renewal showing its first light.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to put on the new self God has created, a life that bears his likeness in real righteousness and holiness. It is God’s making, not ours, and its pattern is Christ.

To put on. It is not enough to strip off the old; one must be clothed with the new: “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27).

The new self. The person we now are, joined to Christ. In 2:15 Christ made “one new man”, one new humanity, out of Jew and Gentile; the new self is each believer’s own share in it. And it is created, God’s act, like the first creation (2:10). Becoming a Christian is not self-improvement but new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

After the likeness of God. Literally according to God, reaching back to Genesis 1:26–27. Humanity was made in God’s image, to reflect him as a mirror reflects the sun: to know him, love what he loves and care for his world as he would. Sin did not smash the mirror; it turned it away, so that we still have every gift and use it for ourselves (Romans 1:21). In Christ, the perfect image of God (Colossians 1:15), the image is being restored, “renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10). Salvation does not make us less human, but truly human again.

In true righteousness and holiness. Literally righteousness and holiness “of the truth”. The old self’s desires were “desires of deceit” (v. 22); this is real. Righteousness leans towards what we owe our neighbour, holiness towards God: together, a life that reflects God’s own character, the real thing and not a mask.

Cut to the measure of his Son. And it is more than Eden restored. Adam was innocent but able to fall; the pattern of the new self is the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), Christ, tried in every way, obedient to death, risen and beyond all falling. God does not patch old clothes; he creates, and he has cut the garment to the measure of his Son. Righteousness and holiness are the clothes of the risen Christ, and when God has finished dressing his children, nothing in heaven or earth will strip them off (Romans 8:29).

The exhausting work of making a self. Our culture hands every young person a task no earlier generation was given: decide who you are, then build it, display it and keep it up. Identity is no longer received from family, faith or place; it is a project with one author, which sounds like freedom and is also a weight. The French sociologist Alain Ehrenberg argued in The Weariness of the Self that the rise of depression in modern societies is bound up with this burden: the typical distress is no longer guilt at breaking the rules but exhaustion at never being enough. Paul lifts the weight. The new self is “created”, God’s workmanship, not yours (2:10). You need not construct it, defend it online or prove it at work. The self you could never finish building is given to you whole, and it is more truly you than anything you could invent.

How do you actually do it? Picture a child taken off the street and adopted into a noble house. His birth has not changed, but his belonging has, entirely. The old instincts linger: he hoards food, flinches at kindness, waits to be thrown out. Putting on his new self is learning to live as what he truly is, a son at his father’s table; he does not earn the sonship by behaving like a son, but behaves like one because he is (1:5). So in a conversation or a temptation, ask what the person you are in Christ would do, and do it by faith before the feeling follows. Measure it by direction, not perfection. The adopted son still flinches, and is a son all the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The new self shows itself in how members of one body treat each other. Each command puts something off, puts something on and gives a reason from the gospel: truth instead of falsehood, because we are members of one another (v. 25); anger settled before sunset, so that the devil gains no foothold (vv. 26–27); honest work that has something to give (v. 28); words that give grace (v. 29); no grieving of the Spirit who sealed us (v. 30); and bitterness exchanged for kindness and forgiveness, as God in Christ forgave us (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology:
Grieving the Spirit, and forgiving as we were forgiven

Verse 30 shows that the Holy Spirit can be grieved, and so is a Person, not a force (see the note on v. 30).

The same verse says he has sealed us for the day of redemption, so this is not a threat to the believer’s salvation. But how we live does affect our closeness with him. A child who hurts his mother is still her child, yet the home is not happy until it is put right. To grieve the Spirit is to wound the relationship from which our assurance and our growth come.

The closing command (v. 32) sets the measure of Christian forgiveness at the cross (see the note on v. 32).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A mixed congregation brings friction. Paul’s command to speak the truth (v. 25) refuses the small deceptions that keep many communities running smoothly. His command that only what builds up should leave our mouths (v. 29) targets the cutting remark and the diminishing word, the sins most likely to do lasting damage in a church under pressure.

Now: The command not to let the sun go down on our anger is demanding, and in marriages, families and churches it is often broken. We carry grievances and let distance harden into walls. Not every conflict can be settled in an evening; some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work. But the direction must always be towards each other. A church that keeps short accounts and forgives as God in Christ forgave will be noticed, and it will be a sign of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they belong to one another, Christians must put away every kind of falsehood and tell each other the truth. Here the new self begins to show in practice.

The pattern. Each command in verses 25–32 has a negative (put off), a positive (put on) and a gospel motive. No one keeps them perfectly; Christ alone did, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so they are a road for the forgiven, not a test to be passed.

Having put away falsehood. Done in principle when you put off the old self, and now the basis for the command. “Falsehood” (pseudos) is more than outright lying: half-truths designed to mislead, flattery, silence when honesty is needed, the careful management of how others see you, exaggeration, false excuses, broken promises. Lying is the mark of the father of lies (John 8:44). This does not mean saying everything we think: the truth is spoken in love (v. 15), and some things are rightly kept private.

Speak the truth. Paul quotes Zechariah 8:16, where it is one of the terms of life for the people God has brought back from exile and promised to dwell among (Zechariah 8:3, 8). Zechariah’s word now belongs to the new people God dwells in by his Spirit (2:22). “Neighbour” reaches to anyone you deal with, but the next phrase narrows the focus to fellow believers.

For we are members one of another. In a body, each part depends on the others telling it the truth. In leprosy, much of the damage to hands and feet is done because the nerves have stopped reporting: the sufferer does not feel the stone in his shoe, so he walks on it all day, and an injury that cannot be felt cannot be treated. A church in which people do not tell one another the truth is a body in exactly that condition: the marriage quietly failing, the man drifting towards a decision that will wreck him, every one a pain signal that never arrives. And the falsehood that does this is almost never a lie. It is one word, said thousands of times on a Sunday: “fine”.

The faithful and true witness. Christ is “the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14), who never flattered, never managed appearances, and never hid the real state of things to spare himself; yet his truth was always full of grace (John 1:14).

In everyday life. Is there one person in your church who knows the real state of things with you, not just the summary? If not, you are a nerve that has stopped reporting, and the body cannot feel where it hurts.

The hard case: is it ever right to deceive? Not to spare oneself, but to shield a life: a family hiding refugees with soldiers at the door; a man asked by a violent husband where his wife has gone. Scripture itself puts the case. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh’s order to kill the boys and gave him an answer that was almost certainly not the whole truth, and God dealt well with them (Exodus 1:15–21). Rahab hid the spies and sent the king’s men the wrong way, and is commended twice in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). The most careful answer in the Reformed tradition is that the commandment forbids false witness against your neighbour, speech that wrongs someone who has a right to what you know. A murderer at the door has forfeited that right; he is an attacker demanding a weapon, and words are the weapon.

Two guards. Two guards keep this from becoming a licence. First, the door is extremely narrow: an aggressor with no right to the answer, and a life at stake. It does not stretch to the awkward conversation, the padded figure or the reputation being managed; reach for Rahab to spare yourself embarrassment, and you have left the category. Second, some in the tradition say such a person does no wrong; others, more cautiously, that he chooses the lesser evil in a fallen world and needs the same grace as the rest of us. Both agree on what he should do. Corrie ten Boom’s family hid Jews behind a false wall in Haarlem and disagreed about what could rightly be said at the door. Not one of them doubted what they owed each other inside the house, and that is Paul’s subject here.

parallels.desc: speak the truth to one another

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger is not always sin, but it must not be allowed to turn into sin, or be kept overnight.

Be angry and do not sin. Paul quotes Psalm 4:4, best read as a concession and a warning: when you are angry, do not sin. He follows the Greek translation; the Hebrew means to tremble or be stirred up, and David goes on, “ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent”: lay the matter before God rather than rehearse it. There is righteous anger. Jesus looked on hard-hearted people with anger (Mark 3:5) and cleared the temple (John 2:13–17). Never to be angry at child abuse, cruelty or injustice would be a moral failure, not holiness. The sin is in what you do with it. A colleague takes credit for your work: the anger is legitimate. Start quietly undermining him, or lie awake rehearsing it and adding to it, and it has crossed into sin.

Do not let the sun go down on your anger. The word here is irritation, being stirred up (parorgismos). Wages had to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15); the debt of anger should be settled the same day. A fair grievance in the evening becomes resentment by morning, and something darker by next week. Before the day ends, go to the person if you can, or at least hand the anger over to God in prayer (Matthew 5:23–24). A late-night argument may be better postponed; the principle is not to nurse anger or let it settle in.

Before that day’s sun went down. Only God’s anger has never once been sinful, and his righteous anger against our sin was not left unresolved. It was poured out on the Son at the cross, and before that day’s sun went down the account was settled in full (John 19:30).

How to tell the difference. Two questions. First, what was injured? Righteous anger is provoked by damage to someone else, or to God’s honour: the child mistreated, the truth twisted. Sinful anger is almost always provoked by damage to me: my standing, being overlooked, corrected or made to look foolish; much moral indignation is wounded pride in a better coat. Second, what does the anger want? Righteous anger wants the wrong put right. Sinful anger wants the person made smaller; you can tell, because when the offender apologises there is a faint disappointment. Anger that does not want to be resolved has already told you what it is.

The anger that goes underground. Some conscientious Christians have decided that anger is unspiritual and permit themselves none. The anger has not gone; it has only stopped announcing itself. It comes out as sarcasm that can always be defended as humour, a coolness that never quite amounts to rudeness, an unreturned message, a decision taken without consulting somebody: all deniable, none accidental. Buried anger is not put to death; it is put to work, and nobody can address a grievance that has never been stated.

Is it a sin to be angry with God? Anger at God always rests on a mistake about God, for he has never done anything that deserves it, so it is not something to defend. But the Psalms show what to do with it: bring it to him, not away from him. The psalmists ask him how long, and why (Psalm 13:1; 22:1; 42:9), in prayer, as children, not as accusers walking out of the room. If you are angry with him in grief, you are not the first, and he does not turn away from you; Job complained bitterly and was answered, not destroyed. Tell him honestly what you feel, keep listening, and let him point you to the cross, where he showed what he is really like. Anger spoken to God in prayer tends to soften into trust; anger nursed against him in silence hardens into unbelief.

parallels.desc: be angry, and do not sin

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger kept overnight gives the devil a foothold, a place inside your defences from which to divide.

And give no opportunity. “Opportunity” is topos, a place: a foothold, an opening inside your lines, like a squatter moving into an empty room.

To the devil. The slanderer, the one who divides (diabolos), and unresolved anger is his best material. He is a real enemy (6:11–12), though not one to blame instead of ourselves: we give the opportunity; he takes it. He need not tempt you into great sin if you will leave a small wound unattended (2 Corinthians 2:10–11). Nor need we fear him: resist him, and he will flee (James 4:7).

He has no claim on me. On the night before the cross Jesus said, “the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me” (John 14:30). In one human life the devil searched every corner for a foothold and found none: no grudge, no lie, no anger kept overnight. That spotless life was laid down for people full of open doors. So the believer takes his stand in Christ, who gave the devil no ground at all, and every anger handed to Christ before sunset is a door shut in his name.

How the foothold grows. Two elders disagree sharply; neither goes to the other, because it feels awkward and the matter was technically settled. A week later they are polite on Sunday, but something has cooled; within a year there are two quiet camps. No one planned it. A small, unresolved anger was given time to harden, and the devil, who is in no hurry, used it. The foothold is usually granted by something we say to ourselves: It would be awkward. It is not a big deal. I have forgiven it, so there is nothing to discuss. Each can be true, and each can be the polite name for avoidance.

In everyday life. Is there a conversation you have been not having, with the person you now sit a little further from? The remedy is embarrassingly ordinary: a message tonight, not tomorrow, or a sentence at the door, Did I take that the wrong way? Most footholds are closed by one short, awkward exchange that turns out far less terrible than the fortnight of imagining it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel turns a taking hand into a working hand, and then into a giving one.

Let the thief no longer steal. Were there really thieves in the church? Evidently. These congregations probably included many day labourers and household slaves living hand to mouth, and petty theft was part of survival (Titus 2:10). The culture barely blinked. In the body of Christ the common thing is no longer the acceptable thing.

But rather let him labour. Hard, tiring work, with his own hands. Among the educated, manual work was widely despised; Paul, trained at the highest level (Acts 22:3), made tents for a living (Acts 18:3; 20:34). The one laying bricks, cleaning floors or driving a van is doing something the New Testament counts honourable.

So that he may have something to share with anyone in need. The great surprise: the gospel never merely empties a life; it refills it, aimed the other way. Paul does not say so that he may support himself, true and necessary as that is (1 Timothy 5:8; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12), but “so that he may have something to share”, for “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). Zacchaeus got there in an afternoon, once Jesus had invited himself to his house: the tax collector who took gave half his goods away, and Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:5–9). Under both stealing and hoarding lies the fear that nobody will provide unless I secure it myself. The gospel answers it at the root: the God who did not spare his own Son will not fail to give his children what they need (Romans 8:32).

What theft includes. Also padding expense claims, wasting paid time, the cash job kept off the books, borrowed tools that never come home, cheating on taxes, failing to pay a fair wage (Leviticus 19:13; James 5:4).

Hung between two thieves. The carpenter of Nazareth honoured the work of hands with his own, and at the last he was hung on wood between two thieves, and promised one of them paradise that very day (Luke 23:43). This Saviour does not only stop the taking hand; he opens it.

What it does not mean. Not that earning well, owning property or saving is suspect; wise saving and providing for one’s family are good, while covetousness wants more for its own sake or trusts wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). Nor does this verse weigh the worth of anyone who is ill, out of work or past working. It describes the direction a redeemed life travels whenever it has the means: from taking, through honest getting, to giving.

In everyday life. Look at your bank statement. Is anything in it there on purpose for giving, planned first? Or does giving come out of whatever survives the month? Generosity funded by the remainder has a notoriously unreliable donor.

I stole in the past. Do I have to pay it back? Where you can, yes. God’s forgiveness is full and free the moment you turn to Christ, and repaying does not buy it; but real repentance wants to put right what it can. The law required a thief to restore what he took and add to it (Exodus 22:1–4; Numbers 5:6–7), and Zacchaeus, unasked, offered to repay four times over (Luke 19:8). So return the item, repay the employer, correct the tax return, even when it costs you. If the person cannot be found, give the amount to those in need, exactly where this verse points; where the sum is beyond you, take wise counsel and do what you honestly can. It may mean owning up. That is humbling, and it is freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians should speak only words that build others up and carry grace to them. The test of speech is not only whether it is true but whether it builds.

Let no corrupting talk. “Corrupting” (sapros) means rotten, used of rotten fruit or bad fish (Matthew 7:17–18). Gossip, slander, crude jokes, swearing, cutting sarcasm, grumbling and flattery are as out of place in the body of Christ as rotting meat at a feast (5:4; Colossians 3:8; Matthew 12:36). This does not rule out humour that builds up and gives joy.

Come out of your mouths. Words come from the heart (Matthew 12:34); changing the speech requires a changed heart.

But only such as is good for building up. The same word as in verses 12 and 16, and it closes a loophole. We screen our speech with one question: is it true? Gossip is very often true; that is what makes it feel permissible. Paul asks whether it builds. Is it constructive? Is it timely, or am I unloading? Is it for them, or for my own relief? Much of what we say passes the first gate and fails the other three.

As fits the occasion. The right word for the moment and the person: comfort for the grieving, warning for the wandering (Proverbs 25:11).

That it may give grace to those who hear. The same grace (charis) this letter uses for God’s undeserved gift. Your words can carry it: an honest encouragement to someone doubting, a gentle truth to someone drifting, a simple acknowledgement to someone who feels invisible. Two members learn that a third, James, has lost his job. Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t cut out for that role. Possibly true, no grace. Or: James has just lost his job and he’s shaken. Could we pray for him now, and someone ring him this week? Same information; grace given; the body moves towards him instead of past him.

Words of grace. When Jesus taught, people marvelled at “the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22), literally words of grace. Grace-giving speech is not a knack but an imitation of the eternal Word made flesh, whose speech raised the dead, stilled the storm and told sinners that their debts were forgiven.

In everyday life. Measure your words by the empty chair. Would you have said it with him sitting there?

Is it gossip to talk to a friend about someone who has hurt me, or to ask for advice? Not necessarily; it depends on what the conversation is for. Asking a wise believer how to respond, seeking a pastor’s help, or reporting wrongdoing to someone responsible for dealing with it is not gossip. It becomes gossip when the aim is to be agreed with, to lower the other person in the hearer’s eyes, or to enjoy the telling. Tell as few people as you need to, say no more than they need to know, and where it is safe, speak to the person himself before you speak about him (Matthew 18:15). A good counsellor will usually send you back to that person, not keep you company in the grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sinful words and broken relationships grieve the Holy Spirit, who loves us and has sealed us as God’s own until the last day. Paul pulls back the curtain and shows who is in the room, hearing every word.

And do not grieve. Not do not anger the Spirit, or defy him, but do not grieve him. Grief is not the reaction of an official whose rules have been broken, but of someone who loves you: a traffic warden is not grieved when you park badly. Before it is a warning, the verse is a staggering statement of how the Spirit regards you. Your sin does not chiefly irritate him; it wounds him, because he loves you, and that the eternal God should open himself to grief over people like us is a mercy almost too high to think about.

Which sins? The command sits among commands about speech and relationships: falsehood, though he is the Spirit of truth (John 16:13); unresolved anger, though he keeps the unity of peace (4:3); corrupting talk, though he builds up the body; bitterness and slander (v. 31), the opposite of his fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). The Spirit who makes believers one is grieved by what divides them. He is not grieved by weakness, failure or honest struggle; in those he helps us and prays for us (Romans 8:26). He is grieved by willing, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

The Holy Spirit of God. He is holy, so sin grieves him; and he is God’s Spirit, so to grieve him is to grieve God, who has made his home in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19). No sin is ever private.

Only a person can be grieved. You cannot grieve a force. The Holy Spirit is a person, who knows, wills and loves (1 Corinthians 2:10–11; 12:11; Romans 15:30). Israel “rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit” in the wilderness (Isaiah 63:10); the church must not repeat Israel’s sin.

By whom you were sealed. In Paul’s world an owner pressed his seal into wax on a parcel or a letter. It said: this is mine, and no one may open it before it arrives. The Holy Spirit living in you is God’s seal on you (1:13–14). You belong to God, and he will bring you safely home.

For the day of redemption. To redeem is to buy a slave’s freedom, and the price is already paid in Christ’s blood (1:7). The day of redemption is the day Christ returns, when our bodies are raised and we are free from sin for good (1:14; Romans 8:23). On that day the last chain falls.

A third kind of sin. We file our sins as rule-breaking or self-harm, and both are strangely bearable. This is sin done in front of someone living inside you, who feels it. A man who will break a rule without a flicker can be undone the moment he realises he has hurt his mother. Paul is speaking to that man, which is to say all of us.

In everyday life. On the edge of the thing you keep going back to, the second look, the cutting reply already loaded, do not reach first for this is forbidden, true as it is. Reach for this: someone who loves me is here, this will hurt him, and he is here to give me strength to turn away. You can grow hard to a rule. It is very hard to keep wounding, to his face, a Person who has decided never to leave.

What it does not mean. Not a threat that sin will make the Spirit leave, or that believers can lose their salvation; they are sealed until the day of redemption. The Spirit grieves precisely because he stays: the grief of a love that will not let go, not of weakness.

I know I have grieved him. What do I do now? Go straight back, today, without waiting until you feel worthy. Name the sin to God plainly and trust his promise: “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). Christ’s blood covers this sin too, and he is pleading for you with the Father now (1 John 2:1). Where you have wronged someone, put it right with them as well. Then do not keep your distance as a self-imposed punishment, like a servant on probation who stays away until he feels presentable. The Spirit’s grief is not cold anger waiting to be paid off but love wanting you back, and the way to stop grieving him is to come home and walk with him again.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security until delivery.

parallels.desc: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every form of resentment, from the bitterness inside to the malice that wishes harm, must be put away. Not some, but every trace: six words, laid down like weapons surrendered.

Bitterness. The settled sourness (pikria) of a soul that has been wounded and chosen to nurse the wound. It is the one that does not feel like sin. Wrath makes a scene you regret, and slander you know is unkind as you say it, but bitterness feels like justice. It grows in genuinely wronged soil, and the resentment feels less like a sin to repent of than a fact to be honoured; perhaps that is why Paul lists it first. It does not punish the person who wronged you. It punishes you, daily, on his behalf: he may be asleep, having forgotten the whole thing, while you lie awake rehearsing it, giving him free lodging in a mind he does not know he occupies. And it spreads: a root of bitterness causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15), leaking into your tone, the warnings you pass on, the coldness a whole room can feel.

Wrath and anger. Wrath (thymos) is often the sudden hot flare (James 1:19–20); anger (orgē) its cold twin, brooding resentment that builds a case and waits.

Clamour. Shouting, brawling (kraugē): a private grievance turned into a public scene.

Slander. Speech that damages another person’s name (blasphēmia), whether false or maliciously true. The same word is used for blasphemy against God, and in the church it attacks the members of Christ’s body, and so Christ himself (Acts 9:4).

Along with all malice. Ill will (kakia), taking pleasure in others’ misfortune, perhaps last because it is the soil the others grow in.

The progression. Read in order, the list shows resentment growing when it is not dealt with: from a bitter spirit within, to outbursts, to shouting, to slander, to a settled wish for the other’s harm. It begins in the heart, and so must the cure.

He did not revile in return. Christ had more cause for bitterness than anyone who has ever lived. “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), and on the cross he prayed for the men who drove the nails (Luke 23:34). The malice poured out on him became the very means of our healing (Isaiah 53:5).
