What it does not mean. Not that Christians must pretend they have never been hurt. Grief over wrong is not bitterness; bitterness is refusing to let the wrong go. Paul does not say the wrong did not happen, but set down the thing you are carrying. Nor does this forbid naming wrong or seeking justice through proper channels.

How do I put bitterness away? Seldom in one go. First, tell God the whole story: “pour out your heart before him” (Psalm 62:8). Second, hand the case over; bitterness is a court that never adjourns, so give the case to the real Judge: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19), as Christ “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Third, stand again at the cross and look at the size of your own debt, cancelled at his cost (Colossians 2:13–14). Fourth, pray for the person by name, asking God to do them good (Luke 6:28); a grudge seldom survives honest prayer for its object. Fifth, when the old speech starts up at two in the morning, decline to finish it. Timothy Keller often pointed out that forgiveness is granted before it is felt: you make the decision, and keep making it, and the feelings follow. And the Spirit who sealed you (v. 30) loosens the grip.

Textual note. Jesus’ prayer, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), is missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but it is found in many others and many scholars think it a true record of his words, so most modern Bibles keep it, often with a footnote.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of bitterness, Christians are to be kind, tender and forgiving, passing on the forgiveness God gave them in Christ. What God did for us is both the measure and the motive of what we do for one another.

Be kind to one another. “Kind” (chrēstos) means useful, good, generous: the word was used of old wine, mellowed and no longer sharp (Luke 5:39), and of Jesus’ easy yoke (Matthew 11:30). God is kind even to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35; 2:7).

Tenderhearted. Literally with good bowels (eusplanchnos), where the ancients located deep emotion: a heart moved by another’s pain, like Christ’s compassion for the crowds (Matthew 9:36), the opposite of the hardened heart of verse 18.

Forgiving one another. Charizomenoi shares its root with charis, grace: gracing one another, releasing them from the debt they owe you. It is hard because it feels like letting them off.

As God in Christ forgave you. A friend borrows your car and dents it. If you forgive him, the dent does not vanish: you pay for the repair yourself. Forgiveness always works like that; the one who was wronged bears the cost instead of making the other pay. At the cross God did exactly this. He did not pretend our debt did not exist; in Christ he paid it himself. Having been forgiven so much, we cannot refuse to forgive others so little (Matthew 18:21–35); we are only passing on what we have received (Romans 2:4; Psalm 103:13).

How it hides. Sarah fell out with Mark six months ago. He spoke sharply to her in front of others and never apologised. She serves beside him on Sundays but keeps her distance, has told two friends, and believes she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day. She has let go of the sharp pain but kept the verdict: he still owes her. The way forward is a decision made in prayer at the cross: Lord, I release this; I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I give the same. Then behaviour follows: a genuine word to him, an end to the quiet commentary, and the decision made again tomorrow if need be.

In the flow. The chapter ends here; the thought does not: “be imitators of God, as beloved children” (5:1–2).

In everyday life. Who do you need to forgive today? Begin by remembering what God has forgiven you. And if you cannot get there yet, pray as someone who wants to want it: Lord, I am not able to release this; make me willing. That prayer is the beginning of obeying.

What it does not mean. This verse can be turned into a cruelty, and it has been said, in a kind voice, to people it then badly hurt. Forgiveness does not mean the wrong was small, or calling evil good, or that you must feel warmly. It does not always mean restoring trust at once: trust is rebuilt over time, and wisdom may require boundaries, especially where there has been abuse. It never means returning to a place where you are still being harmed, or dropping a safeguard. It does not remove just consequences: a forgiven thief may still need to repay, and crimes should be reported to the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:1–4). And it is not the same as reconciliation, which needs both sides. Forgiveness means releasing the debt, refusing revenge, refusing to keep bringing the wrong up, and wishing the other person good. Where the wound is deep, it is often done again on Tuesday, having been done on Monday, without that meaning it was insincere the first time.

If I have forgiven, why do I still remember it and feel it? Because forgiving is not forgetting, and feelings heal more slowly than decisions are made. When God says he will remember our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34), he has not lost the memory; he will never hold them against us. That is your promise too: not that the memory will vanish, but that you will not use it as a weapon. When it returns with the old heat, that is not proof that you never forgave but the moment to forgive again: Lord, I released this, and I release it again. Over time the memory usually loses its sting, until it reminds you more of God’s grace than of the wound.

Where Christians differ: must the offender repent first? Jesus said, if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3), so some Christians hold that forgiveness, like God’s, is complete only when the offender repents. This commentary’s view: both are true when forgiveness is seen in its two parts. In the heart, before God, the wronged person lets go of bitterness and the wish for revenge, whether or not the other repents (v. 31; Mark 11:25). The restored relationship, the forgiveness spoken and received, waits for repentance, as God’s reconciliation with us does. So a believer must not nurse a grudge, but neither must he pretend that nothing happened.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 shows that justification and sanctification belong together. The grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make him righteous: not all at once, but surely. The commands of this chapter are not conditions for being accepted but the life of people already accepted (see the note on v. 1).

The chapter also teaches what it means to be a church: not a set of private spiritual journeys that happen in the same building, but members joined to one another, helped by their gifts and harmed by their sins.

At the centre stands the renewal of the mind, the Spirit’s work and not willpower (this is treated fully at v. 23).
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture full of the patterns Paul describes in verses 17–19: idol worship, sexual licence, and a morality where the main thing to avoid was public shame. To put that off was not a small adjustment but a new identity. Truth-telling, honest work and free forgiveness made the church a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The pressures are the same: the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more, the temptation to manage people instead of telling them the truth. The command still stands, not because we must earn our standing, which is secured in Christ, but because we have been made new. Renewal is what happens when a Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of brooding, and speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one, and then does it again tomorrow.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 is the hinge of the letter. After three chapters on what God has done in Christ, Paul turns with a “therefore” to how such people walk, and lays the foundation for all that follows: a united church, growing up together, made of people who have put on a new self.

The message. God has called you into one family, so walk in a way that fits it. Guard the unity the Spirit has already made. Use the gifts the ascended Christ hands out, so that the whole body grows up into him. And since you have learned Christ, take off the old self like a rotten garment and put on the new self God has created, which shows in truth, settled anger, giving hands, gracious words and forgiveness passed on.

Why it was said. These young churches of converted pagans and Jewish believers had only lately been made one body across an old hostility (2:11–22). The life they had left was all around them (see the introduction), and false teachers would soon rise even among their own leaders (Acts 20:29–30). They needed to know how to stay together, how to grow up and how to stop living as they used to.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–6 call for humble, patient love that keeps the Spirit’s unity, resting on one Lord, one faith and one God and Father. Verses 7–16 show that unity is not sameness: the risen Christ, like the conqueror of Psalm 68 sharing out the spoil, gives grace to each believer and ministers of the word to equip all the saints, until the body is mature, steady and built up in love. Verses 17–24 set the new life against the old: the pagan mind is empty and its heart hard, but the readers learned Christ, and were taught to put off the old self and put on the new. Verses 25–32 show the new self in commands that each carry a gospel reason, ending in forgiveness “as God in Christ forgave you”.

Where it leads. At the centre stands the Christ who came down to the lowest place and “ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (v. 10). Everything the chapter asks flows from him: the unity he bought, the gifts he gives, a maturity measured by his stature, a new self cut to his likeness, a forgiveness he paid for. The church does not grow towards an ideal but “into him who is the head, into Christ” (v. 15).

For us. This is a chapter about ordinary church life: the person you find hard to bear, the gift you have not used, the old desire that still lies to you, the grudge you are keeping. Ask where you still walk like the person you used to be, and look again at the one you learned.

keyVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called,
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the whole letter: everything in chapters 1–3 is the calling, and everything from here to the end is the walk that fits it. The order is the gospel itself. God calls first and the life follows, so obedience is never the price of belonging to him but the way his called people live.

4.reflection:
Paul’s first commands are humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another (v. 2), not great deeds. Why are these the qualities that keep a church one? Who in your church might be quietly bearing with you?

Verses 7–12 say that every believer has been given grace to serve, and that pastors and teachers are given to equip the saints for the work of ministry. What would change in your church if every member took this seriously? Where could you begin to serve?

Paul calls the desires of the old self “deceitful” (v. 22). What promises does your most familiar temptation make, and has it ever kept one? How does knowing Christ himself (vv. 20–21) loosen its grip?

Verse 32 measures our forgiveness by God’s forgiveness of us in Christ. What makes forgiving someone hard for you, and how does remembering what you have been forgiven change it? What does forgiveness not require of you?

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because Christ gave himself for you, love that takes for itself has no place in your life. Paul sets one pattern over everything, Christ’s self-giving love (vv. 1–2), and then names its counterfeits: sexual sin, impurity and greed, which use others for ourselves, and crude talk, which turns them into a joke (vv. 3–4). These are not small matters, for they mark the life of those outside God’s kingdom (v. 5), so do not believe the voices that call them harmless, and do not join in (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as an offering to God

Paul describes Christ’s death in the language of Israel’s sacrifices: an offering God receives with delight. It was the perfect offering all those sacrifices pointed to.

That gives ordinary love a surprising dignity (see the note on v. 2).

Paul calls greed idolatry (see the note on v. 5), and lust shares its root (v. 3). The gospel answers both at the root, with “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Greek philosophers spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the soul, but Paul points the other way (see the note on v. 1).

Now: Sexual freedom is often presented today as self-expression, and greed as healthy ambition. Paul does not answer with a longer list of rules but with who we are: children loved by a God who gave his Son for us. The call to walk in love is not a burden laid on us from outside. It comes from a Father who wants his children to share his likeness and his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live like your Father, because you are his dearly loved child. Paul does not tell us to imitate God in order to become his children, but the reverse: we already are his beloved children, so the family likeness should show.

Therefore. The verse continues 4:32, “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you”. What God has done becomes the pattern for what we do.

Imitators of God. Imitators (mimētai, from which we get mimic): the only place in the New Testament that calls believers imitators of God (compare Matthew 5:48; 1 Peter 1:15–16), in character, not power. Philosophers of the day sought “likeness to God” by climbing upward, through withdrawal, discipline and secret knowledge, becoming of use to fewer and fewer people. Paul reverses the direction. The God we imitate came down, gave himself up for his enemies and died in public between two criminals; so Paul at once defines the likeness as walking in love (v. 2), which sends us down among ordinary people to serve them.

As beloved children. No father explains to a three-year-old how to be like him. The boy simply appears one Saturday with a plastic hammer, or stands with his hands in his pockets the way his father stands. The fastest way to become like the Father is not to try harder but to be with him more (Acts 4:13).

Beloved in the Beloved. God has already “blessed us in the Beloved” (1:6). Joined by faith to his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17), we have the love that rests on him (John 17:23): not strangers on probation, but children he is glad to see (Galatians 4:4–7). And since no one has ever seen God, but the only Son has made him known (John 1:18), to imitate God is to watch Jesus: the hands laid on lepers, the patience with slow disciples, the prayer for the men driving in the nails. The eldest Son wore the family likeness perfectly, and we are being conformed to his image, that he might be “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

Not content to have only one. The Father had one beloved Son from all eternity, and he was not content to have only one. So the Son took our likeness, that we might wear his. Every small family resemblance in a Christian, a grudge let go, a kindness to an enemy, is the Father seeing his Son again in another face, and delighting in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love the way Christ loved you: by giving yourself away. The measure of Christian love is not a feeling but the cross, where Christ gave himself for us freely and at full cost, and God received the gift with delight.

Walk in love. Not soar or feel, but walk: one foot after the other. Love is a direction to be kept, not a temperature to be checked. A man walking north is walking north whether or not he is enjoying the weather.

As Christ loved us. This love (agapē) chooses the other’s good at cost to itself, and Christ loved not admirers but enemies (Romans 5:8). His love never responded to loveliness, which is why it can be commanded of you towards people who have not earned it.

Gave himself up for us. Not only things or time, but himself, to death, in our place (Galatians 2:20), and freely (John 10:18). Freely given and enormously costly: that is the shape of Christian love.

A fragrant offering and sacrifice. A gift God accepts with delight. Israel’s burnt offerings sent their smoke up to God; when Noah left the ark and built an altar, the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and said in his heart that he would never again curse the ground (Genesis 8:21). Every sacrifice pointed to this one: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Not that the Father enjoyed his Son’s pain, but that the offering fully satisfied his holy justice: the punishment our sin deserved was truly borne, so that God can welcome sinners and remain just. Paul’s word for such a sacrifice is propitiation, an offering that turns away God’s just anger (Romans 3:25–26).

Before it is a pattern, it is a gift. If “as Christ loved us” were only a standard to reach, none of us would pass. But before the cross is a pattern to copy, it is a gift to receive, and we are now “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). The smoke from Calvary has never stopped rising, and the Father has never stopped being pleased with it. What pleases God in you is not the quality of your loving this week, but the fragrance of an offering someone else made, which you are covered in. No bad week can sour it.

Your love, the same fragrance. Paul uses “a fragrant offering” once more, of the parcel the Philippians sent him in prison: “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). A bag packed for a friend in trouble, and the apostle reaches for the language of the altar. The meal for the family whose week has collapsed, the bill quietly paid: these go up. That answers the weariness of loving someone who does not notice: the daughter who drives every Saturday to a mother who no longer knows her name; the one who has held a marriage together alone for eleven years, never thanked. The last two words are “to God”: the smoke goes up, not across. Noticed or not, it arrived. Nothing spent in love has gone nowhere.

What it does not mean. Not that love has no limits or must tolerate sin; Christ’s love aims at our holiness (v. 27). Nor does “gave himself up” mean absorbing whatever harm is done to you and calling it love: Christ’s self-giving was chosen and aimed at rescue (see the note on v. 22). The command to walk in love has never contained a command to stand still and be destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sex outside marriage, impurity and greed are love turned inside out, and they have no place among God’s people. Where Christ gave himself for others, these take others for ourselves, so a people set apart for God should not make room for them at all.

Love’s counterfeits. “But” sets these sins against v. 2, where Christ gave himself up for us. Sexual immorality uses another’s body for my pleasure, where Christ gave his body for another’s life. Greed reaches for more than its share, where he who was rich became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9). Impurity feeds on what it should protect, where he gave himself to make his bride clean (v. 26).

Sexual immorality. Porneia: every sexual act outside the marriage of a man and a woman, including adultery, sex before marriage, prostitution, homosexual acts and pornography (the words share a root). Not because the body is evil; it belongs to God (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Sex says with the body what husband and wife have promised in words: “I am wholly yours, for life.” Outside marriage the body makes that promise while the person withholds it (1 Corinthians 6:16).

All impurity. Uncleanness (akatharsia) in thoughts, words, images and desires as well as acts (Matthew 5:28). “All” closes the loopholes: what never reaches the bed still defiles the heart.

Covetousness. Wanting more (pleonexia) than God has given. Greed and lust are one appetite, the conviction that what God has given is not enough (1 Thessalonians 4:6), and greed is the sin respectable people commit and rarely confess.

Must not even be named among you. Paul has just named all three, so he does not forbid the sermon that warns, the confession that admits, or the parent who explains to a teenager what pornography does to a soul (vv. 11–13). He forbids the naming that makes a thing ordinary: the affair discussed as entertainment over coffee. Things become acceptable by being mentioned often enough in a relaxed tone.

As is proper among saints. A saint is not a spiritual hero but anyone God has set apart as his own, as every believer is (1:1): “you are saints, so live in the way that fits.”

The setting. In Ephesus sexual licence was woven into ordinary life and religion: festivals, temple banquets, drunken revels. Prostitution was legal and taxed, and a husband’s use of slaves or prostitutes was not counted as adultery. (The popular claim that the temple of Artemis kept sacred prostitutes is not well supported by the evidence from Ephesus itself.) Sexual sin and idolatry were often one act, which is why Paul ties them together (v. 5). Greed was as respectable: the temple was also the province’s bank (see the introduction), and Demetrius raised a riot with profit and piety in one speech (Acts 19:25–27).

Jesus was tempted. He “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He never once grasped at more than his Father gave, and he now helps the tempted as one who has stood where they stand (Hebrews 2:18). Being tempted, even strongly and repeatedly, cannot in itself be sin.

What it does not mean. Not that owning, earning or saving is wrong. Providing for your family and managing money well are good stewardship (1 Timothy 5:8), and God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Paul was ambitious and said so (Romans 15:20). Greed measures itself against a neighbour and wants a larger share; godly ambition measures itself against the task and wants it done well, for others and for God. Is it held open-handed as a trust, or clutched as security? Likewise, desire for marriage, and sex within it, is good (1 Corinthians 7:2–5).

Nor that temptation is sin. Paul condemns sexual sin, not being tempted, a difference that guards against both excuse and despair. “Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15). An attraction felt is temptation; sin is conceived when the heart says yes, and welcomes, dwells on, replays or acts on it (Matthew 5:28). As Luther put an old saying: “You cannot stop the birds flying over your head, but you can stop them building a nest in your hair.” The unwanted thought that flashes in and is hated is a call to fight, not a verdict of guilt.

What this means in practice. A believer who feels attraction to someone not his spouse, or struggles with unwanted desires of any kind, including same-sex attraction, is not by that fact one of the “impure” of v. 5. He is a soldier in a fight. Turn away at once (2 Timothy 2:22), turn the mind to something good (Philippians 4:8), pray, tell a trusted believer, and remove what feeds the desire (Romans 13:14); God will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). If you fall, do not hide: confess quickly and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Tormenting thoughts lose much of their power in the light (v. 13).

Is this not just an old-fashioned, repressive view of sex? In Ephesus it was the new thing. The world the church entered used slaves, prostitutes and even wives as bodies, and the Christian ethic protected them: one standard for men and women, and no one’s body a thing for another’s pleasure. Every society draws sexual lines (ours draws them at consent); the question is who sets them, and Scripture’s answer is the God who made the body and in his Son gave his own body for us. His limits are a fence around a gift, not a cage around a prisoner. And for those who have crossed them, he is the God who washes: “such were some of you,” Paul told another church, “but you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Where Christians differ: is our fallen nature itself sinful? This differs from asking whether temptation is sin. Roman Catholic teaching holds that the inclination to sin left in the baptised (concupiscence) is not itself sin until we consent. Reformed theology holds that the corruption of nature remaining in believers is truly sin, though in Christ it is pardoned and being put to death (Westminster Confession 6.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 6.5; Romans 7:17–23); it means the sin that dwells in us, not the experience of temptation, which Christ knew without a fallen nature. This commentary’s view: the Reformed view is more faithful to Romans 7, and fits all that is said above. Three things must be kept distinct. Temptation is not sin: Christ faced it, and the believer who turns from it has resisted, not sinned. The fallen nature that makes us open to it is the remnant of sin we fight and grieve over, yet for those in Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1), so it calls for humility and dependence, not guilt over every passing thought. Consenting to temptation, by entertaining, feeding or acting on it, is sin committed, which needs repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians do not treat people and sex as cheap jokes; they give thanks for them as God’s gifts. Paul’s cure for a dirty mouth is not silence but gratitude.

Filthiness and foolish talk. Speech shows the heart (Luke 6:45) and shapes it: what we joke about, we begin to take lightly. Filthiness is obscene talk; foolish talk (mōrologia, fool-talk) is empty speech, especially the kind that drifts into the indecent.

Crude joking. The ready wit (eutrapelia). Aristotle called it a virtue; Paul names it a vice, because of what that cleverness is usually used for: making degrading things funny through innuendo, and turning people into material. It is out of place, like muddy boots at a wedding.

But instead let there be thanksgiving. The surprising cure, which replaces the habit instead of merely suppressing it (4:28). Crude joking treats people and God’s gifts, especially sex, as material for a laugh; thanksgiving treats them as gifts and names the Giver. A man who begins genuinely thanking God for his wife will find the jokes about her drying up without ever having made a rule.

The mouth that gave thanks. The word is eucharistia. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus “took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it” (1 Corinthians 11:23–24): the darkest night in history, and his mouth spoke thanks. Crude joking makes people smaller to get a laugh; the gracious words of Christ (Luke 4:22) made the small great: the woman of the city, the tax collector up a tree, the thief beside him. Those who eat at his table cannot comfortably use their mouths to degrade what he gave his body to redeem.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be humourless; that produces strain, not holiness. There is wit on the lips of Jesus: a camel through the eye of a needle (Mark 10:25), the log in your own eye (Matthew 7:3–5). The target is humour that degrades.

What about the comedy and drama I watch? Laughing along on the sofa is still laughing along. Christians may enjoy good comedy, and drama that shows sin honestly, as Scripture tells of David’s adultery without making it funny or enticing. Ask whether a programme grieves the sin it shows, exposes it, or sells it as entertainment; humour that runs on innuendo and contempt trains your sense of normal every evening you give it. Does it leave me more thankful or more jaded? Do I switch it off when the children come in? If you already know the answer, the remote is in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These sins are not minor faults: a life ruled by them is a life outside God’s kingdom. Greed in particular is unmasked as idolatry, the worship of something other than God.

You may be sure of this. The three sins of v. 3 now become nouns that describe a person by his way of life: the sexually immoral person (pornos), the impure person, the covetous person (pleonektēs). Paul means people whose lives are ruled by these things, not people who have ever fallen into them.

(That is, an idolater). Greed is not like idolatry; it is idolatry. We can see how a man worships a carved image, but not how he worships a bank balance. So ask what an idol does. It tells its worshipper who he is and that he is safe; it receives his best hours; it sets the terms of his joy; and it decides what he will sacrifice: time, integrity, his marriage, his children’s memory of him. In a man who cannot stop wanting more, every one fits (Matthew 6:24; Colossians 3:5). It is the hardest idol to see, because greed wears the clothes of diligence and prudence.

Has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. God’s children inherit his kingdom (1:14, 18); those who live as slaves to these things show that they are not his children. “The kingdom of Christ and God” is one kingdom, shared by Son and Father, a quiet witness that Christ is God, and we inherit only as fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17; Hebrews 1:2). So the question is finally not whether you have kept a list, but whether you belong to him. The greedy man looks for treasure in the wrong place; in Christ are hidden all the treasures (Colossians 2:3).

In everyday life. An idol holds power only while it goes by another name. What loss would feel like the end of you? What did you last lie awake over? Name it, and you can stop asking it for what it was never able to give.

A question that troubles many believers. A Christian who struggles with lust, pornography or greed may fear this verse means he is lost. Three things help. First, Paul describes a settled pattern a person accepts and does not fight, not the believer who falls, hates it, confesses it and keeps fighting (Romans 7:18–25; 1 John 1:8–9): the question is whether you are at peace or at war with your sin. “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24) is the cry of one who belongs to Christ and is not yet what he will be; the believer is not one who never falls, but one who cannot stay down. Second, Paul includes the covetous, so no reader can think this list is only about other people.

Written to the washed. Third, Paul writes to people already saved by grace (2:8–9) and sealed by the Spirit as God’s own (1:13–14). After a similar list he says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). If this verse troubles you, the trouble is itself a sign of life; the person Paul warns is not troubled at all. The cure for a troubled conscience is not to soften the warning, but to run to Christ.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer lose the inheritance? Many sincere Christians in the Arminian tradition (which holds that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) believe that true Christians can fall away for good, and read this verse as a warning that a believer who returns to these sins will lose the kingdom. This commentary’s view: the warning is real and must be taken seriously, but it does not describe a true believer losing what God has sealed (1:13–14; 4:30). God’s children will not settle into a life ruled by these sins; one who does so and never repents shows that he never truly belonged to Christ, whatever he professed (1 John 2:19; 3:9). God uses such warnings to keep his people persevering.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not believe anyone who tells you these things do not matter; God’s judgment says they do. The danger is not only the sin but the soothing words that excuse it.

Let no one deceive you with empty words. Paul’s other letters show what such voices said: the body does not matter; grace makes sin harmless (1 Corinthians 6:12–13; Romans 6:1). Such words work because they are half true. God is gracious; this does not really matter. But grace is not God’s indifference to sin; it is what it cost him to deal with it, and to call sin unimportant is to call Calvary an overreaction. Everyone struggles with this. A reason to be gentle with others, not to stop fighting; “struggle” is often the word of someone who has stopped struggling and would like to keep the word. A loving God would never judge. A father who watched his child being destroyed and felt nothing would not be loving. Wrath is not the opposite of love; indifference is.

Where empty words come from. Rarely from the enemies of the faith. From a friend who wants us comfortable, from a teacher who has learned that the pleasant half of the message fills a room, and most often from ourselves, at eleven at night, building a case in our own favour.

The wrath of God. Not a tantrum, but the fixed resolve of a holy God against everything that destroys those made in his image, shown now (Romans 1:18) and coming in full at the judgment (Colossians 3:6). “Sons of disobedience” are people whose character is disobedience, as all of us were before Christ (2:2–3).

The obedient Son. Here is the wonder: the wrath that comes on the sons of disobedience fell first and fully on the obedient Son, so that all who trust him are saved from it. His holiness took our sin seriously enough to judge it, and his love took it seriously enough to bear it himself.

What it does not mean. Not that believers should fear God’s wrath as their sentence; Christ has borne it for those who trust him (Romans 5:9; 8:1). The warning is aimed at the conscience that wants permission, not at the believer who fights, grieves and returns.

In everyday life. When a line of reasoning arrives that happens to permit exactly what you already wanted, treat its convenience as evidence against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not join in with them. You have been made partners in God’s promise; do not become partners in the way of life that has no part in his kingdom.

Do not become partners with them. “Partners” (symmetochoi, co-sharers) appears only once elsewhere in the New Testament, in this letter, translated “partakers”: Gentiles are “fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (3:6). So Paul is asking which partnership you are really in. And “become” is present tense: do not drift into it.

The setting. Converts in Ephesus lived among family and guild members who still practised these things at temple feasts, guild gatherings and in private homes (see the introduction).

Your partner already. A believer already has a partner, Christ himself, whose promise, body and inheritance are shared with outsiders at the cost of his blood. Holiness here is not first a fence around the world but faithfulness to someone. You cannot be a co-sharer in Christ and in the works of darkness at once, any more than you can give your whole loyalty to two sides.

In everyday life. Compromise is rarely a decision. It is usually a silence: the laugh you gave so as not to seem difficult, the objection you did not raise. Behind most such silences is the fear of not being liked, and the cure is not grim courage but knowing whose approval you already have: “am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?” (Galatians 1:10). Somewhere you would rather not have to describe, ask not “Am I doing anything wrong?” but “If the people I love and the Lord I serve were both watching, what would my being here be saying?”

What it does not mean. Not withdrawal from unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Jesus was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). He sat at their tables yet never shared in their sin; he came among us without becoming like us in our darkness, so that we might share in his light. The line runs not between people but between practices: not whether you go to the party, but whether you take part in what happens there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You do not need to become light; you already are, so live as what you are. Once darkness, believers are now light in the Lord (v. 8), and it shows in goodness, rightness, truth and a heart that asks what pleases him (vv. 9–10). Light also does what light does: it refuses the works of darkness and brings them into the open (vv. 11–12), where what is exposed can be changed, as Christ shines on the sleepers he wakes (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, darkness and the witness of holiness

Paul does not say his readers were in darkness but that they were darkness, and are now light: a change of nature, God’s own work (see the note on v. 8).

The call to take no part in darkness but to expose it (v. 11) asks for something harder than either withdrawing from the world or blending into it (see the note on vv. 11–12). A church that is visibly holy serves the world as well as its own members, because by contrast it shows what the world cannot see about itself.

The short hymn of v. 14 carries the urgency of the passage. The church is the company of people Christ has woken. And it wakes others less by shouting at the darkness than by shining in it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus had a flourishing trade in magic and mystery rites (see the note on vv. 11–12). Christians who lived openly before God, with nothing to hide, were themselves a witness against that culture.

Now: Our world is often less hostile than drowsy, numbed by comfort and distraction and taking its way of life as simply normal. A church that is awake, seeing life in the light of God’s word and living accordingly, is itself an invitation to come and see what happens when Christ shines on someone.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are no longer darkness but light, so live as light. The command rests on a change that has already happened: the Lord has made you new, and your behaviour is to catch up with who you are.

In the flow. The “for” at the start of verse 8 gives the reason for verse 7: you are no longer what they are.

At one time you were darkness. Paul has written that biography already: dead in trespasses, children of wrath (2:1–3); “having no hope and without God in the world” (2:12); darkened in understanding (4:18). And notice: not “in the dark” but darkness itself. It was our nature. Our desires, thinking and will were turned from God, so that even our good deeds were done without love for him (Romans 8:7–8). Left to ourselves we loved the darkness (John 3:19), and could no more change that by trying harder than a dark room can light itself.

But now you are light. Not “you are in the light” or “you have some light”: you are light, a change of nature, not only of place. The Spirit of Christ lives in you, so you begin to love what God loves, want the truth about yourself seen, and shine on those around you (Matthew 5:14–16). You still sin, but you no longer love it: you hate it, confess it and fight it, because your nature has changed sides. And God did not fan a spark in you; darkness has no raw material. It was creation: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6), Genesis 1:3 spoken over a human being. If you suspect God got less than he bargained for with you, remember: nobody was a promising case.

In the Lord. The light is not generated by you. The moon is truly light; sailors have crossed oceans by it. Yet all its light is borrowed, as ours is from him who is the light of the world (John 8:12), and turned from the sun it is a cold rock. Neither fact cancels the other. The honest reader who remembers what went through his mind on the drive home, and decides “light” cannot describe him, is looking for a glow of his own, which the verse never said he had. Turn round and face Christ, as the moon faces the sun.

Walk as children of light. In Hebrew idiom a son of something is marked by it (Luke 16:8; John 12:36). As in 5:1, the family you belong to is the reason for the behaviour, never the price of admission. Most of us try to walk well enough to earn the identity. Paul hands you the identity and then asks for the walk.

In everyday life. Think of the last time you sinned badly enough to be ashamed. Sin in a child of light sits wrong, will not settle, wants confessing. A stain shows on white cloth and disappears on black; that yours showed tells you what colour the cloth is.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light shows itself in goodness, rightness and truth, and in a heart that keeps asking what pleases the Lord. A child of light does not ask how much he can get away with, but what would delight his Lord.

The fruit of light. Fruit grows; it is not manufactured. Jesus said where it comes from: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit” (John 15:5). Goodness, righteousness and truth are not virtues we assemble by effort but the family likeness of the Son, the good shepherd, the righteous one and the truth (John 10:11; 1 John 2:1; John 14:6), ripening in people joined to him. So the remedy for a barren season is not first a grimmer effort at goodness but nearness to Christ, as a branch to the vine.

Try to discern. To test and approve, as a metalworker tests gold (dokimazō). Life keeps producing cases no rule-book addressed (Romans 12:2; Philippians 1:9–10).

What is pleasing to the Lord. Not what is permitted, but what is pleasing. The boundary question, is this allowed?, is asked by someone who wants to know how close he may go. Take a promotion offering more money and sixty hours a week, with two children at home. No commandment is broken. Ask Paul’s question, and the relevant things arrive from every side: the years with those children you cannot get back; whether this is stewardship or, in respectable clothes, the greed just called idolatry (v. 5); your real motive; what your wife would say if she thought you truly wanted the answer. None of that can be looked up. It is what a person sees who knows the Lord well enough to know what pleases him.

What it does not mean. Not that each of us invents our own morality. Discernment is trained by Scripture and constant practice (Hebrews 5:14), like a cook who has tasted for a lifetime and can tell quickly what is good.

How do I discern what pleases him? Start with what he has said; many questions are settled by an honest reading of a passage like 4:25–5:5. Pray before the decision, not after, and about the specific choice: not “Is this allowed?” but “Lord, would this please you?” Watch your motives as closely as your options; the choice you least want to pray about usually most needs it. Let people who love you and know the Lord disagree with you (Proverbs 15:22). And keep looking at the Son. The Father opened heaven to say what pleases him: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and in him you are already accepted. You are not testing the water to win God’s favour, but learning the tastes of a Father who already delights in you.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fruit of the Spirit” (as in the King James Version), from Galatians 5:22. This commentary’s view: “fruit of light” is original.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have nothing to do with sin’s dark works; bring them into the light instead. Christians are to refuse them and, without dwelling on the details, show them for what they are.

Unfruitful works of darkness. Darkness produces only barren works (Galatians 6:8). “Take no part” has the same root as “partners” in v. 7.

Expose them. To bring into the open, convict, show a thing for what it is (elenchō). Not hunting for what people hide; not exposing persons, for Paul says the works; not denouncing a world behaving as one would expect, since judging outsiders is not our business (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). It has three ordinary forms: living so that the contrast shows, as a man who simply does not join in makes something visible without a word (Matthew 5:16); refusing to let a thing pass as normal, with the quiet sentence that declines to laugh or says, “I don’t think that’s right,” and lets the silence sit; and, hardest, going privately to a brother about something you can see and he cannot (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1).

Shameful even to speak of. Verse 12 governs the manner. You can bring a thing into the open without describing it in detail. An account so vivid that hearers are entertained instead of sobered has stopped exposing darkness and started selling it.

The Ephesians had already seen this done. The city’s magic drew its power from being hidden, and when the gospel took hold, those who had practised it burned their books in the sight of all (Acts 19:18–19; see the introduction): the secret brought into the open by the very people who had done it, and its power broken in the light. Some who first heard this letter had probably stood in that crowd. Paul asks them to go on living what they did that day.

The light that came into the world. Jesus described his own coming in these terms: “the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil”; “everyone who does wicked things hates the light … lest his works should be exposed” (John 3:19–20), with Paul’s verb. The world tried to put the light out. Yet he exposed in order to save (John 3:17). The woman at the well, her history laid bare in a few sentences, ran into the town saying he “told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29), not crushed but set free. That is the pattern for all Christian exposing: the truth told, and the person not abandoned. And he was himself stripped and exposed to public shame on the cross, so that our hidden shame might be covered and healed.

Between two ditches. One ditch is withdrawal: a church so far from the world that its light falls on no one but itself. The other is blending in: a church so like the world that there is no difference left to see. Paul asks for the road between: be among people without joining in what is wrong.

In everyday life. Before you speak about someone’s sin, ask what you are hoping for. If part of you hopes to be proved right, or seen as the one who noticed, that is not light; it is the pleasure of holding a torch.

What if the thing I know about is a crime, or someone is being harmed? Then exposing it means telling those who can stop it, quickly. The private approach of Matthew 18:15 is for a brother’s sin against you, never for the abuse of a child, violence in a home or serious fraud, where going quietly to the offender can warn him and leave the victim in danger. God has given the civil authorities the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and reporting a crime to them is obedience, not betrayal. Tell the police or the proper safeguarding body, and your church’s elders, and let no one, a church leader included, persuade you to keep it inside the church instead. Speaking up for those who cannot speak for themselves honours Christ far more than protecting the reputation of his people (Proverbs 31:8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is brought into the light can be changed, because Christ shines on those who wake. Exposure is not the end of the story but the beginning of rescue: the light that shows up the sin is the light that gives new life.

Anything that becomes visible is light. Sin brought into God’s light is seen for what it is, and, confessed, it does not stay darkness: the one who repents becomes light (1 John 1:7–9; on the wording, see below). A hidden sin carried for years loses its grip once confessed to God and a trusted friend, because secrecy is the one condition sin truly needs. Shame’s whole power is one sentence: “If they knew what you are, they would be finished with you.” Confession tests it. Your friend hears the worst, does not recoil, prays with you, and next week asks how you are getting on: the lie disproved by someone still sitting there. Hence “confess your sins to one another … that you may be healed” (James 5:16): the healing comes through the “one another”.

Awake, O sleeper. Sleep pictures a life unaware of God and of danger. The call is first to the unconverted, but it also reaches the man who woke years ago and has dozed off in a comfortable pew (Romans 13:11; Revelation 3:2). He would answer every doctrinal question correctly, but no sin has been fought in years, prayer has become words without an address, and he cannot remember when he last expected God to do anything. He does not know he is asleep, which is why the summons must come from outside: a hymn, a sermon, a friend, a verse that will not leave him alone.

Arise from the dead. More than sleep: without Christ a person is spiritually dead, cut off from God and unable to respond (2:1). A dead man cannot obey a command to get up, so the call must give the life it asks for, and it does: “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

Christ will shine on you. The point of the sentence is not the command but the promise. The light is already shining; only a pair of closed eyes stands between the sleeper and the sunrise. Isaiah promised that the glory of the LORD would rise upon his people (Isaiah 60:1); the church’s song says, “Christ will shine”. The first Christians put Jesus where Isaiah put the LORD: they sang to him as God.

Shone on anyway. Dawn does not wait for the sleeper to deserve it. The Son of God rose on the first morning of the week, and has been rising on sleepers ever since. He called a dead man by name, and Lazarus came out (John 11:43–44). Every believer is a morning he made: a darkness that never asked for light, and was shone on anyway.

Uncertain wording. Two things here are genuinely uncertain. First, “anything that becomes visible is light”: Paul’s Greek is compressed and can mean “everything that is made visible becomes light” or “everything that makes things visible is light” (the King James Version’s “whatsoever doth make manifest is light”). The likely meaning is the first: what is exposed and confessed is itself changed into light, as the readers once were darkness and are now light (v. 8). Second, the source of the quotation. “Therefore it says” is how Paul introduces Scripture (4:8), yet these words are not in the Old Testament. They echo Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1, and are probably lines from an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism; no one knows for certain.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

parallels.desc: awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust
arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is a life filled and governed by the Spirit instead of drifting with the evil days. Watch your steps and buy up the time (vv. 15–16), understand what the Lord wants (v. 17), and instead of being ruled by drink, be filled with the Spirit (v. 18). Paul then shows what that filling looks like, and it is not spectacular: singing to one another and to the Lord, thanking the Father for everything, and humbly putting others first out of reverence for Christ (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The fullness of the Spirit and the worshipping church

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v. 18) is a present, passive command: go on being filled (on how, see the note on v. 18).

“Submitting to one another” (v. 21) is the hinge into the household instructions that follow. Its root is the humility of Christ, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Against the cult of Dionysus, god of wine (see the note on v. 18), Paul sets a church filled not with wine but with God’s Spirit.

Now: Our age has endless ways to fill an inner emptiness: entertainment, substances, the constant pull of the screen. The hunger returns each time. A church that sings with gratitude, gives thanks and puts others first offers the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live carefully and use your time well, because the world is pulling the other way. Wisdom is not drifting with the current but choosing, day by day, to spend your hours on what matters to God.

In the flow. For the third time in the chapter Paul says “walk” (vv. 2, 8, 15), taking up 4:1. The one Christ has woken (v. 14) must now watch his steps.

Look carefully then how you walk. Literally see accurately how you walk, like someone picking his way along a narrow path. Think of a surgeon entering theatre: not anxious, but focused.

Unwise and wise. Wisdom is skill in living God’s way, rooted in the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10). Nobody decides to waste his life. The unwise simply never decide not to.

Making the best use of the time. Literally buying up the time (exagorazomenoi), a merchant’s word from the same root as redemption. Time cannot be saved, only spent; the man with no time for prayer has bought something else with it. And the word for time is kairos, opportunity, and opportunities have expiry dates: a conversation with an ageing parent while he can still follow it; a friend in crisis, asking questions now, who in eighteen months will have rebuilt his defences; a child at the age when he still wants your company. None of these announces its closing time (Colossians 4:5; Psalm 90:12).

Because the days are evil. The current runs against you (2:2; 6:12), and a boat that does nothing drifts downstream. Yet the evil days are not the whole story. Christ gave himself “to deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4), and when he rose, the age to come began, like first light before full day. We live where the two ages overlap, in the season when the risen Lord is gathering his people before he returns. To buy up the time is to spend it on what he is doing.

Never in a hurry. Redeeming the time is not maximising output, and gives no ground for guilt about rest. Jesus had some three years and the weight of the world on him, and still stopped for a blind man on the road (Mark 10:46–52) and slept in a boat during a storm (Mark 4:38). He knew his hour, and when it came he went to meet it, buying with his own life the redemption of a people who had squandered theirs. A frantic life and a wasted life can be equally unredeemed. The question is not how much you got through today, but what you bought.

How do I buy up the time? See where it goes: for one ordinary week, notice what your free hours are spent on, and ask Paul’s merchant question, what did I buy? Put first, before the diary fills, the few things that matter most: God’s word and prayer, the Lord’s Day with his people, unhurried time with those you love. Name one open door this month and walk through it this week. Leave margin: opportunities arrive in the gaps a crammed life does not have. At night hand the hours back to God, the wasted ones included. The motive is gratitude, not panic: we buy up the time because we ourselves “were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not live thoughtlessly; work out what the Lord wants. Most of God’s will for your life is already revealed, and the wise person lives by it.

Foolish. Not low intelligence, but living without thinking about God (aphrōn).

Understand. Christian obedience uses the mind: not “What is convenient?” but “What does the Lord want here?”

The will of the Lord. Christians agonise over this phrase, mostly by confusing two senses. God’s hidden will is everything he has planned, which will surely happen, though he has not told us its details: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29). His revealed will is what he has told us plainly, and it fills the Bible. Most anxiety about “finding God’s will” concerns the hidden one, which house, which career, which person, though that will was never given to you to read. The revealed will sits open on the desk: “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3); “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18). It is not a hidden dot you are ruined for missing, but a direction described in detail, and a person he is making you into. Whoever pursues holiness, gives thanks, tells the truth, loves his wife and does good work is in God’s will, whichever of two reasonable job offers he accepts.

The will has a centre. When this letter first speaks of God’s will, it names its subject: “the mystery of his will … to unite all things in Christ” (1:9–10). It is not first a set of private instructions but one purpose with Christ at its heart, and our lives are caught up in it. So understanding the Lord’s will begins with knowing the Lord, and Jesus said what the Father wants most: “that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6:40). The Son came down to do the will of the one who sent him (John 6:38), all the way to the cross. Whoever asks, “How does this decision serve his purpose to gather all things under Christ?” has found the right question, even before he has found the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let drink control you; let the Spirit fill you. Both can fill a person and change how he speaks and acts, but only one leads to self-control, praise and love.

Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery. “Debauchery” (asōtia) is a life out of control, the prodigal son’s reckless living (Luke 15:13; Proverbs 23:29–35). Drink is often asked to quiet fear, numb shame, or supply a comfort we are not finding in God, which is why Paul’s cure is not only less wine but more of the Spirit.

But be filled with the Spirit. Wine takes away self-control; the Spirit gives it (Galatians 5:23). The point is who is in control, not what it feels like. The command is passive and continuous: keep on being filled. How can anyone be commanded to have something done to him? A sail cannot make wind, but it can be raised or left furled, and a filled sail goes where the wind takes it. Whatever opens a life to the Spirit raises the canvas; grieving or quenching him furls it, and then a man may sincerely complain that he is becalmed. Every believer has the Spirit (1:13); being filled is less like a tank topped up once than like breathing.

The setting. At the festivals of Dionysus, god of wine, drunkenness was thought to bring people close to the divine. Wine promised a counterfeit nearness; the true God gives himself, by his Spirit.

Not drunk at nine in the morning. The contrast had been drawn once before, in public. At Pentecost, when the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit, mockers said, “They are filled with new wine” (Acts 2:13). Peter answered that they were not drunk at that hour, but that Jesus, exalted to God’s right hand, had received the promised Spirit and poured him out (Acts 2:15, 33). The filling is the gift of the ascended Christ, and the Spirit leads back to him: “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). A Spirit-filled life is a Christ-filled life, where the word of Christ dwells richly (Colossians 3:16) and the songs are about him.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on wine, God’s gift “to gladden the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11); the sin is being controlled by it. A Christian should not drink in a way that makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21), and some wisely choose not to drink at all. Nor does it mean being loud or ecstatic; the marks Paul gives are worship, gratitude and humility.

How is a believer filled? Paul’s parallel passage is the best guide: there “let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” is followed by the same results, in the same order and almost the same words, ending with wives, husbands and children (Colossians 3:16–18). These are not two attainments, one ordinary and one rare, but one reality, because the Spirit wrote the word and works through it. In practice: take in God’s word; ask (“how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” Luke 11:13); obey what you already know; confess sin quickly, so as not to grieve him (4:30; 1 John 1:9); do not quench his promptings (1 Thessalonians 5:19); stop numbing your inner life with substitutes; and worship with God’s people.

How would I know? Paul’s test is outward, not a check of your feelings (vv. 19–21): Is there song in you? Thanksgiving, always and for everything? Are you submitting to others, the least likely product of any counterfeit filling? Nobody has to be told when a man is drunk: it shows in how he speaks and treats people. The Spirit does not fill people to make them impressive or dominant, but more like servants. If you want to know which is filling you, ask the people who live with you.

Should I expect to feel something when I am filled with the Spirit? Sometimes, but feelings are not the test. At times God gives a strong sense of his nearness, joy in worship or a peace in a crisis you know you did not produce (Romans 5:5; 1 Peter 1:8); receive it with thanks. But the filled life is as real on grey days, when you obey without any glow and keep loving a difficult person out of plain faithfulness. When the believers in Acts 4:31 were filled, what followed was not a sensation but boldness to speak the word. So do not chase experiences, or doubt the Spirit’s work when you feel flat. Feelings follow sleep, health and temperament; the fruit Paul names follows the Spirit.

Where is the line between drinking and being drunk? Well before you are falling over: when drink takes the controls, and your judgment, speech or restraint is no longer fully your own. An honest test: would you say, do and drive exactly as you would sober? If you drink to feel the loosening, to switch yourself partly off, you are asking wine to do what the Spirit does. Needing a drink to get through an evening, hiding how much you have had, or being irritable without it are signs of dependence: stop altogether, and tell someone. The same applies to anything taken to alter the mind for pleasure, recreational drugs included: your mind is meant to be governed by the Spirit, not handed over to a substance.

Where Christians differ: is the filling a second blessing? Some Pentecostal and charismatic teaching links being filled with a second experience after conversion, often called the baptism in the Spirit and marked by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: every believer is indwelt and sealed by the Spirit from conversion (1:13; Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Being filled is the ongoing life of a Spirit-governed believer, nourished by the word and shown in the fruits of vv. 19–21. Believers may be filled afresh many times, as the apostles were (Acts 2:4; 4:31), and God may grant times of special strength, but no Christian is a second-class believer without the Spirit. Many charismatic and Pentecostal believers love Christ deeply, and their hunger for more of the Spirit is right; the question is only whether Scripture promises a distinct second stage, and Paul here describes a filling every believer is to seek again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Spirit-filled church sings and gives thanks. The first signs of the Spirit’s filling are not spectacular experiences but songs that build one another up, and thanks to the Father, always and for everything, through Jesus. In Greek, singing, thanking and submitting (vv. 19–21) all hang on the command “be filled”: they are what the filling looks like.

Addressing one another. We sing not only to God but to each other (Colossians 3:16). The man in the third row who buried someone on Tuesday cannot get the words out; they are sung over him by those who can manage it this week, and he is carried on a sound he had no strength to make. At three in the morning in your worst week, what comes is rarely a paragraph from a sermon; it is a line you have sung a hundred times. What you sing is what you will believe when you cannot think. Nor does the church sing alone: the Lord Jesus sang a hymn with his friends on the night he was betrayed (Mark 14:26), and he now leads his brothers’ praise in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:12).

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Probably the Old Testament psalms, hymns of praise, and other songs prompted by the Spirit. Paul does not legislate the repertoire; what interests him is the direction the singing travels.

Singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart. Psallō first meant to pluck a string, and the instrument Paul names is you. If you were once told you cannot sing, the Lord is listening to the instrument, and yours is in tune. But “with your heart” is not permission to stand in silence; the other half of the verse needs someone to hear you.

Always and for everything. Not only in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18) but for all things, and anyone who has buried a child may ask whether it can mean what it says. It does not mean calling evil good, a tumour a blessing or a betrayal a gift. Nor is grief a failure of faith: about a third of the Psalms are complaints, and God put “How long, O LORD?” into the church’s hymnbook permanently.

To God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thanks goes to a Father, not to fate, and this letter has said what kind: one who chose you before the world began (1:4) and adopted you at the cost of his Son (1:5). You are not asked to believe that everything that happens is good, but that nothing reaches you except through that Father’s hands, and that he can make what was meant to destroy you serve you. “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28): not feel it, but know it, which you can say with a wet face. And “in the name of” Jesus is not a password: we give thanks through Christ our mediator, who brings us to the holy Father as children admitted at his invitation (John 16:24; Hebrews 13:15). By the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father.

What it does not mean. Job, having lost his property and ten children in one day, fell on the ground and worshipped: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). He does not bless the loss. He blesses the Name: gratitude, in the wreckage, to a Father who has not moved. This verse describes what a Spirit-filled life overflows into; it was never meant to be handed to a grieving person as an instruction across a hospital bed. If you cannot do it today, you have not failed the verse.

Where Christians differ: psalms only, and instruments? Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms (exclusive psalmody), reading all three words as kinds of psalm, a serious position, since all three appear in the Greek Old Testament’s psalm headings. Some also sing without instruments, holding that the New Testament gives no warrant for them in worship. This commentary’s view: the Psalms deserve a far larger place in our worship, but Scripture-filled hymns are also fitting: the New Testament itself contains Christian songs about Christ (5:14; Philippians 2:6–11; Revelation 5:9–10). Instruments help singing rather than replace it; the Psalms call for praise with lute and harp (Psalm 150:3), and nothing in the New Testament withdraws that.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit-filled life puts others first, out of reverence for Christ. This verse completes Paul’s picture of the Spirit’s filling and opens the door to the home, where that humility takes particular shapes.

The hinge. Verse 21 completes the description of being filled with the Spirit and introduces the household sections (5:22–6:9). In Greek v. 22 has no verb of its own; it borrows “submit” from v. 21. So the marriage passage cannot be lifted out and applied on its own: detached from the filling of the Spirit, it is misused.

Submitting. Hypotassomenoi was first a military word: to arrange under, to take one’s ordered place, to put another’s good and rightful leadership before one’s own way. Two things must be said. First, it says nothing about worth. The Son is equal with the Father in being, power and glory, yet in the work of salvation he came as the one sent and obeyed the Father even to death (John 5:30; Philippians 2:6–8), and at the end he will hand over the kingdom to him (1 Corinthians 15:24, 28). That submission belongs to his mission, not to any inferiority of nature: order and equality are not rivals. Second, it is voluntary. The middle voice describes something a person does himself, chosen, not forced. No one in this passage is told to make others submit; a man who sets out to do so shows that what he wants is not submission but control.

Out of reverence for Christ. Literally in the fear of Christ: not dread, but awe before the Lord who loved us to the death. It is both the reason for submitting and its limit. You do not yield because the other person has earned it, but for the sake of the Lord who gave up everything for you. And because the reverence is for Christ, it can never require what Christ forbids. A submission that would demand you sin has lost the only reason it ever had.

What every first reader would have felt. The ancient household codes told the head of the house how to manage his wife, children and slaves. Paul speaks first to the wife, the child and the slave, as responsible people who answer to Christ themselves. And he asks more of the one holding the power: the husband gets three times as many lines, and is commanded to love “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her”. The heavier cost is laid on the stronger.

Leadership in every sphere. The order assumed here is God’s gift in creation, a common grace for believer and unbeliever alike: a family, a company or a nation flourishes only when someone leads and others are willing to follow, or it dissolves into the days when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Scripture applies this to home, work, state and church (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13; Hebrews 13:17). But all human authority is delegated and limited by God: where it commands what he forbids, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). And Christ has redefined it as service (Mark 10:42–45). The study Leadership explores this further.

What it does not mean. Not submission to sin, cruelty or abuse (Acts 5:29). Nor that leaders are worth more: every believer is equally a child of God and equally loved.

Where Christians differ: mutual submission? Egalitarians (for example Gordon Fee) read “submitting to one another” (allēlois) as fully mutual: every believer submits to every other in the same way, husbands to wives as wives to husbands, with no distinct roles of leading and following in marriage. Complementarians (who hold that men and women are equal in worth but given different, complementary roles in marriage and the church; for example John Stott in his own nuanced way, and Wayne Grudem more strongly) note that the following verses specify who submits to whom, wives to husbands, children to parents, slaves to masters, never the reverse, and that husbands are told not to submit but to love. Used of relationships between people, the verb regularly means submitting to someone in authority (Luke 2:51; Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13), and “one another” can mean some to others, as when people “slay one another” in Revelation 6:4 (not everyone killing everyone). This commentary’s view: the complementarian reading, with its truth fully honoured. Verse 21 sets the spirit in which all Christians relate, humble and putting others first (Philippians 2:3–4), and husbands, parents and masters are not exempt from it. Within that humility, the following verses show a particular order God has given in marriage and family, where some lead and others follow, and both serve. Mutual humility does not erase distinct roles, any more than Christ’s humility erased his headship. Many egalitarian Christians reach their view out of love for Scripture and a right concern that women never be belittled or harmed; they are brothers and sisters, and this commentary shares that concern even where it reads the text differently.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “in the fear of God”, following later manuscripts; the earliest read “of Christ”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christian marriage is a living picture of the gospel. Paul speaks to wives first: trust and follow your husband’s lead as part of following Christ (vv. 22–24). He speaks to husbands at greater length: love your wife as Christ loved the church, giving yourself for her good and caring for her as your own body (vv. 25–30). Then he reveals why: marriage was designed from creation to point to Christ and his bride (vv. 31–32). So each spouse has one command to keep, love and respect (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, headship and the gospel mystery

Because marriage pictures the relationship between Christ and the church (see the note on v. 32), its shape is not arbitrary: the husband’s headship and the wife’s willing trust reflect Christ’s self-giving rule of his church and her glad response to him.

The husband’s headship is defined by the cross (v. 25). The head of the church died for her, washes her, and nourishes and cherishes her (v. 29); the husband follows the one who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife’s submission is the free response of a woman secure in Christ, not compliance under pressure, and it never extends to sin or abuse. Neither calling can be lived from one’s own resources. Both depend on the Spirit who fills the church (v. 18), and both rest on Christ, whose love for his bride never fails.
verseByVerse.examples:
