Then: In the Roman world a husband’s authority over his household was very great and was assumed to exist for his benefit. Paul turned that around: the Roman husband used his authority to be served; the Christian husband was to use his to serve.

Now: Christian marriage faces two opposite pressures: a culture that treats marriage as a partnership to be ended when it stops meeting individual needs, and a shallow version of headship, in which a husband demands to be followed but will not give himself up for his wife as Christ did. Ephesians 5 answers both with a love that keeps its promises, gives itself as Christ did on the cross, and is kept going by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives, make your husband’s leadership part of your service to Christ. Paul asks a wife to follow her own husband’s lead freely, as something she does for the Lord, and never in anything the Lord forbids.

Wives, submit. Paul now applies the submission of v. 21 (the verb is carried over; see the textual note below) to each relationship in the home, beginning with the wife, addressed directly as a responsible person who chooses freely before God. To submit is to arrange yourself under, to support and follow his leadership: her own choice, offered to Christ, never the husband’s to demand, and a matter of role, never of worth (see the note on v. 21). In Christ a man and a woman stand on the same ground (Galatians 3:28).

To your own husbands. Not women to men in general, at work or in the church foyer, but a wife to the one man she made promises to. The verse has often been stretched far past that boundary.

As to the Lord: “do it for my sake”. Your best friend goes abroad for a year and asks you, “Please look after my elderly father while I am gone. Do it for me.” So you visit the father and drive him to his appointments. He is the one you are helping, but you are doing it for your friend. That is what “as to the Lord” means: Christ says, do it for my sake. See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

Three things follow. First, the father is real, and you really serve him. No one pretends a husband is Jesus: “as to the Lord” does not mean “as if he were the Lord”, and his word is not Christ’s word. Second, it does not depend on the father being pleasant; you were never doing it for his thanks. So her submission does not rise and fall with her husband’s performance on a given day. It rests on Christ, who is always worthy of trust and never asks his people to go where he has not gone first: he submitted to his Father in the garden (“not my will, but yours, be done”, Luke 22:42), bore an unjust trial without hitting back (1 Peter 2:23), and went to the grave for us. Third, you would never do what your friend would hate. If her husband asks what Christ forbids (to lie, to join in sin, to hide abuse, to give up her faith or her conscience), her loyalty to Christ comes first, and she must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29; compare Colossians 3:18, “as is fitting in the Lord”).

What submission looks like. Mostly the texture of ordinary life: not undermining him in front of the children, speaking well of him, and choosing to trust after her voice has been fully heard; she brings her full wisdom and gifts, and a good husband depends on them (Proverbs 31:10–31). Suppose he is offered a post in another city and she is deeply reluctant, for her friends, work and ageing parents are here. They talk it through honestly, and he still believes they should go. Submission is trusting his judgment once her concerns have been truly weighed, without letting it harden into a grievance, while he carries the decision’s weight and owes her every sacrifice to make it work.

What it does not mean. Not inferiority: husband and wife are equal heirs of the grace of life (Genesis 1:27; 1 Peter 3:7). Not silence, or giving up her judgment or conscience. Not submission of all women to all men. And not a burden uniquely hers: it follows the call to all believers to submit (v. 21), and comes before the far heavier charge to the husband (v. 25). If the wife is called to submit, the husband is called to die.

And if he is not leading, or is not a believer? Many women are married not to an abuser but to a man who is spiritually passive or self-absorbed: he will not pray with her, lets every hard decision drift, and is present in the house but absent from the marriage. Peter writes to her, and to the wife of an unbeliever: “even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1–2). Her position is not hopeless, nor are nagging and despair her only options: her steady life has power, and God can use it to reach a man sermons have not reached, though never by her joining in his sin. That is a real calling, harder than that of the wives of good men, and the church should come alongside her and call the husband to his responsibilities.

What if there is abuse or danger? Then the limit of “as to the Lord” applies: no one is required to submit to violence. A husband who abuses his wife is not exercising headship but violating it catastrophically. A wife in danger should seek safety at once, report crimes to the authorities, and receive the church’s protection. Using this verse to keep a woman in danger is a terrible misuse of Scripture.

Does abuse mean only physical violence? No. Abuse is a pattern of control through fear, and it needs no blow: threats and intimidation, constant belittling, cutting a wife off from friends and family, controlling all the money so that she cannot act, sexual coercion, checking her every move. This is not the hard edge of headship but its opposite, for Christ never rules his bride by fear. A wife who recognises it should tell someone outside the home: a trusted friend, a pastor, and where there is danger, the police or a domestic abuse helpline. Separating for safety is right; no one should tell her that leaving to protect herself or her children breaks her vows, for he has broken them. Whether such a marriage may finally be ended is for the elders to weigh with her, carefully, in the light of Scripture’s teaching on desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.6).

Where Christians differ: is this cultural? Egalitarians see the instruction as a first-century cultural arrangement, like slavery, which the gospel eventually set aside. This commentary’s view: the complementarian view: husband and wife are equal in worth, with different roles that fit together. Paul grounds the wife’s submission not in culture but in two things that do not change: creation (v. 31, Genesis 2:24; compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13) and Christ’s relationship with the church (vv. 23–24). Slavery is regulated in Scripture but never grounded in creation or in Christ; Paul tells slaves to take their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21) and lists slave-traders among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). So the pattern holds today, to be lived gladly and humbly and never used as a weapon. Many faithful Christians read it otherwise, often grieved at how these verses have been misused; the answer to misuse is the passage’s own limits, not its removal.

Textual note. In the earliest Greek manuscripts v. 22 has no verb of its own (“wives, to your own husbands”); “submit” is carried over from v. 21. Later manuscripts supply it, as the King James Version does. The meaning is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband’s headship is real, but it is shaped like Christ’s: responsibility and care, not control. And the church’s willing trust in Christ is the pattern for a wife’s trust in her husband.

Even as Christ is the head of the church, his body. The comparison gives the husband real authority, then changes what it looks like. To be head as Christ is head is to take final responsibility: when things go wrong, to ask not whom to blame but what he failed to do. Adam stood by silent while his wife was tempted (Genesis 3:6), and God called to the man first (Genesis 3:9). It is to start love rather than wait for it, and to lead the spiritual life of the home rather than leave it as her department. Not “I lead, therefore I decide”, but “I lead, therefore I bear the cost of this for her sake.”

And is himself its Saviour. Here Paul marks the limit of his picture: the husband is head as Christ is head, but he is not Saviour. That diagnoses two mirror-image failures: the wife who needs her husband to make her finally secure, and finds him failing at a job he was never given; and the husband who takes that job on, trying to fix her and be her sufficiency, and ends up exhausted or controlling. He is to love her as Christ loved the church, not to be Christ to her, and she must not ask it of him.

Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit. The church submits to one who has already given himself for her entirely: first his love, then her trust. That is a word to husbands first. A husband who wants to be followed but will not give himself has turned the picture upside down; a man who must remind his wife that he is the head is like a man who must remind people that he is funny. Christ washed feet (John 13:5) and went to a cross; such headship is visible and need not be asserted. Yet it is not a condition for the wife. Paul does not say, “Submit if your husband loves you as Christ loved the church.” Her submission is “as to the Lord” and does not wait for him to earn it, as his love does not wait for her to deserve it (v. 25). Each owes Christ their part, whatever the other does.

In everything. Every area of married life, still within “as to the Lord”: the limit is set not by how well he loves her but by what Christ forbids, so no husband may command sin, and nothing here covers abuse (see the note on v. 22).

What it does not mean. Not that the husband rules his wife as a master rules a servant. Godly headship listens, consults, serves and takes responsibility, and she may be the more mature and discerning. A husband who hears her honest disagreement as a threat is protecting his ego; Christ is not threatened by the church’s questions. If he is resting while she is exhausted, he is not leading but being served. A husband who uses this verse to dominate has forgotten that Christ “gave himself up for her” (v. 25).

What should I do if my wife will not follow my lead? Not try to make her. Nothing here tells a husband to secure his wife’s submission; that is her obedience to Christ, not your project. Your command is to love her, without condition (v. 25), so begin with yourself. Ask her, and listen without defending yourself: “Has my leading been safe to follow? Have I listened, carried the cost, kept my word, prayed with you?” Resistance is often taught by years of careless or selfish decisions; where you have failed, own it specifically. Keep leading gently in ordinary things: prayer, kindness, responsibility. If the deadlock continues, ask your pastor or a wise older couple to help you both. Christlike leadership is rarely refused for long, and if it is, your call to love her does not lapse; Christ’s love has never depended on how well his church follows.

Where Christians differ: does head mean authority or source? Some egalitarian scholars (for example Catherine Kroeger and Gordon Fee) argue that in Greek kephalē often meant source, like the head of a river, so that the husband is the source of the wife (as Eve came from Adam), not her authority. Others (for example Joseph Fitzmyer and Wayne Grudem) studied the ancient uses and found that kephalē, used of a person in relation to others, regularly means one in authority or prominence. This commentary’s view: authority, exercised as Christ exercises it. In this letter Paul plainly uses head of Christ for authority: God put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things (1:22); and here the wife’s response to the head is to submit (v. 24), which fits authority, not source. Yet Paul also uses head for the one who nourishes the body and gives it growth (4:15–16; v. 29). Christ’s headship includes both, rule and life-giving, and the husband’s is meant to mirror both. Paul does not leave the word to a dictionary. He defines it himself, with a cross (vv. 25–27).

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love your wives the way Christ loved the church: by giving yourselves up for them. This is the longest command in the passage, and the hardest.

Husbands, love. Familiarity has flattened how strange this was. Marriage in that world was for property, heirs and an orderly household; some moralists urged kindness, but none had measured a husband’s love by a Saviour dying for his bride. And Paul does not say, “lead your wives”, but “love your wives”, and gives the measure at once: a love that gives itself and keeps its promises, not a feeling that comes and goes.

As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The standard is not other husbands, or what she deserves, but Christ, and the measure is the cross: headship means going first in sacrifice, of comfort, preferences, time and if necessary life, for her good. When he gave himself up for her, the church was dead in trespasses and sins, by nature children of wrath (2:1–3). He did not find her radiant and decide she was worth it; the radiance came afterwards (vv. 26–27). This love does not respond to loveliness; it produces it, and that closes every husband’s escape hatch: when she is easier to live with, when she deserves it. Christ did not wait for a bride worth dying for. He died, and so gained one.

Where the power comes from. A husband who reads this honestly is in a hard place. Measured against Calvary, the reasonable conclusion is despair, and it is half right: you cannot love like this, and the standard is not lowered. Only one Husband ever has, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so your failures do not undo your standing. Nor does the command stand alone: Paul’s teaching on the home grows out of “be filled with the Spirit” (v. 18). This love is fruit the Spirit grows, not a test to pass before Christ accepts you, and fruit grows on a branch because the branch is attached (John 15:4–5). It is not temperament, favouring naturally warm men. The husband who grew up where nobody said anything kind is not disqualified; he is asked to stay attached, which he can do.

In an ordinary week. For a husband who keeps failing, the question is not chiefly, “How do I try harder?” (he has tried, in bursts, for years), but whether the man who comes through the door at six is being filled, because a marriage lives largely on the overflow. With his Bible shut for months, the tenderness he truly intends will not be there on a Thursday evening when he is tired and she says the wrong thing. The overflow looks ordinary: he relieves what she carries unasked, taking over the evening after her hard week with the children; gives up his preferences without the pointed silence; prays for her and asks how she is with God; chooses her above career and comfort when they truly conflict; and asks forgiveness specifically and promptly, “I was unkind this morning, and I am sorry; will you forgive me?”, with no “but you also”. Over years, that builds a marriage in which she knows she is safe with him.

What if I no longer feel any love for my wife? Then you are in exactly the place this command was written for. Paul does not tell you to feel love but to love, and the verb is about what you do. Feelings often follow actions rather than lead them, so do what love does: the kindness you stopped bothering with, the attention, the apology, the evening given to her. Pray for her daily by name, and ask God to restore what has cooled. Look honestly at what drains your affection: unresolved resentment, exhaustion, attention given elsewhere, a screen included. Many couples who once felt nothing have found warmth return after patient, deliberate love. If you cannot find a way forward, ask your pastor or a biblical counsellor early, before the walls go up.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many faithful Christians hold that Christ died in the same way for every person, to make salvation possible for anyone who will take it up, and they love the cross no less. This commentary’s view: Paul says Christ gave himself for the church, his bride, which points to a love that had particular people in view and actually saves them (Acts 20:28; John 10:11): a people the Father gave him, none of whom he will lose (John 6:37–39). Reformed churches call this definite (or particular) atonement. The difference is over what the cross actually achieved, and verses like this one are why this commentary holds that it secured salvation for a people he knew by name. That does not narrow the invitation: everyone who comes to him is welcomed (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s love does not leave his bride as she is: he makes her holy, and he will present her to himself without a flaw. What he began by washing her, he will finish on the wedding day.

That he might sanctify her, having cleansed her. “Sanctify” (hagiasē): make holy, set apart for him, now in part and perfectly at the end. He cleanses her of sin’s guilt, what sin deserves before God’s judgment, and of its stain, the dirt and the grip it leaves in us. The guilt he removes once for all when he justifies us, declaring us righteous for his sake; the stain, over a lifetime, as he makes us actually holy (2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:23).

By the washing of water with the word. “Washing” is a bath. A bride was bathed before her wedding, and in Ezekiel 16:8–14 God washes his bride Israel and adorns her. “With the word” is probably the gospel preached and believed (see “Uncertain wording” below).

So that he might present the church to himself in splendour. In an ancient wedding others prepared the bride and presented her to the groom. Here the groom does both, and receives her to himself: not repairing a damaged asset out of duty, but getting her ready because he wants her. It was for the joy set before him that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2), and this is that joy: his bride, ready at last and his for ever. If you belong to him, you are part of what he was looking forward to.

Without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. Not the same defect twice. A spot is a stain that landed on her from outside; a wrinkle is the mark of wear and years. He removes both, the guilt and the exhaustion (Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2, 5), worth hearing if what you feel about yourself is less like dirtiness than fatigue. He is not only washing his bride but making her new. And the goal, “holy and without blemish”, is the one God named before the foundation of the world (1:4): what the Father chose us for, the Son brings to completion.

For husbands. A husband cannot sanctify his wife, but his love aims the same way. Suppose she grew up under a critical father and struggles to believe God loves her. When she waves off a gift, he names specifically what he sees; when she doubts God’s love after a hard season, he opens Scripture with her, not to win an argument but to wash her with the word; he prays against the particular lies she has told him she believes. He is not her therapist or her pastor. He is her husband.

What it does not mean. Not that the husband is his wife’s spiritual improver, noting her faults and holding up the standard until she rises to it. Christ does not cleanse his bride by listing her blemishes, but at his own expense. A husband is not responsible for his wife’s sins, but he is responsible for loving her towards holiness.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself cleanse? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran traditions understand verses like this to teach that baptism itself, as God’s act, washes away sin and gives new birth (baptismal regeneration). This commentary’s view: Christ cleanses, and he does it by his word, the gospel received by faith. Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (John 15:3); God cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (Acts 15:9); we have been born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). So Simon Magus could be baptised and still be in the gall of bitterness (Acts 8:13, 23), while the thief on the cross, as far as we know never baptised, went that day to paradise (Luke 23:43). Baptism is the visible sign of the cleansing (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 29.1), not its cause (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt, but the appeal of a good conscience); to collapse the two is to trust the picture instead of the gospel it pictures. Many believers in those traditions trust Christ alone and treasure baptism as his gift; the disagreement is over what the water does, not over whether Christ saves.

Uncertain wording. “The washing of water” is literally “the bath of water”. It clearly draws on the bride’s bath before her wedding; whether Paul also has baptism directly in mind is debated, though many think he does. “With the word” is less certain. Paul’s term (rhēma) means a spoken word, and he does not say which: the gospel preached and believed (the same term as “the word of God” in 6:17), the confession of faith or the name of Christ spoken at baptism, or, in the wedding picture, the bridegroom’s own pledge. What is clear is that the cleansing is Christ’s work and that a spoken word goes with it. The likeliest meaning is the gospel word through which Christ cleanses (John 15:3; 1 Peter 1:23).
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband should care for his wife as naturally as he cares for his own body, because in marriage she is part of him.

As their own bodies. “In the same way”: as Christ loves the church, his body, not as a possession but as part of himself, for husband and wife are one flesh (v. 31). A man does not ignore a pain in his shoulder because he is busy. James, absorbed in a demanding season at work, has not noticed Sarah pulling back for three weeks, quieter at dinner and carrying something he has not asked about. He will check in when the pressure eases, he tells himself: reasoning he would never apply to a pain in his own chest. Her withdrawal is his signal; her heaviness is his concern.

He who loves his wife loves himself. Paul does not command a man to love himself; he assumes it. A hundred times a day you notice you are hungry, tired or sore, and do something about it. Give her that same attention.

Two measures, one instruction. In v. 25 the standard is Christ’s love for the church; here, a man’s care for his own body. But the church is Christ’s body (1:23; 5:30), so the highest standard and the most everyday one turn out to be one command.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ feeds and cherishes his church every day, and a husband is to do the same for his wife. We are cared for like this because we are part of Christ himself.

No one ever hated his own flesh. Paul is writing not to men trying to destroy their wives but to men who are simply not feeding them, and that is how most marriages fail: not in an atrocity, but in a slow drop in temperature. He has never raised his hand or his voice; the bills are paid; and she has been cold for four years. Nothing was done to her; something was never done for her.

Nourishes and cherishes. Neither verb is heroic. To nourish is to feed up to full growth (6:4): twenty years of meals, no single one of which looks like love. To cherish is literally to keep warm, used of a mother bird on her nest (Deuteronomy 22:6; 1 Thessalonians 2:7). Feed her, and keep her warm.

Just as Christ does the church. Note the tense: Christ does this, now. The giving up of himself is finished (v. 25); the feeding and warming have not stopped for a day since, through his word and at the Lord’s Supper. He who fed five thousand on a hillside, and cooked breakfast on a beach for disciples who had just failed him (John 21:9–13), feeds us still, with himself, until the Lamb is our shepherd and God wipes away every tear (Revelation 7:16–17). That answers an ache. Paul promises a church without spot or wrinkle (v. 27), and you see spots and creases everywhere, in your church and in yourself. Has he changed his mind? No: the presentation is future; the feeding is present. He is not at the far end of the aisle with arms folded, waiting for you to make yourself presentable. He is at the near end, feeding you.

Members of his body. The ordinary word for limbs and organs (melē): not subjects or admirers, but parts of him. Saul of Tarsus had been arresting Christians when a voice knocked him flat on the road: “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The Christ of heaven called it an attack on himself. That is not sentiment but anatomy: touch the hand, and the head says, me. From your side, it is the safest thing in the letter. A body does not amputate a part for being weak; a broken arm gets more of its attention than a sound one (1 Corinthians 12:22–26). For Christ to neglect you he would have to neglect himself, and no one ever hated his own flesh.

What keeping her warm looks like. She never has to wonder whether she is loved, because he shows it every day in small ways. He greets her as someone he is glad to see, asks about her day and listens, touches her with affection when he wants nothing in return, thanks her and tells her what he admires. He keeps harsh words away from her, his own first of all. When she is tired, ill or afraid he comes nearer instead of withdrawing. None of it costs much on any one day; keeping it up, year after year, is what makes a home warm.

In everyday life. One test cannot be cheated: what happens to her face in the two seconds after you come through the door? And to the wife reading this as a list of what she does not have: wanting warmth is not weakness; say so plainly to someone, and if there is more than coldness in your home, tell someone who can act. But you have not gone unfed. Christ has been feeding you all along.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones” (as in the King James Version), from Genesis 2:23. This commentary’s view: probably not original.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage means a new first loyalty and a lifelong union of the whole life. Paul quotes God’s own words from Eden and, as verse 32 shows, he sees Christ and the church in them.

Therefore. Paul has just said we are members of Christ’s body (v. 30), and to prove it he quotes Genesis 2:24, the foundational text on marriage, spoken before the fall and quoted by Jesus (Matthew 19:4–6). The logic only works if that verse was about Christ and the church all along (see the note on v. 32).

Leave his father and mother. A new first loyalty, not mainly a matter of distance. A man can live four hundred miles from his mother and still be run by her: a decision made together on Tuesday quietly reopened on the phone on Wednesday; a husband who defends his wife to nobody and explains her to everybody. And parents can refuse to release as firmly as sons refuse to leave.

Hold fast. Literally to be glued (proskollaō). Glue two boards properly, leave them overnight, then force them apart: the join holds, the wood tears, and each board comes away carrying fibre from the other. That is why the ending of a marriage does not feel like the ending of an agreement. To anyone divorced or left, this is not another sentence passed on you; it explains the shape of the wound. You were not weak when it went on hurting long after others thought you should have recovered: something God joins was pulled apart, and it tore. Where the fault was yours, there is complete forgiveness in Christ; where it was done to you, God himself calls such tearing apart violence (Malachi 2:16). Neither his love for you nor his use of you is reduced by one degree.

The two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole life: two bodies, two lives shared, a promise made, and no one else let in. Even union with a prostitute makes one flesh (1 Corinthians 6:16; see the note on v. 3). Marriage is a bond witnessed by God (Malachi 2:14), not dissolved by fading feeling. Yet the two remain two; a marriage in which one swallows the other distorts the union.

Fulfilled before it was obeyed. Once Paul has said whom it is about, every clause has a second face. “A man shall leave his father”: the Son of God did, not ceasing to be one with the Father, but leaving the glory he had before the world existed (John 16:28; 17:5). “And hold fast to his wife”: he has held fast to a bride who has let go of him a thousand times, and never loosened his grip. “And the two shall become one flesh”: he took flesh to do it. As in Eden the LORD God brought the woman to the man (Genesis 2:22), the Father has been bringing a bride to his Son ever since: “All that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37). So Christian marriage is not finally an achievement to be measured but a picture, and the original holds even in the weeks when the copy does not. For the divorced, the deserted and the never-married, here is a Husband who will never tear himself away.

May a marriage ever be ended? God designed it for life: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6). But Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul allows it when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Corinthians 7:15). This commentary’s view: in cases of adultery or desertion the innocent party is free to divorce and remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6), though reconciliation is better wherever it is possible. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to such desertion, and the elders help judge each case; but anyone in danger should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered.

I divorced and remarried on grounds that were not biblical. Should I now leave my present marriage? No. The sin lay in how the earlier marriage ended; confess it, and it is fully forgiven in Christ (1 John 1:9). Your present marriage is real, made with vows before God, and breaking it would add a second wrong, not undo the first; the law of Moses even forbade a divorced woman who had remarried to return to her first husband (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). Repent honestly, make peace where you can, perhaps with a former spouse or children who were hurt, and give yourself wholeheartedly to the marriage you are in, taking particular questions to your elders. God’s grace was never only for people with tidy histories; it was sent for the rest of us.

Where Christians differ: the definition of marriage. Some churches now affirm same-sex marriage. This commentary’s view: the historic Christian view, held with compassion: Scripture defines marriage as the union of one man and one woman, and that pattern is part of its meaning, since it pictures Christ and his church. Jesus grounded marriage in God’s making them male and female (Matthew 19:4–5), and the picture needs two who are different joined as one, as the Bridegroom and his bride are distinct. Those who differ often do so out of love for gay friends and family, and those who hold the historic view must hold it with the same love, honouring every person as made in God’s image.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the beginning, marriage was designed to point to Christ and his church. That is why married and single believers alike share in the reality it points to.

Mystery. Not a puzzle, but something hidden and now made known (3:3–5). In a city where secret religions sold their secrets to the few who joined, Paul’s mystery is read aloud to a room of ordinary people, and its point is that outsiders have been let in.

It refers to Christ and the church. God did not invent marriage and then find it a useful illustration; he designed it from creation to point to the greater marriage. That reframes the Bible. He wedded himself to Israel: “your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5). When she was unfaithful he grieved as a wounded husband, and showed how he would win her back by telling the prophet Hosea to take back his unfaithful wife (Hosea 2:19–20; 3:1). Scripture opens with a wedding in a garden (Genesis 2:24) and closes with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9); between lies the long story of a Bridegroom coming for his bride. God made man and woman one flesh so that the world would never lack a living picture of the love that would bring the Son of God down from heaven to win us.

For the single. And what of the reader who has no marriage: the man of forty who assumed he would be married by now, the widow, the woman whose husband left? The Lord Jesus never married, and Paul, writing this sentence, was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). The two who understood the mystery of marriage most deeply had, as far as we know, no experience of it, and neither thought himself impoverished. The most complete human life ever lived was a single one.

The sign and the reality. If marriage is the sign, the union of Christ and his church is the reality, and the single Christian already has it in full: the same Bridegroom, the same love, on the same terms. “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), not because something good is taken away, but because no one needs the signpost once they have arrived. Every marriage ends, by its own vows, at a graveside; the one it pointed to never does. And to the eunuch, whom the ancient world pitied because he could never marry or have children, God promised “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:3–5): more, to the one with least.

What it does not mean. If every faithful marriage pictures the gospel, what does a bad marriage say about the gospel? Nothing at all. A sign knocked flat in a ditch does not move the city it pointed to.

Where Christians differ: a sacrament? The Latin Vulgate translated “mystery” as sacramentum, one ground on which the Roman Catholic Church counts marriage among seven sacraments. The instinct is not contemptible: it wants to say marriage is holy, and it is. The Reformers held that marriage is a holy creation ordinance for all people, not a sacrament of grace for the church. This commentary’s view: marriage is honourable and holy, a living picture of the gospel, but not a sacrament, one of the signs Christ gave his church, as baptism and the Lord’s Supper are. It points to the gospel; it does not hand out its grace.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever your spouse does, keep your own command: husbands, love; wives, respect.

However. After the great mystery, Paul comes back down, in one word, to a husband and a wife who have to get through Tuesday.

Each one of you. Paul addresses not the couple but two individuals, each with one command and no condition. He does not write, “love your wife once she respects you”, or “respect your husband once he loves you like Christ”. Yet that is the deadlock of most struggling marriages: she waits for his love, and is not wrong to want it; he waits for her respect, and is not wrong either; each will move once the other has. Your half cannot wait for the other half, and no one can keep it for you. You can only go first.

Love his wife as himself. For a man of few emotional words it means learning to ask and stay: not “are you okay?” but “tell me how you are really doing”, and then sitting with the answer instead of fixing it.

And let the wife see that she respects her husband. Literally “fears”: reverent honour, in how she speaks about him as well as to him. In practice: keeping correction for a private moment; letting him make a low-stakes decision she thinks slightly wrong, and not reopening it; saying something genuinely admiring of him where he can hear it.

He moved first. That is what Christ did. He did not wait for his bride to honour him before he loved her; while she was still turned away, he came and gave himself, and her love for him began there: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). So the spouse who goes first is not being naive, or rewarding bad behaviour, but copying the Bridegroom. It can be done without being sure of the response, because the love that matters most is already given, and no one at the dinner table can take it away.

What it does not mean. Not terror or blind agreement, and not absorbing harm; the limits of v. 22 stand. It governs chiefly manner: the hardest sentence in a marriage can be said with honour or with contempt, in nearly the same words. A wife married to a man who has given her little to admire is not asked to manufacture admiration, but to refuse contempt, which is very often the last thing standing between a marriage and its end. And wives need respect and husbands need love too. Ask your spouse which they are short of, and believe the answer.

In everyday life. A husband who can quote “let the wife see that she respects her husband”, but not what he was told in the same breath, is not studying Scripture; he is arming himself.

5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 stands in the second half of the letter. Paul has spent three chapters telling believers who they are in Christ, and since the “therefore” of 4:1 he has been showing how such people walk; this chapter runs straight on from 4:32, and its marriage passage opens the household teaching that continues to 6:9, before the letter closes with the armour of God.

The message. You are God’s dearly loved children, so live like your Father: love the way Christ loved you, by giving yourself away instead of taking for yourself. Everything in the chapter is that one family likeness worked out: in what you do with your body, your words and your time, in the songs and thanks of the church, and in the most intimate place of all, a marriage.

Why it was said. The believers in Ephesus were mostly converted pagans, living in a city where sexual licence, greed and drunken religion were simply normal life, and where the household belonged to its master (see the introduction). Some voices were already saying that grace made such things harmless (v. 6).

How the chapter makes its case. Three times Paul says “walk”. Walk in love (vv. 1–7): Christ gave himself up for us, so sexual sin, greed and crude talk, which take others for ourselves, are the cross turned inside out. Walk as children of light (vv. 8–14): you are no longer darkness but light, so bear light’s fruit and bring the darkness into the open, where Christ shines on those he wakes. Walk wisely (vv. 15–21): buy up the time in evil days and be filled with the Spirit, a filling that shows in song, thanksgiving and humble submission to one another. That humility then reaches the home (vv. 22–33), where a wife’s trust and a husband’s self-giving love are both modelled on Christ and the church.

Where it leads. The chapter begins and ends in the same place. Christ “loved us and gave himself up for us” (v. 2); Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (v. 25). Then Paul reveals that marriage was designed from the first wedding in Eden to picture this greater marriage (vv. 31–32). Every believer, married or single, belongs to the bride he is washing now and will present to himself in splendour.

For us. This chapter is not a list of rules for earning God’s love but a portrait of the family you already belong to. Ask where your life still takes instead of gives, in your body, your words, your time or your home, and bring it to the one who gave himself for you.

keyVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the whole chapter in one sentence. The walk it commands is defined by the cross it remembers, and everything that follows, from clean speech to a husband giving himself up for his wife (v. 25), is this one self-giving love worked out. Before it is a pattern to copy, it is a gift to receive: the offering that pleased God was made for us.

5.reflection:
Paul grounds every command in this chapter in who believers already are: dearly loved children (v. 1), light in the Lord (v. 8). How does it change obedience to begin with who you are rather than with effort? Where do you tend to reverse the order?

Verses 3–6 describe sexual sin, impurity and greed as ways of taking others for ourselves, the opposite of Christ’s self-giving. Which of them is most often treated as normal or harmless where you live and work, and what “empty words” are used to excuse it?

Paul’s evidence that a church is filled with the Spirit is singing to one another, giving thanks and submitting to one another (vv. 18–21). Why do you think he chooses these marks rather than more spectacular ones? Which is hardest for you?

Verse 32 says the marriage passage is finally about Christ and the church. What does it show you about how Christ loves his people, and how should that shape our marriages, our singleness and our life together as a church?

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a Christian home everyone, strong and weak alike, serves the same Lord. Paul speaks first to those with less power, as people who answer to Christ for themselves: children obey and honour their parents (vv. 1–3), and slaves serve sincerely, as for Christ, who will repay every good thing (vv. 5–8). Then he limits those with power: fathers must not provoke their children but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (v. 4), and masters must stop threatening, because they answer to the same impartial Master in heaven (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, service and the lordship of Christ

These household instructions are sometimes read as Paul simply accepting the social order of Rome. That misses what he does with it. Each relationship is changed from within: both parties have obligations, and both answer to a Lord who stands above every human order.

Paul does not tell slaves that their situation is just. He tells them that no situation, however unjust, is beyond the reach of Christ, and that faithful work done for him will be rewarded by him, whatever the human master gave or withheld (v. 8).

The word to masters (v. 9) is just as searching: the master has a Master, and before the impartial God distinctions of rank count for nothing, a truth that undermined slavery itself (see the note on v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Roman law the father of the household held great legal power over his wife, children and slaves. Paul addresses children and slaves directly, as people who can answer to God for themselves, and he lays duties on fathers and masters towards the weak that Roman law did not require.

Now: A Christian home where authority is used in love, where children are both corrected and encouraged, and where Christ is spoken of and his word read, quietly shows the world around it a different way to live.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children who belong to Christ obey their parents as part of obeying him, because it is right. The two words “in the Lord” give both its motive and its limit.

Children. Picture the letter read aloud in a crowded room in Ephesus, the children at the edge of it, half listening, until the reader says: “Children.” The moral writers of the day spoke about children rather than to them. Paul speaks to the child, gives him a reason, and expects him to answer for himself, as a member of the church who can hear Christ and respond. The word covers children still living under their parents’ authority, not adults.

Obey. Literally to listen under (hypakouō): to listen and do what is said. It is a different word from the one used for wives, who were told to arrange themselves under (hypotassō). A wife is not a child, and a husband must not apply this verse to his wife. A child obeys because he does not yet know enough to run his own life, and the command changes as he grows. And it is both parents: in the Roman world the father held legal power, but Paul gives the mother equal standing as one to be obeyed. On leading and following in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

In the Lord. First, the reason: a Christian child obeys his parents as part of following Jesus, so that obeying his mother and father is a way of obeying Christ (Colossians 3:20 says this pleases the Lord). Second, the limit: he obeys as a Christian, so he can never be required to obey a parent against Christ. A ten-year-old told to tidy her room, be home by six or stop hitting her brother obeys, and in doing it she is obeying the Lord. If a parent told her to lie to a teacher or to steal, “in the Lord” says no. Everyday life is almost always the first kind; the second is rare, but real.

For this is right. Paul gives three reasons in three verses, each of a different kind. It is right (dikaion): it fits the way God made the world, so that even someone who had never seen the commandment would sense it (v. 1). It is commanded, written into the law at Sinai (v. 2). And it is blessed: it carries a promise (v. 3). Paul never says: “Obey because your parents can shout louder.”

The child who obeyed. Only one child in history had every right to disregard his parents: he had made them. At twelve he astonished the teachers in the temple, and Luke ends the story: “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (Luke 2:51). Then eighteen years of silence. The Son of God spent most of two decades doing what he was told in a small town by a carpenter and his wife. Long before the hard obedience of the cross (Hebrews 5:8) came the ordinary obedience of a boy. A child who obeys is not doing something beneath the dignity of heaven. He is doing what the Lord of heaven did first, for longer, with far less reason to.

Not my will, but yours. That obedience was never grudging: the boy in the carpenter’s house became the man in Gethsemane who prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). And God now counts that perfect obedience as belonging to everyone who trusts him: to every child who has sulked and slammed a door, and to every parent who has failed a child. The same Lord took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), and he has not changed.

What it does not mean. Not obedience in sin: when a parent commands what God forbids, “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Nor submission to abuse: a parent’s authority is borrowed, never absolute, and no parent has the right to injure a child. If you are a young person reading this in a house where you are being hurt, frightened, or asked to keep a secret about what an adult does to you, this verse is not telling you to submit to it. Tell someone, a teacher, a pastor, another adult you trust, and keep telling until somebody acts. That is not disobedience; it is obedience to the Lord in whose name the command was given. Any adult who quotes this verse to keep a child quiet has turned Christ’s words against the very person Christ stopped a letter to address. Nor must grown children who have left home obey their parents for life: marriage creates a new household (Genesis 2:24; 5:31). But honour never ends (v. 2).

What if my parents are not Christians and will not let me go to church? Obey them in everything you lawfully can, and honour them even when you disagree; God does not ask you to deceive them or sneak out. Being kept from church is hard, but it is not the same as being commanded to sin, and no parent can stop you praying, reading your Bible or trusting Christ. Ask respectfully whether you may go, or meet a Christian friend, or have the pastor call; a parent who sees a child growing kinder and more honest often softens. Pray for them by name, and remember that this lasts only while you live under their roof. If they ever command you to deny Christ or to do what God forbids, then you must obey God rather than men, respectfully and without contempt.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “in the Lord” in this verse; most include it, and modern translations keep it. Little turns on it, since the whole of Paul’s household teaching is set under Christ (5:21; 6:5–9).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honouring your parents is a lifelong duty, and it is the first command to which God attached a promise. Obedience belongs to childhood; honour lasts for life.

Honour. More than obedience. To honour (timaō) is to treat as weighty, to respect and value. For adults it means speaking of parents with respect, not retelling their failures as entertainment even when every word is true; courtesy as they grow slower and more repetitive; listening to their wisdom (Proverbs 23:22); and practical care when they grow old (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Jesus condemned religious leaders who used a loophole called Corban, declaring their money dedicated to God to avoid supporting their parents, so “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:9–13). That is what he thought the commandment required: money, provision, the unglamorous cost of caring for people who can no longer care for themselves.

This is the first commandment with a promise. Paul quotes the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) to children who were not Jews. The law no longer divides Jew from Gentile (2:14–15), and no one is saved by keeping it, but its moral commands still show every Christian what love for his neighbour looks like (Romans 13:8–10). Why “first”? The second commandment speaks of God’s steadfast love to thousands (Exodus 20:6), but that describes what God is like, attached to a warning. This is the first command that says: do this, and here is my promise.

That it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land. In Exodus the promise ran: “in the land that the LORD your God is giving you”, a promise about Canaan. Paul quietly drops the last clause. A promise about one territory becomes a promise about life anywhere, offered to Greek children in Asia Minor with no stake in Canaan, as all through the letter the good things promised to Israel are held out to every nation.

The Son at the cross. Watch Jesus keep this commandment. On the cross, bearing the sin of the world, he sees his mother standing there, and with what breath he has he arranges her care: “Woman, behold, your son!” “Behold, your mother!” And “from that hour the disciple took her to his own home” (John 19:26–27). He was redeeming the world, and he stopped to make sure his mother would have somewhere to live. And the Father he obeyed is the one “from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (3:15); to those whose earthly parents failed them, he is the parent who never leaves (Psalm 27:10).

In everyday life. Notice how you speak about your parents when they are not there: to your spouse, a friend, your children. Our real assessment lives in the stories we choose to repeat, and we are training the next generation in exactly how they will one day speak about us.

What it does not mean. Not a guarantee that every obedient child will live long, or that early death proves disobedience. Godly children die young. If you have buried a child who loved and honoured you, this verse is no verdict on that child, and no word against your grief. Like the Proverbs, it states how God normally works, not a mechanical rule: a person who learns to honour rightful authority and receive correction generally lives a longer, less damaged life, and a society where the generations honour one another holds together. The promise finds its final fulfilment in eternal life. Nor does honouring parents mean pretending their faults do not exist, or placing them above a spouse.

And if my parents did not deserve it? Paul attaches no clause about sufficiently good parents, and many readers had a father who was frightening, a mother who was cruel, or a parent who simply left. They may read this verse with dread, as if it demanded that they pretend. It does not. Honour is not approval, and it is not pretending: the Bible records the failures of its own heroes without ceasing to treat them with dignity. Honour is compatible with a boundary: the adult child who limits contact with a destructive parent, calmly and without contempt, for the sake of his own household, has not broken this commandment. It is compatible with grief, and with the long work of forgiving. What it rules out is contempt: the sneer, the public mockery, the settled determination to make them pay. At its core the duty is small enough to survive almost any history: to refuse to treat the people who gave you life as though they were nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers must not use their power to crush their children, but must bring them up with nurture, correction and teaching that lead them to the Lord.

Fathers. The natural counterpart to “children” would be “parents”; Paul says “fathers”, the one who held the power. In Roman law the father (paterfamilias) could decide whether a newborn lived or was abandoned to die, sell his children into slavery, or punish them severely even when grown. Into that world Paul says: limit your power by love. The principle applies to mothers too, but fathers bear particular responsibility for the spiritual leadership of the home. And the prohibition comes first: in a relationship that unequal, the damage a man can do without meaning to is the first problem to deal with.

Do not provoke your children to anger. The tense describes a settled pattern, not a bad afternoon. Every father loses his temper; Paul forbids the atmosphere. Colossians names the outcome: “lest they become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21). That is the injury: not an angry child, but a child who has quietly stopped trying, because nothing he does will be enough. And almost none of the provocations is a sin a man would confess. Criticism that only notices what is missing. Expectations that keep moving. Comparison with a sibling. Promises casually broken. Sarcasm, which a child cannot answer and does not forget. Inconsistency, punishing one day what was ignored the next. Rules without reasons. Hypocrisy, demanding what he does not do. Absence: the father in the house and behind a screen. And the commonest of all: warmth when things go well and coldness when they do not, so that a child grows up managing his father’s mood and learns, without being told, that love is earned by performance.

Why it matters so much. A child’s first working model of a father is the man at his kitchen table, and nobody easily thinks his way out of it. The father who is arbitrary teaches his children that God is arbitrary; the father who is never satisfied teaches them that God is never satisfied, and they may spend thirty years unlearning it.

But bring them up. To nourish, to feed up to full growth (ektrephō), the verb used of a husband nourishing his own body (5:29): warmth and tender care, as a gardener tends a plant.

In the discipline and instruction. Discipline (paideia) is training, including correction, the word used of God disciplining his children in love (Hebrews 12:5–11): setting boundaries, correcting wrong, giving consequences and praising what is right. The father who never corrects fails this verse as surely as the one who crushes. The two errors look opposite and share a root: both are easier than the patient, costly work of shaping a person who will one day not be under your authority at all. Instruction (nouthesia) is literally putting in mind, teaching by word. Children need not only rules but reasons.

Of the Lord. This is the goal: not only well-behaved children, but children who know the Lord. The child belongs to God, and the father is bringing him up for God, not into his own image or the career he wishes he had had. With young children it looks like presence, affection, calm and consistent boundaries, and God woven into ordinary talk (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). With older children, genuine interest in their world (the father who does not know his child’s best friend has not yet earned the right to be heard), and correction that is private and aimed at character. With teenagers, fewer orders and more honest conversation, and above all a father’s real walk with God in plain view: praying, confessing sin, coming back to Christ after failure. Children pick up more from what they see than from what they are told.

The Lord who trained twelve. “The discipline and instruction of the Lord” has a living pattern, for the Lord himself spent some three years bringing up a band of slow, quarrelsome men. He corrected plainly: “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:23). He explained again what they had failed to grasp (Mark 8:17–21). He never withdrew his warmth when they failed: “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). And when they argued about who was greatest, he set a child in the middle of them and taught them (Mark 9:36). If you want to see firm correction without lost patience, look at him.

The approval came first. At the Jordan, before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed anyone, a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). That is the Father who has adopted us in the Beloved, his dear Son (1:5–6). He is pleased with his children because of what his Son has done, not because of what they have done. He disciplines us for our good (Hebrews 12:10), never in a temper, and he does not tire of his children.

The child as the project. In much of the modern West childhood has become something to be managed. The sociologist Annette Lareau gave a name, concerted cultivation, to the way many middle-class parents organise their children’s lives: lessons, clubs, tutors and a diary as full as an executive’s. Much of that is love. But underneath there is often fear, and the child quietly becomes the parent’s proof, or his trophy, or his second chance: if he does well, I was a good parent; if he struggles, I have failed. A child carrying his parents’ righteousness on his back feels it long before he can name it. Paul’s phrase cuts the knot. The children are brought up “of the Lord”: they are his before they are yours, and their lives are not your verdict. You have a verdict already, given in the Beloved before you had raised anyone. Parents who know they are accepted are free to let their children be children, and even to let them fail.

In everyday life. Do not ask yourself whether you provoke your children. Ask one of them: “Is there something I do that makes you feel you can never quite get it right?” Then say nothing until they have finished, and do not explain. And to the father whose children are grown, who recognised himself in that list: it is not too late to say so. An apology to an adult child, specific, without excuses, without a single “but you also”, is one of the most powerful things in the world. God has been a Father to your children in ways you never managed, and he is able to repair what you broke.

What it does not mean. “Of the Lord” does not mean that fathers can make their children Christians: only God gives new life (2:1–5). Nor are children’s faith and failures entirely the parents’ fault: children are responsible persons too (Ezekiel 18:20).

What if there is no Christian father in the home? Then God has not left your children without a Father, nor you without help. Timothy was raised in the faith by his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois, while his father seems to have been an unbelieving Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and he became one of Paul’s most trusted men. A single mother, or a believing mother whose husband is indifferent, can do everything this verse describes: nurture, correct, teach and pray. God calls himself the father of the fatherless and the protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). And godly men in the congregation can befriend, include and show faithfulness to children who have no believing father at home. If you are carrying this alone, ask for that help. It is not a failure; it is the family of God doing its work.

Our children have turned away from the faith. Did we fail them? Perhaps in some ways, as every parent does, but their unbelief does not prove it. God himself, the only perfect Father, grieved over children he had reared who rebelled against him (Isaiah 1:2). New birth is God’s work, not the parents’ (John 1:13). If you see real failures, confess them to God, and where it would help, apologise to your adult child plainly. Then keep the door open: love them without nagging, keep a place for them at the table, take an interest in their lives, and do not turn every visit into a sermon. Let them see a parent who still walks with Christ and is kind. Above all, keep praying, for years if need be. Many prodigals have come home in their thirties and forties, and the father in the parable was watching the road (Luke 15:20).

Where Christians differ: physical discipline? Proverbs says that whoever spares the rod hates his son (Proverbs 13:24), and many Christians understand that to allow measured physical correction of young children, given calmly, never in anger, never to injure, and always with love and explanation. Others take the rod as a figure for discipline in general, and some believe physical discipline is unwise in every case. This commentary’s view: whatever a parent decides, this verse rules out anything that provokes, humiliates or harms a child. Discipline that crushes a child’s spirit (Colossians 3:21) is not the Lord’s discipline, and abuse must never hide behind Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian slaves were to serve their earthly masters sincerely, as service offered to Christ himself. Looking past the master to Christ changes the motive of their work and sets its limit.

Bondservants. Slaves (douloi). Perhaps a third of the people of a city like Ephesus were slaves, and so were many of the first Christians (1 Corinthians 7:21), though some were masters. Roman slavery was not based on race: people became slaves through war, debt, crime or birth. Some were teachers, doctors or managers; others laboured in mines and fields in terrible conditions. But a slave was legally property, and it was still bondage and an assault on human dignity.

Speaking to the property. The household codes of the day spoke to the owner about managing his property. Paul speaks to the property, as a person with a conscience, a Lord, and choices to make about his work.

Obey your earthly masters. Literally masters according to the flesh: their human masters. The phrase hints at a contrast, for they have another Master in heaven (v. 9). The earthly master’s authority is real but limited. On authority and submission at work and in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

With fear and trembling. Not cringing terror of the master. Paul uses the same phrase of the Christian life itself: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). It is the seriousness of someone who knows God is watching: the trembling has been redirected upward, over the master’s head.

With a sincere heart. “Sincere” (haplotēs) means single, undivided: no hidden motives, no one face for the master and another behind his back. For a slave, whose whole existence invited a double life, that was a startling thing to ask and a great gift: you may be owned, but you need not be divided.

As you would Christ: “do it for my sake”. A friend going abroad asks you to look after his elderly father: “Do it for me.” You really do help the father, but you do it for your friend (see on 5:22). The slave is not told that his master deserves this, and no one pretends the master is Jesus. He is told to look past the master to Christ, who stands behind every task and receives it as done for him. That changes the motive: not fear of the whip or hope of the master’s favour, but love for the Lord who sees everything. And it sets the limit: what is done for Christ’s sake can never include what Christ forbids, such as lying or stealing for the master, joining in his sins, or submitting to his abuse. In practice it meant doing the work well, honestly and without sulking, whether anyone checked or not. See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

A Lord who took the slave’s name. The word for slave here, doulos, is the word Paul uses for what the Son of God did: though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (doulos), and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). So a slave in Ephesus told to serve as to Christ was hearing from a Lord who had once taken the slave’s own place and name. That Lord has since been raised and seated in heaven, and everyone who belongs to him, this slave included, has been raised and seated there with him (2:6): the slave already shares his Lord’s honour.

Today. An employee is not owned, and the New Testament is emphatic about the wickedness of withholding wages. But the principle reaches everyone who works under conditions they did not choose and cannot change: the manager who will never be fair, the job taken because the mortgage exists. Paul’s answer is neither resignation nor resentment, but a change of employer at the level that matters: you still do the job your manager gives you, but you are working first for Christ, who sees what the manager misses and will repay what the manager never will (Colossians 3:23–24).

Where Christians differ: does the Bible endorse slavery? In the nineteenth century, slave-owners in the American South quoted texts like this to defend slavery. Paul does not endorse the institution; he regulates it while undermining it from within. He lists slave-traders, “enslavers”, among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), which alone condemns the Atlantic slave trade at its root; he urges slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21); he tells masters that they and their slaves have the same Master, who shows no favouritism (v. 9); and he asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). In the church, slave and free were equals at the Lord’s Table (Galatians 3:28). It is honest to admit the difficulty: Paul nowhere commands Christian masters to free their slaves, and for centuries some Christians found that silence convenient. Why not call for revolt? A slave revolt in the first century would have been drowned in blood, as the thousands crucified after Spartacus showed, and would have branded the young church as sedition. This commentary’s view: the gospel undermined slavery from within, and Christians such as William Wilberforce rightly led its abolition. Modern slavery and human trafficking are evils Christians must oppose.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world; many early believers were slaves or owned slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Work wholeheartedly for Christ, not merely for the eyes of whoever is watching. Humble work done honestly and with goodwill is doing the will of God.

Not by the way of eye-service. Eye-slavery (ophthalmodoulia), a word found in no surviving Greek writing before Paul: work that exists only while it is being looked at. It is not laziness, for eye-service can be very energetic, but a matter of where the effort is aimed: the report polished because the right person will read it, the visible task done first. It produces a person always adjusting to an audience, which is exhausting in a way hard work never is. Its companion is the people-pleaser (anthrōpareskos), who works to look good, not to be good.

But as bondservants of Christ. The deepest identity of a Christian slave was not that he belonged to a master but that he belonged to Christ, the title Paul uses of himself (Romans 1:1). Every Christian, slave or free, belongs to Christ.

Doing the will of God from the heart. Look at what this man does all day: cleaning, carrying, cooking, minding someone else’s children. Nothing religious about any of it, yet when he does it well, he is doing the will of God. That removes a division many of us carry unexamined: sacred activities, and then everything else. We are created for good works (2:10), and here is what one looks like on a Tuesday: a floor properly swept by a man nobody is watching. Luther taught that the farmer in his field and the woman at her household tasks please God as truly as the priest at the altar. The nurse on the night shift, the mother whose day’s work will be undone by bedtime, the man who drives a van: none is doing something less spiritual than the one leading the service on Sunday.

Rendering service with a good will. Not grudgingly, but wanting the person you serve to do well: a great thing to ask of a slave about the man who owns him, or of an employee about a manager who took credit for her work. Such goodwill is not manufactured by trying to like him; it becomes possible when you are really working for Christ, so that the manager is no longer the one who has to repay you.

I delight to do your will. Only one person has ever done the will of God from the heart without a divided moment. Hebrews hears Christ speaking Psalm 40 as he comes into the world: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). His food was to do the will of him who sent him (John 4:34), at the carpenter’s bench as much as at the cross. And “by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). The slave sweeping an unwatched floor from the heart walks in the footsteps of the Servant whose obedience saved him.

In everyday life. Think of the part of your work no one senior will ever inspect, and do today’s dullest task as if Christ had asked you to do it, because he has.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must accept unjust treatment without protest, stay in an exploitative job, or never speak up for fair conditions. Paul told slaves to take freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21); James condemns employers who withhold wages (James 5:4); and Paul himself used his Roman rights (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Working heartily for the Lord and standing up for yourself are not in competition. What is forbidden is the divided heart: turning up for the hours while holding back honest effort.

Does this mean I should not care what my boss thinks of me? No. It is right to want your employer to be pleased with your work, and good to be glad when it is noticed; Joseph and Daniel both won the trust of those over them (Genesis 39:4; Daniel 6:3). The fault Paul names is letting human approval become your master: working well only when it will be seen, bending your conscience to the mood of the office, or being flattened for a week by one cool remark. The cure is not to stop caring but to change whose opinion weighs most: when the work is done for Christ, a manager’s praise becomes a pleasant extra instead of oxygen, and criticism becomes useful information instead of a verdict on your worth. You can receive both calmly, because you already know whose “well done” matters most (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord will repay every good thing done for him, whoever did it. No faithful work is lost, even when no one on earth noticed it.

Knowing. Not hoping, but resting on something known, as certain on the worst Thursday of your working life as on the best. Feelings are not asked to carry this.

Whatever good anyone does. No threshold, no category excluded: the meal cooked for a family who did not think to say thank you, the shift quietly covered, the expense claim filled in honestly, patience held with the same difficult relative for the ninth year running. Jesus set the bar at exactly this height: whoever gives a cup of cold water to a disciple “will by no means lose his reward” (Matthew 10:42). And Hebrews makes it a matter of God’s character: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work” (Hebrews 6:10).

This he will receive back from the Lord. To collect what was deposited (komizō), the word Paul uses of the judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10). A slave’s work did not bear his name: whatever he built or mended was credited to the man who owned him. Paul tells him that a complete and accurate record exists, kept by the only one who was actually watching, and that it will be read back to him in person. It is this world’s record, the one everyone can see, that has the names wrong.

Whether he is a bondservant or is free. The slave’s faithful work will be rewarded as fully as the free man’s.

The Servant who seemed to labour in vain. This promise has already been kept once, for Christ. In Isaiah the Lord’s Servant says that he has laboured in vain and spent his strength for nothing, yet his right is with the LORD and his recompense with his God (Isaiah 49:4). From outside, his life looked like that: a short ministry, his friends scattered, his body in another man’s tomb. Then God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9). The Lord who will hand back your hidden work had his own handed back to him on the third day.

Read back to you with joy. The woman who has cared for a parent with dementia for six years; the believer who served one small church for thirty years and whose name is in no history: none of it was thrown away. He who has numbered the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) keeps a fuller record of your love than you do, and on that day he will read it back to you with joy.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works: salvation is by grace through faith (2:8–9). What is promised is not wages earned but reward given: the Father’s pleasure in what his own Spirit produced in you (2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts. Salvation is not what is handed back on that day; it is why you are standing there at all. Nor are the rewards necessarily material, or in this life: most will not be settled here, but nothing is pending for ever. The wait is real; the loss is not.

Is it not selfish to serve God for a reward? Not when the reward is the kind that belongs to the deed. A man who marries a woman for her money is mercenary; a man who marries her for love and is rewarded with her company is not, because the reward is the very thing he loved. What Christ promises is of that second kind: his “well done”, his joy, and more of himself (Matthew 25:21). Nor does the reward turn grace into wages.
